2026-06-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A cut vinyl decal goes onto a clean, dry surface under firm squeegee pressure. Avery Dennison's instructions call for squeegeeing before and after the application tape is peeled away, with extra attention to the edges.
glance: Transfer tape, vinyl film, adhesive and substrate
Firm, short and overlapping, from the top center downward and outward
Peeled back from a corner at a 180° angle
Squeegee again with very firm pressure, including all edges
Avery Dennison's application bulletin for its films

sections.heading: The layers and the surface
body: The infographic shows a decal as a stack. From the top down it labels transfer tape, vinyl film, adhesive and the substrate, which is the surface the decal goes on. It gives painted aluminum, acrylic and glass as examples of suitable substrates.

Avery Dennison's application bulletin for its films says every application surface must be considered contaminated and must be cleaned, and that the surface must be completely dry. On a painted surface, the drying or curing period of the paint system must be followed. The bulletin warns that failing to do so can result in poor decal performance and difficult removal. It also directs the applicator to the film's product data bulletin for recommended substrates and for minimum and maximum application temperatures.

sections.heading: Hinge, peel and squeegee
body: The infographic lays out the work as a strip of steps: clean, hinge, peel, squeegee, remove and check edges. The bulletin's own step-by-step procedure uses a top hinge. Once the decal is in position, a masking tape hinge is applied along its top edge. The decal is then flipped up over the hinge and the liner is removed.

The bulletin says to squeegee from the top center downward and outward, with firm, short, overlapping strokes. The infographic's squeegee panel gives a similar instruction: firm, overlapping strokes from the center outward. Avery Dennison says not to use application fluid, the so-called wet method. Water or fluid that is not squeezed out can remain between the surface and the decal and reduce its ultimate adhesion.

sections.heading: Removing the tape and checking edges
body: Application pressure helps seat the adhesive. Avery Dennison recommends squeegeeing the decal before the premask is removed and again afterward. The premask, which the bulletin also calls application tape, comes off by peeling back a corner and pulling it back at a 180° angle. The infographic labels this tape transfer tape. The second squeegee pass is aimed particularly at edges that could lift as the tape peels away. The bulletin calls for very firm squeegee pressure over the entire decal, including all edges.

Any air bubbles are punctured with a straight pin and squeegeed from the edge of the bubble toward the puncture. The infographic shows an air-release path as well, with a caption that says air escapes through tiny channels in the adhesive when pressure is applied. Its last step is to check edges. It contrasts a good seal with edge lift and states that edge lift can lead to moisture, dirt and premature failure.

2026-06-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: In an aquarium, bacteria turn the ammonia that fish produce into nitrite and then into nitrate. The process needs oxygen, and making nitrate does not mean the nitrogen has left the aquarium.
glance: Other bacteria oxidize nitrite to nitrate
Oxygen, and a biological filter where the bacteria can colonize
Six to eight weeks to build up enough bacteria
Water changes or separate denitrification systems

sections.heading: Where the ammonia comes from
body: Ammonia is the primary waste product of fish metabolism. A University of Florida IFAS Extension publication on ammonia says most of it leaves a fish by diffusion through the gills. The decay of uneaten feed and other organic matter adds more, but in most aquaculture or hobbyist systems the digestion of the feed the fish eat is the primary source. The infographic puts it differently: fish waste and uneaten food break down and release ammonia into the water.

Ammonia is colorless and, even at levels toxic to fish, odorless, so the only way to know it is present is to test the water. In water it exists in two forms, un-ionized ammonia and ionized ammonium. The un-ionized form is approximately 100 times more toxic to fish. In healthy ponds and tanks, the publication says, ammonia levels should always be zero.

sections.heading: Two steps, two groups of bacteria
body: Nitrification happens in two biological steps. Ammonia-oxidizing bacteria, including Nitrosospira and Nitrosomonas, convert ammonia to nitrite. Nitrite-oxidizing bacteria, including Nitrospira and Nitrobacter, convert nitrite to nitrate, which is much less toxic. The infographic labels both groups as beneficial bacteria.

Both groups need oxygen. If oxygen levels are not sufficient, the bacteria can stop functioning or die, and ammonia and nitrite levels increase. In tanks and aquariums, the publication says, a biological filter must be provided as a place where the bacteria can colonize. A new biofilter requires six to eight weeks to build up enough bacteria to reduce ammonia and nitrite effectively.

sections.heading: Where the nitrate goes
body: Making nitrate does not mean nitrogen has left the aquarium. The publication says that in natural systems and ponds, plants take up nitrate as a fertilizer, so levels typically remain low. In closed systems with little or no water exchange, nitrate can accumulate, and water changes or separate denitrification systems are needed to remove it.

The infographic shows both routes in a planted freshwater tank. It states that plants use nitrate and ammonium for growth, that roots absorb nutrients such as ammonium and nitrate, and that regular water changes remove excess nitrate and other dissolved wastes. It also states that beneficial bacteria thrive around roots and in the substrate, and that root surfaces release natural compounds that feed them. These root-zone details appear on the infographic, not in the extension publication.

sections.heading: Keeping the cycle steady
body: The infographic closes with care guidance: test water regularly, avoid overfeeding, and add plants gradually so the aquarium can adjust and stay balanced. The extension publication supports the first two. It says testing is the only way to know ammonia is present and that overfeeding is a major cause of high ammonia concentrations. The advice about adding plants appears only on the infographic.

2026-06-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Direct thermal receipt paper carries a heat-sensitive coating of dye and developer that forms marks when heated. The print can fade in sunlight or under prolonged fluorescent light, and plasticizers in some tapes and sleeves can fade it as well.
glance: Heat activates a dye and developer coating
Between 60 °C and 100 °C, depending on the grade (Jujo Thermal papers)
Direct sunlight and prolonged fluorescent light
Plasticizers in PVC film and some tapes, and sweat
In the dark, below 25 °C, relative humidity below 65%

sections.heading: How the mark is made
body: Direct thermal paper uses a heat-sensitive coating of dye and developer. The infographic shows the paper in cross-section: base paper fibers at the bottom, a thermal coating that holds a colorless dye and a developer, and a protective top coat. Its caption says no ink or toner is used, and that heat triggers a reaction in the coating that turns it dark. A second panel shows the heat elements of a thermal print head in contact with the paper as a dark mark forms.

Jujo Thermal, a maker of thermal paper, gives figures for its own papers. They begin to develop color at temperatures between 60 °C and 100 °C and reach what the company calls an applicable density at 70 to 120 °C, depending on the grade. The paper also shows similar signs of development at high temperature or in high humidity. Frictional heat from scratching, or pressure from hard metal objects or fingernails, causes an image to develop too.

sections.heading: What fades the print
body: The manufacturer says the printed image tends to fade in direct sunlight, and that it also shows a tendency to fade under conventional fluorescent light over prolonged periods. For that reason it advises filing printed paper soon after printing. All papers turn yellow with time, especially in direct sunlight for prolonged periods.

The storage material matters as well as the light. PVC film contains plasticizer, and prolonged contact with it reduces the paper's image-forming property and fades the printed image. Plasticizers in some tapes can fade the print as well, and so can sweat. Adhesives that contain volatile organic solvents, such as alcohols, esters and ketones, cause color formation in the paper.

The infographic groups the causes of fading as heat, sunlight and UV, abrasion, hand oils, plasticizers from some plastics, solvents and cleaners, and humidity or poor storage. It shows a receipt going from fresh to fading to aged and discolored, and describes fading as gradual and irreversible.

sections.heading: Keeping a receipt legible
body: For long-term storage, the manufacturer says its papers should be kept in the dark, at an average ambient temperature of less than 25 °C and a relative humidity of less than 65%. For files and cases it recommends polyolefins or polyester.

The infographic's storage panel gives similar general advice: keep receipts cool, dry and dark, and keep them apart from vinyl or plastic sleeves and chemicals. It suggests paper folders or envelopes, and scanning or photographing important receipts to keep a digital copy.

2026-06-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: An automatic fire sprinkler head is held closed by a heat-responsive element, normally a liquid-filled glass bulb. When a fire heats the head to its operating temperature, the element breaks or releases and water sprays out over the fire.
glance: A heat-responsive element pressing on a sealing mechanism
Liquid-filled glass bulb; other heads use a fusible metal link
The head reaches its predetermined operating temperature
Only those closest to the fire

sections.heading: Parts of the head
body: The infographic shows a cutaway of a typical head with its parts labeled: the frame, the threaded inlet that connects to the sprinkler pipe, the heat-sensitive element, a compression screw, a cap or plug, the seat and orifice, and the deflector plate.

In normal conditions, according to the British Automatic Fire Sprinkler Association, the heat-responsive element holds the waterway of the head closed by applying pressure to a sealing mechanism. The element is normally a liquid-filled glass bulb. Other heads use a fusible metal link in its place. The association's table of operating temperature ratings matches each rating to a color of bulb filling, from 57 °C (orange) to 182 °C (mauve). A bulb rated 68 °C (155 °F) has a red filling.

sections.heading: What happens in a fire
body: Sprinkler heads are spaced on or close to the ceiling, where heat collects as it rises during a fire. Each head operates only when it reaches its predetermined operating temperature. The element then breaks apart or releases, and water pressure in the sprinkler piping overcomes the sealing mechanism and sprays water on the fire. The infographic shows this as a sequence: standby with the orifice sealed, heat releasing the element so the plug drops away, then water flowing through the orifice.

The water is distributed by a deflector over the location of the fire. The infographic shows the stream striking the deflector plate and breaking into droplets that spread below the ceiling. Besides extinguishing or controlling the fire, the association says, the water helps to cool the hot gases produced and pre-wets areas immediately next to the fire to inhibit fire growth.

sections.heading: Only the heads near the fire open
body: Sprinklers operate independently of one another, so only those closest to the fire open. Sprinklers in areas where there is no fire remain closed and do not release water. The infographic makes the same point with a ceiling of several heads, one of them spraying over a fire. Its caption says heat must reach the element to activate it, and unexposed heads remain closed.

sections.heading: Corrosion, paint, damage and cover plates
body: The infographic lists visual clues that a head may have a problem: corrosion, paint blockage, bent or damaged parts, and a missing cover plate. Its captions say rust or corrosion can weaken components, paint can interfere with operation or hide damage, and physical damage can prevent proper operation.

The association notes that the air or water inside sprinkler piping may be corrosive, so the sprinkler frame must be made of materials that resist that corrosion, even after many years in the field. It also describes concealed sprinklers, which sit flush with the ceiling behind a small metal disc. The disc is soldered to a support bracket. Heated in a fire, this melts and lets the disc fall away, exposing the sprinkler head.

2026-06-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A quartz watch keeps time by a quartz crystal that oscillates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied. A frequency of 32,768 Hz became the standard, though the first quartz wristwatch used 8,192 Hz.
glance: A quartz crystal oscillating at a precise frequency under an applied voltage
±0.2 seconds per day, ±5 seconds per month

sections.heading: The crystal sets the pace
body: A quartz timepiece uses a property of a quartz crystal: it oscillates at a precise frequency when a voltage is applied to it. That frequency serves as the standard for keeping time, in place of the pendulum or balance wheel of conventional timepieces. The Seiko Museum Ginza says the change increased the precision of timepieces dramatically.

The first Seiko Quartz Astron contained a quartz oscillator with a vibration frequency of 8,192 Hz. A frequency of 32,768 Hz became the standard for later quartz timepieces, so not every early quartz watch used the same frequency. The infographic labels 32,768 Hz as a typical quartz oscillator and states that the crystal vibrates that many times per second.
The infographic adds that the performance of a quartz watch can be influenced by temperature, battery condition, magnetism, shock, moisture and aging.

sections.heading: From battery to hands
body: The infographic lays out the signal path in a battery-powered watch with hands. Battery power feeds an oscillator circuit, the quartz crystal vibrates, the timing pulses are divided, a stepper motor advances, and the gear train moves the hands. Its cutaway labels the coin cell battery, integrated circuit, quartz tuning-fork crystal can, stepper motor coil and gear train, along with the dial, hands, crown, case, gasket and caseback.

Several of these parts appear in the museum's account of Seiko's quartz watches. It lists a miniature, low-power, shock-resistant quartz oscillator of the tuning-fork type, a second hand that ticks once per second to save power, and an open-type stepping motor that allowed a space-saving arrangement of the coil, stator and rotor. The museum says the use of these technologies in Seiko's watches made them the global standard.

sections.heading: How quartz reached the wrist
body: The quartz clock was invented in America by Warren Marrison in 1927. Bulova launched a tuning fork watch in 1960 that vibrated at 360 Hz and was accurate to within two seconds per day. The museum says the pursuit of even higher precision led to quartz watches.

On December 25, 1969, Seiko launched the Seiko Quartz Astron 35SQ, which the museum describes as the world's first quartz wristwatch. Its accuracy was ±0.2 seconds per day and ±5 seconds per month, at a time when a few seconds to a few dozen seconds per day was considered normal for high-precision mechanical wristwatches.

2026-06-26-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The waggle dance is how a honey bee forager tells her nestmates where to find food. The angle of her straight run gives the direction relative to the sun, and the time she spends waggling gives the distance.
glance: A forager back at the colony with nectar or pollen
On the surface of the wax comb
More than 150 meters from the hive
The angle of the waggle run relative to vertical
The duration of the waggle run; longer for farther food

sections.heading: When a forager dances
body: NC State Extension describes the dance as something an experienced forager most often does when she returns to her colony with a load of food, either nectar or pollen. If the food is good enough, she will often dance on the surface of the wax comb. Returning foragers use the dance to recruit nestmates to the food.
The waggle dance is the form performed by bees foraging at food sources more than 150 meters from the hive. It passes on two things: direction and distance.

sections.heading: The shape of the dance
body: The dancer runs straight ahead for a short distance, returns in a semicircle to her starting point, runs the straight course again, and then makes a semicircle in the opposite direction. That completes a full figure-eight circuit. During the straight run her body, especially the abdomen, wags vigorously from side to side.
The infographic shows this on a patch of comb. One bee stands on a straight line labeled waggle run, curved arrows beside it are labeled return loop, and a row of other bees faces her at close range.

sections.heading: Reading direction and distance
body: Direction comes from the angle of the waggle run. The angle the bee takes relative to vertical on the comb represents the angle to the flowers relative to the direction of the sun outside. The infographic's sun angle panel draws the outdoor half of that relationship, with a hive, the sun and a line labeled food direction.

Distance comes from time. As the distance to the food increases, the waggle run lasts longer, and the extension publication calls the duration of the straight run the simplest and most reliable indicator of distance. The infographic's distance cue panel reads: shorter, less vigorous waggle run for closer food, and longer, more vigorous waggle run for farther food.

sections.heading: Scent finishes the search
body: According to NC State Extension, the most commonly accepted view is that recruits go to the area the dance describes and then home in on the flower patch using odor cues. Around its main scene the infographic adds a nectar source panel, a cutaway labeled hive context, and close-ups of wax cells, pollen grains, antennae and wing veins.

2026-06-27-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A freehub is the ratcheting mechanism on the rear hub of most modern derailleur bikes. Its pawls lock onto ratchet teeth when the rider pedals and let the wheel turn independently of the cassette while coasting.
glance: The ratcheting mechanism attached to the rear hub
The cassette cogs, on a splined cylinder
Bearings and a clutch system, usually ratcheting teeth and pawls
Pawls engage the ratchet teeth so the cassette drives the hub
The wheel turns independently of the cassette
Liquid lubricant, recommended by most manufacturers

sections.heading: What the freehub is
body: The freehub is the ratcheting mechanism attached to the rear hub of most modern derailleur bikes. It uses a splined cylinder to hold the cassette cogs. The cogs themselves have no moving parts. All the moving parts are in the freehub body, which contains bearings and a clutch system, usually ratcheting teeth and pawls.

The infographic's cutaway labels the hub shell, pawls, cassette splines, bearing, axle, seal and ratchet teeth. A second strip sets the internal parts out in order: cassette body, pawls, springs, ratchet ring, bearing, seal, axle end cap and hub shell.

sections.heading: Pedaling and coasting
body: In a typical pawl-and-ratchet freehub, pedaling makes the pawls engage the ratchet teeth, so the cassette can drive the hub. While coasting, the wheel turns independently of the cassette. The infographic draws the two states one above the other, as a pedaling load path and a coasting click path.

Park Tool's service guide notes that the freehub's pawls and bearings operate only while the bike is coasting, when there is very little load or stress on the freehub. When the bike is pedaled, the pawls lock onto the ratcheting teeth and the freehub bearings take very little stress.
The guide also describes a different clutch. In the DT-Hugi design, the clutch is made up of two star ratchet gears whose angled teeth face one another, each pushed by a spring.

sections.heading: Lubrication and wear
body: Because the internal parts see so little load, Park Tool says bicycle grease is typically not required inside a freehub, and most manufacturers recommend a liquid lubricant. Some of its brand-specific procedures do call for grease on particular parts. For Campagnolo freehubs, for example, the springs and pawls are greased before they are installed.

With enough use a freehub wears out. The pawls may begin to slip and the bearings may become rough. If cleaning and lubricating does not resolve slipping, sticking or noise, the guide says to replace the freehub unit with a new one. The infographic's wear check shows a worn pawl tip, dry and dirty grease, and a contaminated seal as examples. It also lists materials: hardened steel for the pawls and ratchet, aluminum for the hub shell, bearing steel, a rubber seal and grease for lubrication.

2026-06-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A refrigerator door seal is a flexible gasket that includes a magnetic strip. The gasket closes the gap around the door by compressing against the cabinet, which limits warm-air leaks.
glance: An extruded magnetic strip shaped for the gasket
Closing the gap around the door
Water bars, tea bar machines, upright freezers and medical freezers
Insulation, freshness and preventing cold leakage

sections.heading: The gasket and its magnetic strip
body: A magnetic refrigerator seal can use an extruded magnetic strip shaped for the door gasket. The strip is one part of the seal. The gasket is the material that closes the gap around the door.

HIGA Magnetic Materials, which makes such strips, offers them with cross-sections and pole layouts made to order. The company says it developed extrusion screw materials for magnetic granules, for efficient extrusion, and that its own magnetizing fixtures and magnetic circuit design improve magnetic performance. It lists the strips as used in magnetic door seals for refrigerators, water bars, tea bar machines, upright freezers and medical freezers.

The infographic's cutaway labels the parts at the door edge: the cabinet frame, a flexible vinyl gasket with a hollow compression chamber, the embedded magnetic strip, the contact surface, the door liner and the metal door shell.

sections.heading: How the seal closes and leaks
body: HIGA describes the job of a magnetic door seal as providing insulation and freshness and preventing cold leakage. The infographic shows two actions behind that. The flexible gasket compresses against the cabinet to form a seal, and in a step labeled magnetic pull-in, the magnet pulls the gasket tightly to the steel face. Arrows mark cold air staying in and warm air staying out.

A gasket that is dirty, twisted or poorly seated can let warm air leak in and can develop a condensation risk. The infographic shows gaps letting warm air in and cold air out, with moisture forming on warm surfaces near the leaks. It contrasts a good continuous contact line, with even pressure all the way around, with a wavy or damaged corner where gaps cause leaks.

A care panel on the infographic shows inspecting the entire seal with a light, cleaning with mild soap and water, using nonmetal tools to avoid cutting or tearing the gasket, and drying and reseating it so it is fully seated all the way around.

2026-06-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A handheld rotary can opener clamps onto the rim of a can, feeds itself around and cuts the lid. A 1931 patent describes the arrangement: a cutter wheel and a feed wheel on two pivoted levers, geared together.
glance: Two pivoted levers with handles, a cutter, a feed wheel and gears
Through the can end, inward of the seam, not through the side wall
The can rim, held between the two wheels

sections.heading: The parts
body: The patent, granted to Charles Arthur Bunker on December 29, 1931, describes a pair of levers pivoted on a plate, each with a handle. A cutter is mounted so it can rotate on one lever, and a feed member on the other, in alignment with it. The cutter is beveled. Gears on the cutter and feeder mesh when the handles are moved toward each other.

The infographic shows a handheld rotary opener with similar parts. Its cutaway labels two handles, a hinge, a turning knob, a drive gear, a serrated feed wheel, a hardened cutting wheel, axle pins and rivets, with the can lid and rim in cross-section beneath.

sections.heading: Clamping onto the rim
body: In the patent's account, the handles are first spread to separate the cutter and the feed wheel. The bead of the can, also called the chime, goes between them, with the cutter on the inner side of the can wall. Closing the handles makes the feed wheel engage the lower edge of the bead and forces the cutter into and through the top of the can.
The infographic's sequence starts the same way: open jaws approach the rim, then the handles squeeze to seat the wheels.

sections.heading: Cutting around the lid
body: Once the can end is pierced, turning the crank handle rotates the cutter, and the cutter and feed wheel travel around the bead formed by the can's seam. The rim guides the opener while the cutting wheel moves along the inside edge, and the wheels keep the opener positioned so the cutter can make a continuous cut around the top. The feed wheel bears on the outer wall of the can and the lower edge of the bead.

One stated purpose of the patent concerns where the cut is made: through the end of the can, inward of the seam between the end and the side wall, instead of through the side wall as had been done before. Its cutter also turns the cut edge downward against the body of the can. The infographic shows the last step differently, with the cutting wheel shearing the lid while the lid edge lifts.

The infographic's comparison panel shows good contact, with the feed wheel and cutting wheel tracking smoothly on the rim, beside two problem signs: wheels that are not aligned, so one side digs in, and a dull or damaged wheel that skips on the rim and leaves marks.

2026-06-30-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A zipper has three main components: two rows of meshing elements, a slider and fabric tape. The slider, which has a Y-shaped tunnel inside, brings the elements together so they mesh when moved one way and separates them when moved the other.
glance: The component with teeth that mesh with each other
Moved by hand; has a Y-shaped tunnel inside
Within one hundredth of a millimeter, according to YKK

sections.heading: Three components
body: YKK, a zipper maker, divides a zipper broadly into three components. The elements are the component with teeth that mesh with each other, and they run in two matching rows. The slider is the component moved by the user's hand. The tape is the fabric component.

The infographic's exploded view labels more pieces: the slider body and pull tab, a top stop and a bottom stop, the zipper tape, coil or molded teeth, stitching and the fabric edge. Its materials panel shows a brass or plated metal slider, nylon coil and polyester tape.

sections.heading: Inside the slider
body: YKK calls the slider the key to opening and closing. It has a Y-shaped tunnel inside. Pulling the slider up causes the elements to mesh, closing the zipper. Pulling it down widens the gap between the meshing elements and opens the zipper. The uneven sections on the left and right elements mesh together like gears.

The infographic shows closing as a sequence: separated teeth enter the slider, the channel guides them together, the teeth interlock, and a closed chain exits at the bottom. Its cutaway labels the slider's pull tab, crown, throat, Y-shaped channel and bottom exit.

sections.heading: Why shape and size matter
body: Smooth opening and closing depends heavily on the shape and dimensions of each component, YKK says. If there is a measurement error in the elements, the zipper will not open properly, and a zipper that should be closed will come open from the center. Making the elements requires high precision, to within one hundredth of a millimeter.
The infographic's comparison panel shows good alignment beside two faults, skipped teeth and a loose slider. Its close-up panel points to a worn slider channel, a bent tooth and frayed fabric.

2026-07-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A mechanical pencil holds its lead in a clutch, called a collet in the patent described here. Each press of the button carries the lead forward by a small step, and on release the collet grips the lead again.
glance: A collet with split jaws made of spring material
A tapered receiver tube, acting through rolling balls
Advances the lead by a small step
US4521126A, a patent titled Mechanical pencil
Exact construction varies by pencil design

sections.heading: The clutch that grips the lead
body: The mechanism described here comes from a patent for a mechanical pencil. The gripping part is a collet with split jaws made of spring material. Left alone, the jaws tend to spring open, away from the lead. A receiver tube with a tapered guide face works with the collet, and rolling balls sit between the two. In the normal position, a wedging action among the collet, the receiver tube and the balls clamps the jaws on the lead and holds it firmly for writing. Exact construction varies by pencil design.

sections.heading: What one press does
body: In the patent, when the button is operated, the receiver tube and the collet advance together toward the tip, with the lead still gripped, until the receiver tube stops against the tip piece. Pushing farther lets the receiver tube spring back at once on its own, while a pusher drives the collet on toward the tip piece, where the collet is fully opened. When the button is released, springs return the pusher and the collet, and the retracted collet firmly grasps the lead again. The lead has advanced by a small step instead of sliding freely.

The patent describes a fault in earlier pencils of this kind. An opened chuck was likely to close first and then retract, so the small length of lead just pushed out could be pulled back into the pencil and lost. Returning the receiver tube separately is the patent's answer. Its drawings show a button that slides along a slot in the casing, and the text says a general type of push button on the rear end of the casing may be used instead.

sections.heading: What the infographic shows
body: The infographic shows a push-button pencil in cutaway. Its labels name the push button, a removable eraser cap, an internal knock rod that moves the clutch, a return spring, a lead reservoir that stores leads, clutch jaws that open to advance and close to grip, a lead sleeve that guides the lead, and a fixed nose cone. A second strip lays the parts out in order. Close-up panels show the texture of the graphite lead, the jaws gripping the lead, the spring, the plastic barrel threads and wear marks on the nose cone tip.

Its four-step strip reads: press button, clutch opens, lead slides forward, release and clutch grips. The captions say the knock rod moves rearward and pulls the clutch jaws open, and that the spring then pushes the rod forward so the clutch closes. The patent describes the directions differently. Its pusher moves forward toward the tip to open the collet, and springs carry the parts back when the button is released.

A materials panel lists graphite lead, a stainless or brass clutch, a molded plastic barrel, a rubber eraser and spring steel. A last panel, marked as examples to observe only, compares a good grip, where the lead is held firmly, with a worn clutch that lets the lead slip under light pressure and a broken fragment in the clutch that blocks movement.

2026-07-02-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Some dinoflagellates, a kind of microscopic plankton, give off blue light when breaking waves or other water motion disturb them. Not every bloom glows. It depends on which organisms are present.
glance: Certain dinoflagellates, a kind of microscopic plankton
Disturbance by waves or other movement in the water
A dark beach at least two hours after sunset
Scientists think it startles or confuses predators

sections.heading: What makes the water flash
body: Red tides occur when microscopic plankton called dinoflagellates multiply rapidly and form dense blooms that can discolor the water. At night, when the cells of some species are disturbed by waves or other movement in the water, they emit a neon-blue glow that can be seen with the naked eye. The Scripps Institution of Oceanography says scientists think the light is a predator-avoidance mechanism that startles or confuses organisms that might eat the plankton.

The infographic lays this out as a sequence: calm water, a paddle or stir disturbance, a breaking wave, a bright flash and a quick fade. Its cell panel shows mechanical shear from wave action leading to light emission from a single magnified dinoflagellate.

sections.heading: Which blooms glow
body: Not every bloom or red tide glows. Scripps says bioluminescence occurs only when certain species of dinoflagellates or other organisms are present. In Southern California the species most often responsible is Lingulaulax polyedra, formerly named Lingulodinium polyedra. Each cell measures 35 to 60 micrometers across and contains pigments that give it a reddish-brown color. On sunny days the cells swim toward the surface, where they concentrate and intensify the coloration of the water.
Another bloom-forming dinoflagellate common in Southern California waters, Prorocentrum micans, is non-toxic and non-luminescent, but it can still contribute to red tide events.

sections.heading: When it is easiest to see
body: During a red tide dominated by light-producing species, Scripps says the displays are best seen from a dark beach at least two hours after sunset. Visibility is not guaranteed, because these events are unpredictable and vary in intensity and location. The infographic gives its own conditions for a brighter glow: dark water with less ambient light, stronger turbulence in the wave wash, and a bloom with many cells near the surface.

sections.heading: Glowing water and safety
body: A red tide is not the same thing as a harmful algal bloom. Many red tides are relatively harmless, while others can cause harm through toxin production or other mechanisms, depending on the species present. Scripps says most red tides along the California coast are not considered dangerous to humans, but they can sometimes cause skin or eye irritation or respiratory discomfort. Off the coast of Washington, glowing blooms have been linked to Alexandrium catenella, which produces the neurotoxin saxitoxin, and those blooms are often harmful.

The infographic carries a similar caution, that not all glowing water is safe, and adds that some harmful algae blooms do not glow. It shows the glow being watched from the beach edge at a respectful distance, without entering the surf.

2026-07-03-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Retroreflective sign sheeting contains tiny glass beads or cube-corner reflectors that send much of a headlight's light back toward its source. The sign does not glow on its own. It looks bright to a driver whose eyes are close to the headlights.
glance: Sheeting applied to the face of a traffic sign
Microscopic glass beads or cube-corner reflectors
Sends much of the incoming light back toward its source
The driver's eyes are close to the headlights
None; it does not glow by itself

sections.heading: Scattered light and returned light
body: Most objects reflect light. The most common kind is diffuse reflection, in which light scatters after striking a rough surface such as trees, clothing or carpet. Only a very small amount of that scattered light reflects back toward the light source.

Retroreflection is the ability of a surface to reflect light back toward the light source. Retroreflectivity is the measurable property of a material's ability to redirect light back to its source. The infographic draws the same contrast. Its comparison panel shows ordinary matte vinyl scattering light in many directions and retroreflective vinyl returning light in a narrow cone toward the source. It also states that the material does not glow by itself and that it returns much of the incoming light toward the source.

sections.heading: Inside the sheeting
body: To make a sign retroreflective, sign manufacturers apply sheeting to its face. The sheeting contains either microscopic glass beads or cube-corner reflectors. The Minnesota Department of Transportation's Signs 101 manual says that if every bead and cube corner could be made perfectly shaped, all the reflected light would return directly to the headlights. Real sheeting does not have perfectly shaped lenses.

The infographic shows the sheeting as a stack of layers: a clear protective face film, a colored translucent film, a retroreflective layer of microprismatic cube corners or glass beads, a pressure-sensitive adhesive and an aluminum substrate. Its light-path strip follows the light in order. Headlights approach the sign, light enters the sign face, light refracts and reflects inside the retroreflective layer, light exits and returns toward the source, and the driver sees a bright sign. Close-up panels show cube corners, embedded glass beads and a sign surface sparkling under headlights at night. A sign-shop panel shows a reflective vinyl roll, an aluminum sign blank, a felt squeegee, a release liner and test swatches under a hand light.

sections.heading: Why the driver's position matters
body: Drivers see more reflected light the closer their eyes are to the headlights. The manual calls the angle formed between the headlights, the sign and the driver's eyes the observation angle. The smaller that angle, the higher the retroreflectivity. Retroreflective materials are also more efficient when the light source is approximately perpendicular to the sign face, which is why the manual says it is important to orient signs to face approaching traffic.

sections.heading: Why signs use it
body: The manual says the MN MUTCD requires traffic signs to be either retroreflective or illuminated, so that they show the same shape and color both day and night. Because making a sign retroreflective is more cost effective than illuminating it, retroreflective sheeting is used on all signs. The manual also notes that some signs may look almost new during the day but be completely ineffective at night, a problem that is usually a function of the type and age of the retroreflective material.

2026-07-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Comb jellies are oval, gelatinous sea animals that swim by beating eight rows of tiny comblike plates. As the plates move, they break up light into a shimmering rainbow, an optical effect that is distinct from light an animal produces itself.
glance: Oval and gelatinous, more than 95 percent water
Beats eight rows of tiny comblike plates
Comb rows break up light as the animal swims

sections.heading: Eight rows of beating combs
body: The Monterey Bay Aquarium describes the comb jelly as an oval-shaped animal with eight rows of tiny comblike plates that it beats to move through the water. Its soft body is thin skin stretched over a body composed of more than 95 percent water, with no bones or shells to weigh it down. The infographic labels the plates as fused cilia plates, or ctenes, and shows the comb rows on a transparent body.

sections.heading: Where the rainbow comes from
body: As a comb jelly swims, its comb rows break up light and produce a shimmering rainbow effect. The beating cilia split incoming light into colors. This is an optical effect, and it is distinct from biologically produced light.

The infographic lays out the light path step by step. White aquarium light hits the moving plates, and diffraction and interference separate the colors. As the cilia beat, the shimmering bands travel. The animal itself remains mostly transparent. A comparison panel sets this shimmer, caused by external white light scattering from moving plates, against true bioluminescent blue-green light, which it describes as produced by an internal chemical reaction in other marine animals. The infographic calls the rainbow effect mostly structural light scattering from moving cilia.

sections.heading: A predator made mostly of water
body: Comb jellies are voracious predators. The aquarium lists their diet as plankton, small crustaceans and other jellies, and says some species can expand their stomachs to capture other jellies half their own size. The infographic shows trailing tentacles and labels their colloblasts as prey-catching cells.

The aquarium describes a jelly as a gelatinous creature with few specialized organs. Many jelly species have a gravity-sensitive structure called a statocyst that helps with orientation in the water, and the infographic marks a statocyst on its cutaway. Comb jellies belong to the phylum Ctenophora. Relatives listed by the aquarium include the sea gooseberry, the lobed comb jelly and the bloody-belly comb jelly. Their ecosystem is the open ocean, and range and size vary with species.

2026-07-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A heat dome occurs when a persistent region of high pressure traps heat over an area. It can linger for days to weeks while the sun makes conditions on the ground progressively hotter.
glance: A persistent region of high pressure that traps heat over an area
The behavior of the jet stream, a band of fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere
Pavement, buildings and other hard surfaces absorb and retain more heat
There is no physical dome or glass lid

sections.heading: High pressure that stays in place
body: A heat dome occurs when a persistent region of high pressure traps heat over a particular area, according to NOAA. It can linger for days to weeks. Descending air can warm, and the resulting weather pattern can keep very hot conditions in place. Air descending down mountains can also contribute to a heat dome, as it warms even more.

A heat dome is not a literal glass dome. The infographic states that heat domes are not physical domes or glass lids. It describes them as areas of high pressure with sinking air and weak mixing that allow heat to build and persist.

sections.heading: The jet stream's part
body: Heat domes are typically linked to the behavior of the jet stream, a band of fast-moving winds high in the atmosphere that moves in meandering, wavelike patterns. When the jet stream meanders north, it moves slower and can sink, which lowers humidity. This allows the sun to create progressively hotter conditions on the ground.

The infographic shows the jet stream arching around the area of high pressure, with cooler air and storms on either side. NOAA's article reports that during a heat wave in June 2023, storms formed along the edge of a ridge of high pressure. A meteorologist quoted there said such storms are sometimes called ridge-riding storms.

sections.heading: How the heat builds near the ground
body: The infographic lays out the build-up as a chain. A strong area of high pressure parks over a region. Air sinks, compresses and warms. The jet stream arches around the high and steers storms away. Sinking air keeps clouds from forming, so strong sunlight heats the ground, buildings and water every day. With less vertical mixing, warm air lingers near the surface. Dry soil and hot surfaces then release stored heat, which makes the next day hotter.

Its timeline runs from sunny, hot weather at the start, through drying soil and pavement that stores heat, to dangerous heat stress and warm nights. NOAA's article adds a point about cities. Because of the heat island effect, temperatures there are generally higher than in surrounding rural areas, since dense concentrations of pavement, buildings and other hard surfaces tend to absorb and retain more heat.

sections.heading: Warm nights and the June 2023 heat wave
body: NOAA's article was written during a heat wave that affected more than 50 million people across the southern U.S. and Mexico in June 2023, brought on by what it calls a heat dome. Overnight temperatures were expected to be abnormally warm and to give little to no relief. The Weather Prediction Center said there might be more danger than in a typical heat event, because of the longevity of near-record or record high nighttime lows and elevated heat index readings.

According to the weather service, heat causes more deaths across the United States each year than any other weather event, including tornadoes, floods and hurricanes. The infographic's side panel lists reasons the heat feels worse: high humidity slows the evaporation of sweat, pavement and buildings store heat, nights stay warm so bodies and homes cannot recover, and the longer the pattern stalls, the more heat accumulates.

2026-07-05-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Frost flowers are delicate ice crystals, not plants. They form when water vapor turns straight to solid ice on young sea ice in cold, calm conditions, and they become salty by interacting with brine.
glance: Ice crystals, not plants and not alive
On the surface of young sea ice
Water vapor becomes solid ice without first turning into liquid water
They roughen the surface and dramatically affect its electromagnetic signal

sections.heading: Crystals grown from vapor
body: Frost flowers are ice crystals, not plants or living things. The National Snow and Ice Data Center defines them as crystals of ice that form when water vapor becomes a solid, bypassing the liquid phase, and deposits itself on the sea ice surface. The center's glossary adds that frost flowers roughen that surface and dramatically affect its electromagnetic signal.
They form over young sea ice in cold, calm conditions. They are produced by vapor gradients over the ice, and their salt comes from interaction with brine.

sections.heading: The process the infographic lays out
body: The infographic shows a slab of young sea ice, labeled new, thin and dark, resting on relatively warmer ocean water under very cold air. Brine channels, described as salty water in microscopic veins, run through the ice, and a very salty film sits on its surface. Water vapor rises from that surface, and frost flowers stand on top of it.

Its process panel runs in order: new sea ice forms, brine concentrates near the surface, very cold calm air makes a strong vapor gradient, ice crystals nucleate on the surface, and branching frost flowers trap or wick salty brine. A second strip follows the crystals from simple plates and needles to branching arms, feathered dendrites, clusters and flower-like mats.

sections.heading: What holds frost flowers back
body: The infographic lists conditions that suppress frost flowers. Older, thicker ice gives a weaker vapor gradient. Wind mixing disturbs the surface and breaks the crystals. Warmer air weakens the gradient, so there is less growth. It also describes the crystals as fragile surface structures, delicate and easily broken, to be observed without disturbing them.

2026-07-07-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A snapping shrimp, also called a pistol shrimp, shuts its claw so fast that the water jet it drives forms a cavitation bubble. The collapse of that bubble makes the loud snap and can give off a brief flash of light.
glance: Snapping shrimp, also called pistol shrimp
Collapse of a cavitation bubble, not the claws striking each other
At least 5,000 K inside the bubble

sections.heading: Where the sound comes from
body: Snapping shrimp produce a loud crackling noise that is intense enough to disturb underwater communication. The sound does not come from the claws striking each other. When the shrimp's snapper claw snaps shut, it forms a high-velocity water jet. A large cavitation bubble is generated under the tensile forces of that jet, and the sound originates from the bubble's violent collapse. The collapse also produces the characteristic pressure pulse. A report in the journal Nature says the shrimp create these bubbles to stun their prey.

sections.heading: The flash inside the bubble
body: Lohse and colleagues reported in Nature that a short, intense flash of light is emitted as the bubble collapses. The recordings of sound and light they show are from the snapping shrimp Alpheus heterochaelis. According to the authors, the flash indicates that extreme pressures, and temperatures of at least 5,000 K, must exist inside the bubble at the point of collapse.

The researchers named the effect shrimpoluminescence and wrote that it was, to their knowledge, the first observation of this mode of light production in any animal. They chose the name for its apparent similarity to sonoluminescence, the light emitted from a bubble that is periodically driven by ultrasound.

sections.heading: The snap, step by step
body: The infographic follows the snap in order. Water fills the socket while the claw is open. The movable finger of the claw, labeled the dactyl, swings in and strikes the socket, and a narrow jet of water shoots out at high speed. The jet creates a zone of very low pressure, where water vapor forms a bubble. The bubble collapses violently, the collapse produces a shock wave that travels outward, and a tiny blue-white flash follows.

The infographic also states that the collapse heats water to thousands of degrees locally, and that the shock wave and bubble activity can stun or damage small prey. It notes that the flashes are very brief, tiny and hard to see. Its observation notes describe watching the animals in their habitat, at a distance, without touching or feeding them.

2026-07-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Thermal runaway is a chemical reaction inside a lithium cell that drives an uncontrolled rise in temperature and pressure. The cell can release flammable electrolyte and gases, and its heat can push the cells next to it into the same state.
glance: A chemical reaction in the cell causing uncontrolled temperature and pressure rise
Heat from one cell raises adjacent cells to a threshold temperature
Flammable electrolyte and gases, including hydrocarbons and hydrogen
Vent gases can be trapped in confined spaces

sections.heading: What thermal runaway is
body: A Federal Aviation Administration report, a summary of its studies of lithium cells in aircraft cargo compartments, describes thermal runaway as a chemical reaction within a cell that results in a dramatic, uncontrolled rise in temperature and pressure. Lithium cells use a hydrocarbon-based electrolyte that is flammable, unlike the water-based electrolytes of traditional batteries. As the temperature rises, pressure inside the cell increases and activates its pressure-relief ports, releasing the electrolyte. The electrolyte may ignite on contact with hot cell cases or from burning packaging.

The report says many circumstances may start it. They include internal cell failure, heating such as exposure to an external fire, physical abuse, rapid discharge, over-charging, or a manufacturing contaminant that shows itself later.

sections.heading: How it spreads from cell to cell
body: A cell in thermal runaway produces enough heat to heat up the cells next to it. Once those cells reach a threshold temperature, they go into thermal runaway too. The report calls this thermal runaway propagation.

The infographic lays the process out in numbered steps. Abnormal heat begins in a small area. Heat causes the separator to shrink, which increases the risk of an internal short. Exothermic reactions release heat and gas and raise internal pressure. Gas then vents out, and hot gases and surfaces transfer heat to nearby cells. A detail panel adds that heat can conduct along metal tabs and busbars, contributing to heat transfer from cell to cell.

sections.heading: Flammable gas as a second hazard
body: A lithium-ion cell in thermal runaway can release flammable vent gases, so the event is more than a temperature rise inside a single cell. According to the report, the flammable gases include hydrocarbons and high concentrations of hydrogen, and cells at a higher state of charge give off greater volumes of flammable gas. Cells shipped in confined spaces, such as fire-resistant containers or plastic-wrapped pallets, may trap vent gases and lead to explosive conditions.

The lithium polymer cells in the report's tests are encased in a plastic film. When heated, they build pressure and inflate the film until it bursts, releasing the electrolyte all at once. The infographic's cutaway is of a pouch cell, with a vent path labeled as designed to open upward and away.

sections.heading: Design ideas the infographic lists
body: The infographic shows the pouch cell as layers: copper and aluminum current collectors, a graphite anode coating, a microporous separator film, a cathode coating and electrolyte-soaked porous layers. Ceramic insulating barriers stand between neighboring cells. A closing panel, marked as non-actionable concepts, lists cell spacing, thermal barriers, pressure vent paths that direct gas away, BMS monitoring of voltage, current and temperature trends, and early isolation of cells or modules.

The infographic states that insulation and spacing slow the spread. The report describes one packaging test with a different result. When the cardboard separators in a shipping box of cells were replaced with fiberglass ones, the fiberglass did not perform as well as the original cardboard, and thermal runaway propagated at a faster rate than in the baseline test.

2026-07-09-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Electrochromic glass changes how much visible light it lets through when it is switched electrically. It has memory, so it needs power only to make a change.
glance: Low dc power, needed only to make a change
Windows in buildings, automobiles and aircraft
Tungsten oxide and lithium nickel oxide films with a polymer ion conductor

sections.heading: What the glass does
body: Electrochromic glazing changes its visible light transmission when it is switched electrically. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory describes these smart windows as able to dynamically control the light transmitted by windows in buildings, automobiles and aircraft.

The laboratory says electrochromic glazings typically change visible light transmission from 10% to 70%, with moderately fast switching times and low dc power consumption. They have memory, so they need power only to make a change in transmission. Researchers evaluate the absorbing and transmitting states together with switching speed and stability, and exact performance differs among materials.

sections.heading: Layers and moving ions
body: The laboratory's own example window is constructed of thin films of tungsten oxide and lithium nickel oxide, laminated with a polymer ion conductor. Its visible transmittance ranges from 0.68 to 0.10, and its solar transmittance from 0.47 to 0.07.

The infographic shows the device as a stack: outer glass, a transparent conductor, a tungsten-oxide electrochromic film, an ion-storage counter layer, an ion-conducting polymer, an edge seal, a spacer and a laminated backing. Its materials strip names the conductor as an ITO or FTO coating and the counter layer as nickel oxide. A numbered strip shows a clear state, ions moving under low-voltage switching, color centers forming as ions and electrons enter the tungsten-oxide film, and a gradual return toward clear when the polarity changes.

sections.heading: How fast it switches
body: The infographic's observation panel lists slow tinting, low power to switch, privacy and glare control, and large panes that can tint unevenly near the edges. The laboratory describes switching times as moderately fast. Its simulated office sequence starts with the glass at full transmittance, a visible transmittance of 74%. The glazing begins to color at its maximum rate at 15:00:12 on the sequence's clock and reaches its maximum coloration, a visible transmittance of 3.2%, at 15:17:42.

sections.heading: Why buildings use it
body: The laboratory reports that energy simulations of office buildings indicate smart windows with lighting controls in arid climates can provide 30 to 40% energy savings over conventional windows. The savings are realized in cooling, lighting and peak utility electric loads. The infographic's comparison panel sets a clear daylight state beside a tinted, cool blue-gray state and marks reduced heat and glare in the tinted one. It pictures a building facade, a skylight panel and a lab bench sample.

2026-07-10-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A termite mound has no fans, yet air moves through it. In the mounds one study measured, the daily swing in temperature drove air around inside the mound and helped flush carbon dioxide from the nest.
glance: Odontotermes obesus, a termite common in southern Asia
Highly porous, with no visible holes to the outside
A measured mechanism, not a design used by every termite species

sections.heading: The mounds that were measured
body: The study behind this infographic, published in PNAS by King, Ocko and Mahadevan, measured mounds of Odontotermes obesus, a termite that is common in southern Asia. The structure these termites build includes an underground nest that holds the brood and a symbiotic fungus.

Inside the mound the basic layout is a large central chimney with many conduits near the surface, in parts of the mound the authors call flutes. The walls are highly porous, yet healthy mounds have no visible holes to the outside, and any breach in the surface is quickly repaired.

sections.heading: Air that reverses between day and night
body: The slender, exposed flutes heat quickly during the day and cool during the night. By day, air is pushed up the flutes and down the chimney in a closed loop. At night the situation is reversed. In the mounds studied, these day-to-night temperature changes drove the reversing airflows, and the flows helped flush carbon dioxide from the nest.

During the day, when the flows were relatively small, carbon dioxide gradually built up to nearly 6% in the nest. The walls treat gases in two ways. Their high porosity gives little resistance to gases diffusing across them, but their small pores make the mound very resistant to air being driven through by pressure.

sections.heading: What the infographic shows
body: The infographic shows a cutaway mound with labels for central chimneys, porous outer buttresses, lateral galleries, nest chambers, fungal comb and nursery chambers. Its day panel says the sun heats the outer walls, warm air inside rises and exits through upper chimneys, and cooler outside air is drawn in low through pores and lateral tunnels. Its night panel says cooler, denser air sinks down the chimneys while warm nest air moves out through lower pores and passages.

A gas exchange panel shows oxygen moving in and carbon dioxide moving out through the wall, with the line that air moves passively through pores, with no fans. The study describes some of this differently: a nest below ground, walls with no visible holes that strongly resist air being pushed through them while letting gases diffuse, and air circulating in a closed loop inside the mound.

sections.heading: How far the finding reaches
body: The result is a measured mechanism in the mounds that were studied, not a single design used by every termite species. The authors point out that their data come entirely from one species. They also describe the mechanism as very generic and likely dominant in similarly massive mounds.

2026-07-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A solar sail is a large, lightweight, mirror-like surface that takes momentum from sunlight. Each photon that hits it gives a small push, and the pushes add up to a tiny, continuous thrust that needs no onboard propellant.
glance: A large, lightweight, mirror-like surface on a spacecraft
Momentum transferred by photons of sunlight
Changing the angle of the sail

sections.heading: Momentum from light
body: Light is made up of massless particles called photons. Photons carry momentum even though they have no rest mass. When they hit a reflective sail, they transfer momentum to the spacecraft. A NASA teaching activity puts it this way: every photon that hits the sails can create a small thrust forward. The small pushes add up over a large illuminated area.

The activity describes solar sails as large, lightweight, mirror-like surfaces that capture the momentum from sunlight to push the spacecraft forward. Its diagram shows light particles bouncing off the slightly curved surface of a sail and moving the sail forward. It adds that a solar sail's velocity depends on its size and its mass.

sections.heading: How a sail differs from a rocket
body: Thrust is the force that accelerates a rocket through the air and through space. In a traditional chemical rocket, hot gas exhaust is pushed out from the back, and these rockets take tons of liquid and solid fuel. Ion thrusters eject ions instead, using an inert gas like xenon as propellant. A solar sail gets a tiny continuous thrust from sunlight without onboard propellant. As in an ion thruster, each particle creates only a small thrust.
The activity names Starshot, a proposed mission, as one that would use solar sails to travel to Alpha Centauri, the star system nearest our solar system.

sections.heading: What the infographic shows
body: The infographic shows a sailcraft with a reflective sail, a central bus, lightweight booms and attitude vanes, with incoming and reflected sunlight drawn as arrows. Its numbered sequence runs from incoming sunlight, to photons reflecting off the sail surface, to a tiny momentum transfer, to continuous gentle acceleration, to steering by changing the sail angle. It states that reversing direction changes a photon's momentum and gives the sail a tiny push, and that tilting the sail redirects the thrust.

A comparison panel sets an absorbing dark surface, where photons stop and the momentum change is smaller, beside a reflective bright sail, where photons reverse direction and the momentum change is greater. Another panel shows stronger sunlight near Earth orbit and weaker light pressure farther from the Sun, and states that light pressure decreases with the square of the distance from the Sun. The NASA activity asks how distance from the Sun affects a sail's acceleration and does not state the answer.

Close-up panels show crinkled aluminized film, a boom hinge, edge seam reinforcement, a micrometeorite pinhole patch and a mirror coupon. A closing note reads that thrust is tiny but continuous and that solar sails need no onboard propellant.

2026-07-13-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Red sprites are brief flashes that thunderstorms generate high above the clouds. They are the most frequently observed kind of transient luminous event, and NASA asks photographers to help record them.
glance: A type of transient luminous event (TLE)
High above the clouds, in the mesosphere above strong thunderstorms
60 to 250 miles from the storm, in NASA's Spritacular project

sections.heading: Flashes high above the storm
body: Transient luminous events, or TLEs, are colorful, bright, faster-than-lightning flashes that thunderstorms generate above the clouds, as NASA describes them. They can take a variety of shapes, each with its own name. The most frequently observed are called sprites, after the fairies of folklore.

A sprite's brief flash occurs high above the clouds. It does not follow the near-ground path of an ordinary cloud-to-ground lightning strike. One photograph on NASA's page is captioned as a cluster of red jellyfish sprites hovering above a large storm cloud.

sections.heading: From lightning stroke to red glow
body: Sprites occur in the mesosphere above strong thunderstorms. They are associated with major electric-field changes driven by lightning, and they glow mainly through emissions from excited nitrogen.

The infographic lays this out as a chain reaction: a strong cloud-to-ground stroke leaves a charge imbalance, the electric field changes rapidly above the storm, thin upper-atmosphere nitrogen is excited, and a brief red-orange glow spreads into tendrils. Its altitude scale puts the thundercloud in the troposphere and the sprite far above it. Its color panel shows a red upper glow and says the lower filaments can shift to blue-violet.

sections.heading: Sprites, blue jets and elves
body: Sprites are distinct from blue jets and elves. The infographic compares the three. It shows a red sprite above the thunderstorm anvil, red-orange with blue-violet lower filaments, in columns and branches. It shows a blue jet rising from the cloud top as a narrow blue cone or column, shorter than a sprite. It shows elves as a flat, disk-like ring, red or pink, that expands outward very high above the storm and is very brief.
NASA's page also pictures a gigantic jet, another kind of TLE, captured on February 10, 2007 above Tucson, Arizona.

sections.heading: How sprites get photographed
body: Spritacular is a NASA project that invites photographers from all over the world to contribute observations of TLEs, to help researchers better understand them. It asks observers to locate a nearby storm and place themselves 60 to 250 miles away, where they can see clear, dark sky above the clouds, and to aim a camera above the storm. The equipment it lists is a DSLR or mirrorless camera and a tripod. The page carries a safety note about using caution when observing a thunderstorm and keeping a quick exit to safety.
The infographic's observation panel makes similar points: image from a distant horizon, use a sensitive camera, and expect sprites to be extremely brief, so that cameras often catch them more easily.

2026-07-14-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Magnetotactic bacteria live in water and sediment and carry a chain of tiny crystals of magnetic iron minerals. The chain works like an internal compass, aligning the swimming cell with Earth's magnetic field.
glance: Magnetosomes, each a membrane-wrapped crystal of a magnetic iron mineral

sections.heading: A compass built from crystals
body: A magnetosome is a tiny crystal of a magnetic iron mineral with a membrane around it. Early studies indicated that the membrane contains phospholipids and proteins. A mature magnetosome holds a single crystal of magnetite or greigite, with a shape and size that depend on the species, mostly between 30 and 100 nm. A review published by the American Society for Microbiology notes that the number, size, shape, arrangement and chemical composition of the crystals vary considerably between groups of these bacteria.

In the two Magnetospirillum species the review concentrates on, the crystals are cuboctahedral magnetite, about 45 nm in size when mature. The infographic draws magnetite and greigite crystals as octahedrons and labels that a common shape. Its scale panel gives its own approximate sizes for a sediment grain, a bacterium and a crystal, and its crystal range is narrower than the review's.

sections.heading: Why the crystals form a chain
body: The force on a single magnetosome in Earth's magnetic field is too weak to align a cell effectively. Stacked into a line, the magnetosomes add their magnetic moments together and form a much stronger magnetic dipole, strong enough to align the whole cell with the rather weak geomagnetic field, much as a compass needle is aligned. The review says the findings suggest this alignment is a passive, physical effect.

The infographic states the same idea in steps: iron is stored as orderly magnetosome crystals, the crystal chain gains a combined magnetic moment, and the swimming cell tends to align with the local geomagnetic field. It also states that proteins help position and hold the magnetosomes in a straight chain.

sections.heading: Alignment is not the whole trip
body: All magnetotactic bacteria characterized so far use flagella to swim. Lining up with the field reduces three-dimensional trial-and-error swimming to movement along a line. Together with responses to chemicals such as oxygen, this guides the bacteria efficiently to their preferred oxygen concentration in layered environments. The infographic separates the jobs: magnetic alignment for orientation, flagella for movement, and chemical or oxygen sensing for choosing a favorable zone. Its sediment jar shows oxygen-rich water above, a low-oxygen transition zone, and oxygen-poor sediment below.

The infographic cautions that the bacteria do not simply always swim north, and that behavior varies with species, habitat and hemisphere. The review gives some background. In early studies, cells exposed to a magnetic field seemed to prefer one direction along it over the other. In Earth's northern hemisphere predominantly north-seeking cells were isolated, and in the southern hemisphere predominantly south-seeking cells. The review says it is not currently understood exactly how this swimming polarity is controlled.

2026-07-14-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Basalt columns form when a cooling lava flow contracts and fractures. The cracks advance inward from the cooling surfaces and divide the rock into columns, most of them hexagonal.
glance: Cooling causes contraction, which in turn causes fracturing
Mostly hexagonal, with anywhere from three to seven sides
From the top and bottom of a flow inward toward the center
Perpendicular to the main cooling surfaces

sections.heading: Cooling, contraction and cracks
body: Columnar jointing consists of sets of regularly spaced, parallel fractures, called joints, that intersect in a roughly prismatic pattern. The National Park Service gives the cause as a short chain: cooling causes contraction, which in turn causes fracturing. The fractures propagate from the top and bottom of a flow inward toward the center, dividing the cooling body into columns.

The jointing forms after a lava flow or other igneous body has solidified, but while it is still at high to medium temperature. It is thought to form during rapid cooling. The developing fracture system is thought to let fluids circulate, which can further hasten the cooling.

The infographic follows the same order in stages: hot lava is emplaced, the boundaries lose heat first, contraction builds tensile stress, cracks meet in a polygon network, and crack tips advance inward as cooling continues, leaving columns.

sections.heading: Why the columns are polygons
body: Most columns are hexagonal, but they may have anywhere from three to seven sides. The predominantly hexagonal pattern arises because contractional stress is most efficiently relieved by three fractures that intersect at angles of 120 degrees, which creates six-sided polygons. The infographic's caption notes that the columns are not perfect hexagons.

Columns are oriented perpendicular to the main cooling surfaces of lava flows and other igneous bodies. The infographic illustrates this with a top surface, a bottom surface and a sloped surface: where heat leaves, cracks form at right angles to that surface. It also states that basalt columns are intact rock bounded by joints, not single crystals or growth structures.

sections.heading: Irregular joints and other rocks
body: Some lava flows have irregular columnar jointing known as entablature, typically found in the interior portion or near the top of a flow. Its irregular fracturing is likely due to a different cooling rate in the flow's interior. The infographic makes a comparison of its own, between ordered columnar joints and irregular blocky joints, which it says are formed by cooling, weathering or unloading.

Columnar jointing is most commonly found in basaltic lava flows. It also occurs in lava flows of other compositions, pyroclastic flow deposits, some lava domes, volcanic necks and some shallow intrusions.

sections.heading: Columns in the field
body: Devils Postpile National Monument has columns up to 60 ft (18 m) long, in a basalt flow up to 400 ft (122 m) thick that pooled after it erupted approximately 100,000 years ago. A high percentage of its columns, 55%, are hexagonal. The infographic's own field view is labeled Giant's Causeway, Northern Ireland.

2026-07-14-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Dragline silk from orb-weaving spiders changes its mechanical behavior with humidity. Wet dragline fibers can supercontract: they shorten when free to move and develop a contraction stress when held in place.
glance: Dragline (major ampullate) silk of orb-weaving spiders
Supercontraction: wet fibers shorten, or develop contraction stress if restrained
Predicted range of 13% to 42%, rising with humidity

sections.heading: What supercontraction means
body: Humidity changes the mechanical behavior of dragline silk. Wet dragline fibers can supercontract. A fiber that is free to move shortens. A fiber that is restrained develops a contraction stress instead. The magnitude varies among species and silk types. The infographic states that strong supercontraction is characteristic of many orb-weaver dragline silks, and that other web silks generally show little to modest supercontraction.

sections.heading: What the measurements found
body: A study in the Biophysical Journal by Vehoff and colleagues quantified the effect of relative humidity on dragline silk from two spiders, Nephila clavipes and Nephila senegalensis. The analysis is based on 126 single fiber measurements. The shape of the stress-strain curve varied significantly with humidity. Below 35% relative humidity the curve consisted of two linear regimes. Above 75% it took an elastomeric shape.

The strain at which a fiber broke rose with humidity in a linear way, predicting an extensibility range from 13% to 42% for spider dragline silk. The elastic modulus fell as humidity rose. The breaking force varied little with humidity. The authors conclude that the influence of humidity is sufficient to explain the great range of mechanical properties reported for the silk in the literature.

sections.heading: Water inside the fiber
body: X-ray fiber diffraction points to a composite structure in the silk: beta-sheet crystallites embedded in an amorphous matrix. The study's authors write that water can easily permeate the fiber and is incorporated in the amorphous matrix. They assume that this hydration interferes with hydrogen bonds between the amorphous chains, which leads to a loss of rigidity. Weighing measurements that the authors call very preliminary indicate that almost two-thirds of the fiber mass at full hydration is due to water uptake.

The infographic lays out a sequence in stages built on the same structure. In a dry fiber under tension, the chains are stretched, and hydrogen bonds and other interactions hold the structure in place. Water molecules diffuse into the amorphous regions. Some interactions are disrupted and the chains move more freely. The chains then relax into new positions and the fiber shortens, often reversibly. The infographic labels this a simplified model, not a universal one.

2026-07-14-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Many mantis shrimp have compound eyes that detect polarized light, which is not the same as color vision. Experiments showed that the mantis shrimp studied could detect circular as well as linear polarization, a finding that should not be extended to all species without further evidence.
glance: Linear polarization and, in the animals studied, circular polarization
Professor Justin Marshall, University of Queensland, published in Current Biology
12 in mantis shrimp and three in humans, according to Marshall
Not to be generalized to all species without further evidence

sections.heading: Polarization is not color
body: The infographic separates brightness, color, linear polarization and circular polarization as different kinds of visual information. It draws ordinary light with mixed orientations, linearly polarized light with one aligned orientation, and circularly polarized light as a rotating electric field. People are sensitive to light intensity and color, the University of Queensland's Professor Justin Marshall says, but need cameras and filters to see different types of light. The infographic states that humans do not normally perceive polarization directly.

sections.heading: What the Queensland research found
body: In a news release dated March 20, 2008, the University of Queensland reported that research led by Marshall had found that mantis shrimp can see circularly polarized light. The release calls this a completely new type of vision, never seen before in the animal world, and says the research was published in the journal Current Biology. Marshall is quoted as saying that the animals can see both linear and circular polarized light, and that they have 12 color channels where humans have only three.

He describes the mantis shrimp as having a very small brain but one of the world's most complex visual systems. The experiments concerned the mantis shrimp that were studied, and the finding should not be generalized to all species without further evidence.

sections.heading: What the ability may be for
body: After tests of the animals' physiology and behavior over a number of years, Marshall concluded that circular polarization vision is used for sex. He says only the males have the ability, and that it is probably a secret communication channel between males and females that keeps predators from knowing what is going on.

The infographic gives a broader list. It states that mantis shrimp can use polarization cues to detect prey and predators, to navigate and orient, and to recognize reflective signals. It also states that many stomatopods detect linear polarization, that some groups detect circular polarization, and that abilities vary by group and species.

sections.heading: The eye, and polarization in daily life
body: The infographic shows a stalked compound eye with a midband region across it, labeled as specialized for polarization sensitivity, between a dorsal and a ventral region. An exploded view of one unit of the eye, an ommatidium, shows a corneal lens, a crystalline cone, retinular cells and microvillar photoreceptor elements.

The release notes where people meet polarization. Polarized sunglasses show the effect of linear polarization by cutting out glare for driving and boating. Circular polarization is used in 3D glasses for movies, filters for cameras and medical imaging systems.

2026-07-14-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Water rises through a tree as a passive process. Evaporation from the leaves creates tension in the water-carrying xylem, and because water molecules hold together, that pull draws a connected column of water up from the roots.
glance: Transpiration, the evaporation of water at the leaf surface
Xylem, from the roots to the leaves
Equivalent to –2 MPa, varying greatly with humidity
Passive, with no ATP required for water movement
Up to 90 percent of what the roots take up

sections.heading: The pull starts in the leaves
