body: Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant through evaporation at the leaf surface, and it is the main driver of water movement in the xylem. Inside the leaf, water on the surface of the cells evaporates into the air spaces. That lowers the water potential and increases the tension on the water in the xylem. At the leaf surface the negative pressure is equivalent to –2 MPa, a value that varies greatly. It can be negligible at high relative humidity and substantial at low relative humidity.

Water moves from where water potential is higher to where it is lower. For water to travel from the soil to the air, the potential must fall at each stage, from soil to root, stem, leaf and atmosphere. The OpenStax biology textbook describes transpiration as a passive process in which metabolic energy in the form of ATP is not required for water movement. The infographic makes a statement of its own, that roots do not mechanically pump water to the canopy.

sections.heading: Why the column holds together
body: The cohesion of water molecules to each other helps keep the water column connected, so the pull from the leaves can draw water upward from the roots. The textbook says that at night, when stomata shut and transpiration stops, the water is held in the stem and leaf by the adhesion of water to the cell walls of the xylem vessels and tracheids and by cohesion. This is called the cohesion-tension theory of sap ascent.

The infographic lays out the route in order: soil water enters fine roots, water moves into the xylem, cohesion holds the narrow columns, evaporation from moist leaf-cell walls creates tension, and water vapor diffuses through open stomata. Its xylem panel labels vessels as wide conduits and tracheids as narrow conduits.

sections.heading: Stomata, day and night
body: Each stoma on the leaf surface is surrounded by two guard cells, which open and close in response to cues such as light, leaf water status and carbon dioxide. Transpiration is regulated primarily through this opening and closing. When stomata are open, water vapor is lost, and up to 90 percent of the water taken up by roots may be lost through transpiration.

The textbook says stomata shut at night and transpiration stops. The infographic shows stomata mostly closed at night, with lower evaporation and weaker tension, and mostly open in the daytime, with higher evaporation and stronger tension.

sections.heading: When the column breaks
body: The formation of gas bubbles in the xylem, called cavitation, interrupts the continuous stream of water from the base to the top of the plant. The break in flow is termed an embolism. The textbook says that the taller the tree, the greater the tension needed to pull water and the more cavitation events, and that in larger trees embolisms can plug xylem vessels and make them nonfunctional. The infographic shows an air embolism blocking one conduit while flow continues around the blockage through neighboring pathways. It adds that transport varies with species and conditions.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: An octopus changes its appearance with pigment-filled cells in its skin called chromatophores, which expand and contract to change the colors that show. Changing them rapidly helps the animal adapt its pattern to its surroundings.
glance: Chromatophores, elastic cells that contain colored pigments
Stretched open or squeezed shut from moment to moment
Pigment cells, muscle fibers and nerves working together
Reddish-pink with a delicate, veinlike pattern
Capabilities and cell arrangements vary among species

sections.heading: Pigment cells that open and close
body: Chromatophores are pigment-filled cells that can expand and contract, which alters the colors visible at the skin. The Monterey Bay Aquarium describes the giant Pacific octopus, Enteroctopus dofleini, as having millions of these elastic cells under its skin. The octopus adjusts its skin color by stretching the chromatophores open or squeezing them shut from moment to moment. The infographic shows the two states side by side: expanded, with the color visible, and contracted, with the color hidden. It states that the chromatophores expand by radial muscle action.

sections.heading: Eyes, nerves and muscles
body: The aquarium calls the giant Pacific octopus's camouflage one of the most sophisticated systems in the animal world, a complex orchestration of pigment cells, muscle fibers and nerves. It says the octopus uses its eyes to match the patterns and colors of its background nearly perfectly. Experiments have shown that the octopus is color-blind, which the aquarium says makes these feats that much more mystifying.

The infographic draws the control path as a chain: the eye observes the surroundings, the brain selects a coordinated body pattern, motor signals travel through skin nerves, and radial muscles expand the chromatophore sacs. It labels the result coordinated patterning, not exact color copying.

sections.heading: More than pigment
body: The infographic shows further layers that the aquarium's page does not describe. It labels iridophores, which reflect structural color in a way that depends on angle, and leucophores, which scatter ambient light, above deeper muscular tissue. A separate panel shows papillae changing the skin's relief: smooth skin, a contraction that lifts bumps, and relaxed skin that flattens again. The infographic notes that capabilities and cell arrangements vary among species, and that camouflage combines neural control, pigment, reflection, posture and texture.

sections.heading: What the disguise is for
body: Lacking a shell, the giant Pacific octopus protects itself with camouflage. The aquarium says it avoids encounters with predators by staying in its den, hiding in the kelp forest and using its camouflage. It also catches prey by surprise, using camouflage, jet propulsion and the grip of its eight arms. Changing color may be a way to communicate with a mate or scare off predators. The species is usually reddish-pink with a delicate, veinlike pattern, fading to white on the underside of the arms.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Black smokers are seafloor chimneys built from minerals that solidify when hot vent fluid meets near-freezing seawater. Deposits of iron sulfide make them black.
glance: A chimney of mineral deposits at a hydrothermal vent
It is formed from deposits of iron sulfide
Where seawater meets magma, at spreading ridges and convergent plate boundaries
Chimneys formed from deposits of barium, calcium and silicon

sections.heading: Seawater that meets magma
body: Hydrothermal vents form where seawater meets magma. NOAA describes them as hot springs produced by underwater volcanoes at spreading ridges and convergent plate boundaries. Seawater percolates down through fissures in the ocean crust, the cold water is heated by hot magma, and it reemerges to form the vents. Seawater in hydrothermal vents may reach temperatures of over 700° Fahrenheit. It does not boil because of the extreme pressure at the depths where vents form.

The infographic's cutaway shows the same loop. Cold seawater infiltrates fractures in the ocean crust, is heated near a shallow magma heat source, and rises as buoyant vent fluid. The cutaway labels a water-rock reaction in which metals and reduced sulfur enter the fluid.

sections.heading: How the chimney builds up
body: A venting black smoker emits jets of particle-laden fluid. The particles are predominantly very fine-grained sulfide minerals, formed when the hot hydrothermal fluid mixes with near-freezing seawater. The minerals solidify as they cool and build up chimney-like structures. Black smokers are chimneys formed from deposits of iron sulfide, which is black. The infographic labels the dark plume as particle-rich, not smoke or lava.

The infographic lays out growth in stages. Hot fluid rises from a bare fissure. A porous, anhydrite-rich mound forms where the fluid meets sulfate-bearing seawater. A narrow conduit focuses the flow, and sulfide minerals deposit on its walls, thickening the chimney and building it upward and outward. Continued deposition makes branching spires. An older chimney may fracture, and new vents form on its flanks. A separate panel shows mineral layers becoming brittle, a blocked conduit redirecting the flow, a wall collapsing, and growth resuming from side vents.

sections.heading: Inside the wall, and white smokers
body: The infographic shows a cross-section of a mature chimney wall, marked as simplified and variable among vents. From the hot central conduit outward it shows a porous inner zone rich in copper and iron sulfides, a zinc-rich sulfide zone, an iron-sulfide zone and an outermost crust of sulfate-rich minerals against cold seawater. It names chalcopyrite, sphalerite, pyrite and marcasite as key sulfide minerals.

White smokers are chimneys formed from deposits of barium, calcium and silicon, which are white. The infographic shows them as generally cooler, with a paler plume, and notes that compositions vary by site. Vent chemistry, mineral assemblages, temperatures and organisms all vary among sites.

sections.heading: Life around the vents
body: Scientists first discovered hydrothermal vents in 1977, while exploring an oceanic spreading ridge near the Galapagos Islands. They found the vents surrounded by large numbers of organisms that had never been seen before. These communities depend on chemical processes that result from the interaction of seawater and hot magma. The infographic shows microbial mats, tubeworms, mussels, and vent shrimp and crabs, with a chain running from vent chemicals to microbes to animals, and labels the system as needing no sunlight.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Frost flowers are delicate ice crystals that water vapor deposits directly onto young sea ice. Rejected brine can coat them with salts, and weather affects how they grow.
glance: Water vapor becomes a solid and deposits on the sea ice surface
Rejected brine can coat the crystals with salts
A rougher surface and a dramatically changed electromagnetic signal

sections.heading: Vapor that becomes ice
body: The National Snow and Ice Data Center defines frost flowers as crystals of ice that form when water vapor becomes a solid, bypassing the liquid phase, and deposits itself on the sea ice surface. Their texture roughens that surface, and the center says they dramatically affect its electromagnetic signal.

The infographic carries the heading that frost flowers are ice crystals, not plants. Its close-up of crystal growth shows water vapor molecules depositing directly onto crystal tips and edges. It shows plate-like, needle-like and dendritic forms, and says temperature, humidity, wind, ice age and location shape the patterns.

sections.heading: From open lead to flower field
body: The infographic's formation sequence begins with an open lead that starts to freeze. Thin new ice forms, and its surface stays moist relative to the air. Supersaturated vapor deposits as ice, branches multiply, and mature clusters spread. The central cutaway sets comparatively warm seawater under porous new sea ice with a briny, wet surface, below much colder, calm air. Arrows mark heat and water vapor rising from the surface.
Its scale strip steps down from a dark lead in sea ice seen by satellite, to a field of flowers, to a single cluster centimeters across, to a branch millimeters wide.

sections.heading: Salt, weather and the air above
body: Rejected brine can coat the crystals with salts. The infographic shows the pathway: as seawater freezes, salts are rejected, concentrated brine moves up through pores, and salty brine droplets can coat the frost flowers. Its chemistry panel separates the ice crystal framework, built by vapor deposition, from a surface coating of sea salts and other concentrated compounds that come from the brine.

Weather affects growth. The infographic shows cold, calm air favoring large, delicate structures, and wind breaking and removing them. It also shows salty frost-flower surfaces, and nearby saline snow or brine, as able to take part in reactive halogen chemistry in the polar atmosphere, with the note that importance varies by place and study. Local conditions and chemical importance vary.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A gecko's toes are lined with tiny hairs whose split tips come into close contact with a surface. The combined attraction of forces between molecules holds the animal up without glue, suction or static electricity.
glance: Van der Waals forces between hair tips and the surface
Up to 500,000, each with hundreds to a thousand split ends
The angle of the hair to the surface governs sticking and release

sections.heading: Hairs that split into tiny tips
body: A gecko's foot carries up to 500,000 tiny hairs, according to a UC Berkeley news release on the research. Each hair ends in hundreds to a thousand split ends, tiny pads called spatulae. Each spatula is only 200 billionths of a meter wide, which is below the wavelength of visible light. With these hairs a gecko can adhere even to molecularly smooth surfaces such as polished glass.

The infographic lays out the same structure as a scale ladder: adult gecko, toe, lamella, seta, spatula tip. It labels the lamellae as overlapping ridges that run across the toe and the setae as hairs that branch into flattened tips. One of its labels gives millions of setae on each lamella. The Berkeley release gives up to 500,000 hairs per foot and also speaks of millions of foot hairs.

sections.heading: Why it is not glue
body: The hair tips make close contact with the surface, and their combined van der Waals attraction lets the gecko grip without secreting glue. Van der Waals forces are forces between molecules. The release says their sum can amount to 1,000 times the weight of a gecko.

The researchers had reported earlier that the hairs stick without suction, glue or static electricity. Many animals that stick with a film of liquid have glands on their feet that secrete it, and geckos have no such glands. In the tests, gecko toes stuck equally well to a surface that repels water and a surface that attracts it. The release says the experiments confirmed van der Waals forces as the most likely adhesive mechanism.

sections.heading: Gripping and letting go
body: The angle a hair makes with the surface is critical for controlling both sticking and release. The infographic shows this as two sequences. In attachment, the toe approaches, makes light contact and rolls on, the setae align under shear, and many tips share the load. In release, the toe hyperextends and peels from the tip back, the setal angle changes, and contact drops with no glue left behind.

The infographic also shows that claws can help on rough surfaces such as bark but are not the setal mechanism, and that contamination on wet or dusty glass can reduce performance. Anatomy and performance vary among species and surfaces.

sections.heading: Copying the idea
body: Engineers at UC Berkeley made synthetic hair tips that stick almost as well as the geckos' own. The infographic's biomimicry panel shows reusable dry-grip material research and a wall-climbing inspection pad, under the label inspired by, not a perfect copy.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A whale fall is the carcass of a whale that has died and sunk to the seafloor. It gives deep-sea life a sudden, concentrated supply of food, and its skeleton can support communities for years to decades.
glance: The carcass of a whale that has died and sunk
Eaten by scavengers in a matter of months
Enriched by organic fragments for over a year
Can support rich communities for years to decades
Found in 2019 at 10,623 feet near Davidson Seamount

sections.heading: Food from above
body: The ocean's depths are supplied by nutrients falling down from the surface waters. When a whale dies and sinks, NOAA explains, its carcass gives deep-sea organisms a sudden, concentrated food source. The carcass becomes both food and habitat.
During a 2019 expedition, researchers discovered a whale fall 10,623 feet below the surface near Davidson Seamount, in NOAA's Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary.

sections.heading: A succession of communities
body: Different stages in the decomposition of the carcass support a succession of communities. Scavengers consume the soft tissue in a matter of months. Organic fragments, or detritus, enrich the nearby sediments for over a year. The skeleton can then support rich communities for years to decades, both as a hard surface for invertebrates to colonize and as a source of sulfides.

The infographic draws this as four phases: mobile scavengers, enrichment opportunists, a sulfide-associated bone community, and a later hard-substrate community of sponges, corals and other organisms that stay fixed in place. It names hagfish, sleeper sharks, amphipods and large crustaceans among the scavengers. It labels the phases as overlapping and variable, not a fixed clock, and notes that not all whale falls develop every phase.

sections.heading: Energy from bone chemistry
body: As organic material in the bones breaks down, the resulting sulfides can support microbes that use chemical energy and, in turn, the animals that depend on them. The microbes form the basis of ecosystems for as long as the food source lasts. NOAA says this forms a new food web that supports single-celled and multi-celled organisms and sponges.

The infographic shows the pathway as a chain: bone organic matter, anaerobic microbes, sulfide, sulfur-oxidizing microbes, then grazers and associated animals. It labels the chain as local chemical energy, not sunlight. It also shows red-plumed Osedax worms on a whale rib, with root-like tissues that enter the bone, and notes that symbiotic bacteria help the worms reach bone-derived nutrients and that they have no mouths or teeth.

sections.heading: Why whale falls differ
body: The infographic lists carcass size, depth, oxygen, currents and region as things that change the succession, its duration and the species present, with no universal timetable. It also compares a whale fall, as an island of organic matter, with the sparse background seafloor and with a hydrothermal vent, where chemosynthesis is driven by geologic fluids.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Every year, Saharan winds carry mineral dust across the Atlantic to the Amazon basin. Some of it settles there and delivers phosphorus, a nutrient that plants need and that is in short supply in the Amazon.
glance: From the Sahara across the Atlantic to the Amazon basin
A 10,000 mile long, intermittent atmospheric river of dust
182 million tons each year, by the CALIPSO satellite's measure
27.7 million tons, or 15% of the total

sections.heading: A river of dust between two continents
body: The Sahara and the Amazon basin are connected by what NASA calls a 10,000 mile long intermittent atmospheric river of dust. Every year, intense Saharan winds send enormous clouds of dust on a trans-Atlantic journey to the Amazon basin. Much of the dust originates in an ancient lakebed in Chad.

The infographic names that source as the Bodélé Depression in Chad and labels it a major source region, not the whole Sahara. It traces the journey in steps: surface gusts, saltation, the release of fine dust, turbulent uplift, easterly transport, aging in humid air, scavenging by clouds, wet and dry deposition, and export by rivers.

sections.heading: Phosphorus for the forest
body: The dust is rich in phosphorus. Phosphorus is essential to plant growth and is in short supply in the Amazon, and NASA says the desert dust dumped into the forest every year helps to diminish this deficit. The nutrients are the remains of long-dead organisms of the Sahara.

The infographic frames the dust as one external input in a complex nutrient budget, and says the dust delivers other minerals along with phosphorus. Its balance panel sets inputs (dust, rainfall, litter cycling and rock weathering) against losses (leaching, river export, erosion and gaseous losses) in highly weathered soils. It shows dust landing on leaves and litter, washing down to the forest floor, and reaching roots and fungi before erosion and rivers carry nutrients away.

sections.heading: Measuring the dust from orbit
body: NASA's CALIPSO satellite, launched in 2006, uses a lidar to scan the atmosphere for the vertical distribution of dust and other aerosols. NASA reports that it quantified the trip for the first time: of the 182 million tons of dust that leave the Sahara each year, 27.7 million tons, or 15% of the total, are scattered over the Amazon basin.

The infographic gives no tonnage. It says the minerals arrive in small but meaningful amounts and that numbers and mechanisms are refined over time. It lists several lines of evidence for where the dust comes from: satellite aerosol views, air-mass back trajectories, mineral fingerprints, isotope ratios and collected dust samples.

sections.heading: A link that changes from year to year
body: CALIPSO showed that the connection varies, changing as much as 86 percent between 2007 and 2011. Researchers found a possible connection with rainfall in the Sahel, the strip of semi-arid land on the southern border of the Sahara: when rainfall there is higher, the volume of dust is lower. The exact reason is unknown.

The source fractions, atmospheric routes, delivery and ecological importance of the dust vary by season and study. The infographic adds that dust can influence clouds under some conditions while clouds and rain also remove dust, with no single universal weather effect.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A ground-based gravitational-wave detector such as LIGO is an L-shaped laser interferometer. It sends laser light down two perpendicular arms, recombines the returning beams, and reads tiny changes in the arm lengths as changes in the interference signal.
glance: L-shaped Michelson interferometer with two equal-length arms
Tiny differences in the optical path lengths of the two arms
A change in distance 1,000 times smaller than a proton
About 300 bounces in each arm, about 1200 km of effective travel

sections.heading: The basic interferometer
body: LIGO describes its detectors as, at their cores, Michelson interferometers. Each is L-shaped with two equal-length arms. A beam splitter sends laser light along the perpendicular arms. The returning beams are recombined, producing an interference signal that responds to tiny differences in their optical path lengths.

LIGO's arms are 4 km (2.5 mi) long, and LIGO says its interferometers are by far the largest ever built. The instrument has to measure a change in distance 1,000 times smaller than a proton, which is why it must be larger and more sensitive than any interferometer built before.

sections.heading: Making the arms act longer
body: As simple Michelson interferometers, instruments with 4 km arms would still be too short to detect gravitational waves. LIGO places an additional mirror in each arm near the beam splitter, 4 km from the mirror at the end of the arm. The space between them is a Fabry Perot cavity. The laser in each arm bounces between the two mirrors about 300 times before it is merged with the beam from the other arm. That increases the effective distance each laser travels from 4 km to about 1200 km and builds up the laser light within the interferometer, both of which increase sensitivity.

sections.heading: Building up laser power
body: The laser first enters the interferometer with a power of about 40 Watts, but the instrument needs to operate closer to 750 kW. Power recycling mirrors make up the difference. They continually reflect laser light that has already traveled through the instrument back into the interferometer. The added power sharpens the interference fringes that appear when the two beams are superimposed. Signal recycling mirrors further enhance the signal received by the photodetector, and the interferometers were built with mechanisms to damp out unwanted vibrations, or noise.

sections.heading: What the infographic adds
body: The infographic shows a passing gravitational wave lengthening one arm while the other shortens, then the reverse, and labels the arm deformation as exaggerated enormously. It states that the detector measures the differential change in the lengths of the two perpendicular arms, encoded as changing laser interference, and that this is not wind, sound in air or electromagnetic waves. Its footer describes gravitational waves as ripples in spacetime produced by accelerating asymmetric masses.

A numbered chain runs from compact objects that inspiral and merge, to waves that propagate outward and cross Earth, to arm lengths changing in opposite directions, to shifted laser phases and calibrated data that reveal the waveform. Other panels set several kinds of noise beside a coherent astrophysical signal, with the note that noise is modeled and reduced, not eliminated. Another shows that two or more widely separated detectors can reject local noise and constrain sky location, though not as a perfect pinpoint with two sites.

The infographic describes the mirror motion as far smaller than an atomic nucleus and says there is no universal displacement, because it depends on the source and distance. LIGO's own page gives the comparison as 1,000 times smaller than a proton. A final panel shows calibrated strain data being processed and scaled into audio in the human hearing range.

2026-07-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: In the most common cloud-to-ground lightning, a stepped leader of negative charge works down from the cloud, streamers of positive charge reach up toward it, and a bright return stroke travels back up the connected channel.
glance: A channel of negative charge that zigzags downward in roughly 50-yard segments
Channels of positive charge, normally from taller objects in the area
Travels about 60,000 miles per second back toward the cloud
One, or perhaps as many as 20, in a negative flash
Roughly 5 to 10 times as many as reach the ground

sections.heading: Leader, streamer and return stroke
body: Most lightning starts inside a thunderstorm and travels through the cloud. In the most common type of cloud-to-ground lightning, a channel of negative charge called a stepped leader zigzags downward in roughly 50-yard segments in a forked pattern. NOAA's National Severe Storms Laboratory says the leader is invisible to the human eye and shoots to the ground in less time than it takes to blink.

As it nears the ground, the stepped leader causes streamer channels of positive charge to reach upward, normally from taller objects in the area, such as a tree, house or telephone pole. When a leader and a streamer connect, a powerful electrical current begins flowing. This return stroke, the bright part, travels about 60,000 miles per second back toward the cloud along the existing channel.

A negative cloud-to-ground flash consists of one or perhaps as many as 20 return strokes. Lightning flickers when the process rapidly repeats itself several times along the same path. The channel that carries the current is one to two inches in diameter, surrounded by a region of charged particles.

sections.heading: Charge in the cloud and on the ground
body: The infographic states that its dimensions and brightness are exaggerated for explanation. Inside the cloud it shows ice crystals, graupel and supercooled droplets colliding in strong updrafts, with pockets of positive charge and a region of negative charge. The exact charge structure of a storm and the behavior of a flash vary.

Near the ground the infographic shows induced positive charge on the surface, electric field lines crowded around sharp or elevated objects, and several upward streamers competing. It carries the label that the tallest object is not always struck. Abandoned leader branches stay faint, and one streamer makes the successful attachment.

sections.heading: Where thunder comes from
body: Rapid heating of the lightning channel produces thunder. The infographic shows the steps: rapid heating, expanding air, pressure or shock waves, waves that bend and reflect in uneven air, and delayed, rolling thunder at the observer. Its channel diagram has a narrow, hot conducting core inside a sheath of superheated air, with a cylindrical pressure wave moving outward. It separates the flash, which is seen, from the sound wave, which is heard.

sections.heading: Other paths lightning takes
body: There are roughly 5 to 10 times as many flashes that remain in the cloud as flashes that travel to the ground, though individual storms may have more or fewer reaching ground. Most flashes that do not reach the ground stay within the cloud and are called intra-cloud flashes. Lightning can also travel from one cloud to another.

Less commonly, a downward positive leader followed by an upward return stroke lowers positive charge to earth. These positive flashes typically have only a single return stroke and are more likely to have a sustained current flow. A bolt from the blue starts inside a cloud, leaves the side of the storm and travels horizontally before going to ground, so even a storm that is 6 miles away can be dangerous. The infographic's safety panel reads: when thunder is heard, seek proper shelter.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The electric eel is a South American freshwater fish whose three electric organs make up most of its body. It uses strong pulses to hunt and to defend itself, and weak ones to navigate and communicate.
glance: A South American knifefish in the genus Electrophorus, not a true eel
Main organ, Hunter's organ and Sachs' organ, about 80 percent of the body
Up to 800 volts, according to the zoo
Quiet, slow-moving waters and flooded forests of the Amazon and Orinoco Rivers

sections.heading: Three electric organs
body: The Smithsonian's National Zoo describes three specialized electric organs: the main electrical organ, the Hunter's organ and the Sachs' organ. Together they make up about 80 percent of the fish's body. The strongest pulses come from the main organ and two-thirds of the Hunter's organ. The remainder of the Hunter's organ and the Sachs' organ produce the weaker discharges.

The infographic's cutaway places the main organ toward the front, Hunter's organ in the middle and Sachs' organ toward the tail, behind a compact region of vital organs near the head. Its scale ladder puts the electric organ at a smaller share, measured along the body's length, than the zoo's figure. It also notes that organ proportions and discharge vary among Electrophorus species.

sections.heading: How the cells add up
body: The organs are built from electrocytes, modified cells derived from muscle, which activate in coordinated stacks. The infographic labels a stack as living cells in series. Its firing sequence has five steps: a motor command reaches the nerves, a neurotransmitter is released at one face of the cell, ion channels open, one electrocyte develops a voltage difference, and many cells activate nearly together so that their voltages add.

sections.heading: Strong pulses and weak pulses
body: The organs generate both strong and weak pulses. Stronger pulses are used in predation and defense, while weaker outputs support navigation and communication. Electric eels communicate using low electric organ discharges, produced in pulses that are much shorter than the gaps between them.

When hunting, the eel emits a doublet of pulses. The zoo says the doublet affects the prey's muscles, making it twitch involuntarily and alerting the eel to its presence. A series of high-voltage pulses, as many as 400 per second, then paralyzes the prey. The zoo gives the eel's output as up to 800 volts. The infographic adds that discharge strength varies with species, body size and context, and that no single set of numbers fits all circumstances.

sections.heading: Where it lives and how it breathes
body: Electric eels live in the quiet, slow-moving waters of ox-bow lakes, streams, pools and flooded forests of the Amazon and Orinoco Rivers. They are obligate air-breathers, which means they surface for air periodically. The infographic shows an eel at the surface gulping air, and electric field lines spreading through fresh water, where nearby objects alter the field the eel senses.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Mantis shrimp can detect the polarization of light, which is how light waves are oriented, not their color. University of Queensland researchers reported in 2008 that the animals they studied could see both linear and circular polarized light.
glance: How light waves are oriented, not their color
The studied mantis shrimp distinguish linear and circular polarization
Professor Justin Marshall, University of Queensland

sections.heading: Seeing how light is oriented
body: Polarization describes how light waves are oriented, not their color. People notice the effect of linear polarization through polarized sunglasses, which cut out glare, and use circular polarization in things such as 3D glasses for movies and filters for cameras.

University of Queensland researchers found that the mantis shrimp they studied could distinguish both linear and circular polarization. The university described the ability to see circular polarized light as a completely new type of vision. Professor Justin Marshall, of its School of Biomedical Sciences and the Queensland Brain Institute, said the animal has a very small brain but one of the world's most complex visual systems, with 12 color channels where humans have three. The research was published in Current Biology.

sections.heading: How the eye is laid out
body: The infographic shows each compound eye divided into a dorsal hemisphere, a midband and a ventral hemisphere. It draws the midband as six rows, some labeled for linear polarization and some for circular polarization, and notes that their functions vary by group. A close-up of one optical unit, an ommatidium, labels the corneal facet, crystalline cone, retinular cells, rhabdom, microvilli, pigment cells and nerve output.

In the infographic's linear polarization panel, incoming light meets microvilli that share one orientation. In its circular polarization panel, labeled for some stomatopods, light first passes a retarder-like layer, and the receptors then compare right-handed and left-handed light. Another panel shows the eyes rolling independently around the viewing axis, which changes receptor alignment.

sections.heading: What it may be for
body: Marshall said only the males have the ability, which implies it has something to do with sex. He said it is probably a secret communication channel between males and females that keeps predators from knowing what is going on.

The infographic's signaling panel sets polarization contrast from the shrimp's body patches beside ordinary color contrast and labels it not a universal language. Its accuracy panel lists species, sex, body region, adaptation state and conditions such as light, depth and temperature as sources of variation. Visual mechanisms and sensitivities vary among stomatopod species.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A few darkling beetles of the Namib Desert drink fog. They stand head-down facing into the wind, and the water that collects on their backs runs down to their mouths.
glance: Particular Namib beetles, including Onymacris unguicularis
Head standing, facing into the wind
Collects on the wing covers and runs down to the mouth
Two of approximately 200 in the area have been observed to fog-bask
As much as 100 km inland from the coast

sections.heading: The fog-basking stance
body: Darkling beetles of the Namib Desert have different ways of getting water from fog. Some dig trenches in the sand. Others use their own bodies as fog collectors. A fog-basking beetle takes up a head-standing posture facing into the wind. Fog water collects on its wing covers and runs down to its mouth.

The paper traces the fog to the cold current that runs along the coast, and says it can reach as much as 100 km inland. The infographic's coastal strip shows that setting with the labels Benguela current, moist marine air, coastal fog, dune belt and inland drying.

sections.heading: Which beetles do it
body: Fog-basking is documented in particular Namib beetles, including Onymacris unguicularis. It is not a trait of all darkling beetles. According to the paper, only two of approximately 200 beetle species living in the area have ever been observed to fog-bask, and both belong to the genus Onymacris.

The authors tested four species in a fog chamber. Only O. unguicularis could be seen actively collecting water from the fog. The infographic makes a similar point in a panel titled strategies vary, which sets fog-basking beetles beside beetles labeled as using other strategies.

sections.heading: Bumps, grooves and an older model
body: A familiar explanation of fog collection involves a bumpy back. In that account, the structures are believed to be water-attracting peaks surrounded by water-repelling areas, with fog water settling on the peaks of smooth bumps on the wing covers. The paper notes that applying this mechanism to fog-basking beetles has been questioned.

The beetles well known to fog-bask have smooth wing covers with regular grooves. In this study the wing covers of all four species were found to be completely water-repelling, and the authors conclude that the fog-basking behavior itself is a more important factor than structural adaptations when O. unguicularis collects water from fog.

sections.heading: What the infographic lays out
body: The infographic shows the process as six numbered steps: Atlantic fog, inland fog, impact, pinning, coalescence and ingestion. On its central beetle, labels follow the droplets from impact to coalescence to runoff toward the mouth, with gravity marked. Side panels cover the forces on a droplet, a water budget of fog, food moisture and metabolic water, and fog-collecting meshes labeled analogy, not exact copy.

It marks the bump model as an older simplified model that is not universal and is debated, not settled, and an accuracy panel says behavior, texture, wax chemistry and fog reliance all vary. The infographic's microtexture panel labels pits and ridges on a waxy cuticle and notes that structures differ among species. The paper describes the well-known fog-basking beetles as smooth with regular grooves.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A fulgurite is a tube of glass made when lightning passes through sand. The discharge melts sand around its path, and the melt cools into glass that keeps some of the shape of the route.
glance: A glassy tube formed in sand by lightning
From fulgur, the Latin word for lightning
50,000 degrees F, by the National Park Service's figure
Form and composition vary, and not every strike makes one

sections.heading: Sand melted by lightning
body: A lightning discharge through suitable sand can briefly melt material around its path. The melt cools into a glassy fulgurite that preserves some of the shape of the route the discharge took. At Great Sand Dunes National Park and Preserve, the National Park Service describes fulgurites as blackish tubes of glass.

The Park Service gives lightning a temperature of 50,000 degrees F, hotter than the surface of the sun. It says the bolt vaporizes the area where it shoots through the sand and melts the surrounding sand into dark glass.

sections.heading: The sequence in the infographic
body: The infographic lays out the formation in order: a dry dune, attachment of the lightning, a current path through the sand, local melting, rapid quenching and, later, exposure. Its cutaway labels a hollow tube with a glassy wall, fused grains, vesicles, mineral inclusions and a sand-coated exterior. A grain-scale panel shows separate grains before the strike, a transient melt during it, and quenched glass bridges after.

sections.heading: Why no single shape
body: Fulgurite form and composition vary with lightning energy, current path, moisture, grain size, mineralogy and cooling, and not every strike makes one. The infographic shows the current path branching where moisture, minerals, pore space and grain contact vary. It shows different results in different materials: branching tubes in sand, massive forms in soil and a thin glassy coating on rock.

It also shows what happens afterward. A buried fulgurite is fragile. Shifting sand exposes it, it breaks into segments, and the pieces become rounded fragments. A comparison panel sets fulgurites apart from roots, animal burrows, volcanic glass, slag and manufactured glass by a sand coat, a branching tube, a glassy wall and an irregular path.

sections.heading: An old name and a park request
body: Fulgur is the Latin word for lightning. Cicero used the expression condere fulmina, meaning to dig up thunderbolts, which the Park Service says indicates that early Romans had knowledge of fulgurite formation in sandy areas of Italy.

At Great Sand Dunes, the presence of fulgurites in the sand is a reminder that lightning can and does strike the exposed dunefield during storms. The Park Service asks visitors who find one to study and enjoy it but leave it in the sand for the next visitor.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A honey bee's waggle dance works like a set of directions to a flower patch. The angle of the waggle run on the comb gives the direction relative to the sun, and a longer run stands for a longer flight.
glance: The waggle run of a figure-eight dance on the comb
The food lies directly away from the sun
60 degrees left of vertical means 60 degrees left of the sun
A longer waggle run for farther food, roughly linear
Recruits home in on the flower patch using odor cues

sections.heading: Turning the comb into a compass
body: The angle of a returning bee's waggle run conveys direction relative to the sun. NC State Extension gives examples. If the food source lies directly away from the sun, the straight run points vertically down. If the food source is 60 degrees to the left of the sun, the waggle run is 60 degrees to the left of vertical.

The infographic's sun compass panel shows the rule with three labels: toward the sun is up on the comb, away from the sun is down on the comb, and an angled run keeps the same offset from the sun. Across the bottom it draws a bee flying over a landscape toward a flower patch, with the caption that the dance angle equals the flight direction relative to the sun.

sections.heading: Why the dance changes through the day
body: The direction in the dance is relative to the sun, so a forager's dance for one particular food source changes over time. In the publication's example, a source due east has foragers dancing approximately straight up in the morning and approximately straight down in the late afternoon.

The infographic labels this time compensation, with the caption that the sun moves and the flower stays, and draws it for morning, midday and afternoon. A neighboring panel is labeled polarized skylight cue.

sections.heading: Distance, and how exact the message is
body: As the distance to the food increases, the waggle run lasts longer. NC State Extension describes the relationship as roughly linear. The infographic shows three runs marked nearer, farther and farther still, says the duration of the waggle run correlates with distance, and adds the note that calibration varies.

The infographic also calls the direction a vector, not a point, and shows recruits searching near the target. The extension publication gives the most commonly accepted view: recruits go to the area the dance describes, then home in on the flower patch using odor cues.

sections.heading: From dancer to recruits
body: If the quality of the food is high enough, a forager will often dance on the comb, and the complete waggle dance is a figure-eight circuit. Recruits follow the dancing bee to get the information, then leave the hive and travel to the place. They use that information to search for food.

The infographic shows a six-step recruitment sequence: returns, nectar sample, dance floor, repeated circuits, followers attend, search. It lists several signal channels around the dancer (vibration through the comb, air movement, odor and antennal contact) and says food quality and colony need drive motivation.

In the research that NC State Extension describes, marked foragers were trained to food placed at known distances from a colony, and the angle and duration of their dances were then measured. The infographic's panel on how the dance is studied shows observation-hive video, a vibration sensor, a marked dancer, feeder training and decoded bearings.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A hydrothermal vent chimney grows where hot, mineral-rich fluid from the ocean crust meets cold seawater. As the fluid cools, minerals precipitate into chimney walls and sometimes a dark plume.
glance: Seawater that percolates into the ocean crust and is heated by hot magma
Extreme pressure at depth keeps it from boiling
Chimneys formed from deposits of iron sulfide
Chimneys formed from deposits of barium, calcium and silicon

sections.heading: Seawater's loop through the crust
body: Hydrothermal vents are the result of seawater percolating down through fissures in the ocean crust near spreading centers or subduction zones. The cold seawater is heated by hot magma and reemerges to form the vents. Hot seawater circulating through the crust carries dissolved minerals. It may reach temperatures of over 700° Fahrenheit, and it does not boil because of the extreme pressure at the depths where vents form.

The infographic draws this loop as a descent of cold seawater through fractured crust, heating and a water-rock reaction at depth, and a buoyant upflow of hot fluid through the active conduit in the middle of the chimney. Its pressure panel says that under great depth pressure, very hot fluid can remain liquid.

sections.heading: Where hot fluid meets cold seawater
body: When the vent fluid cools against seawater, minerals precipitate, forming a chimney and sometimes a dark plume. NOAA describes a venting black smoker as emitting jets of particle-laden fluid, in which the particles are predominantly very fine-grained sulfide minerals formed when the hot hydrothermal fluid mixes with near-freezing seawater. Black smokers are chimneys formed from deposits of iron sulfide, which is black. White smokers are formed from deposits of barium, calcium and silicon, which are white.
The infographic marks this meeting as a mixing front at the top of the chimney, with hot vent fluid on one side and a particle plume on the other.

sections.heading: Layers of the chimney wall
body: The infographic shows growth in stages: a hot-fluid jet, an anhydrite scaffold of calcium sulfate, a porous young wall of sulfide deposits, a chalcopyrite-rich lining of copper-iron sulfide, outer zones of sphalerite and iron sulfides, and a branched chimney with sealed and new conduits. Its magnified wall section runs from the hot conduit through a chalcopyrite-rich inner lining and mixed-sulfide zones to an iron-sulfide exterior, with anhydrite remnants, porous channels and cold seawater in cracks. It marks the zones as variable.

The archive note for the picture credits a Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution feature, The birth of a black smoker, for the anhydrite scaffold, the chalcopyrite lining, the sulfide zoning and the wall porosity. Those details are not on the NOAA page.

sections.heading: Life on chemical energy
body: Scientists first discovered hydrothermal vents in 1977 near the Galapagos Islands, and found them surrounded by large numbers of organisms that had never been seen before. These biological communities depend on chemical processes that result from the interaction of seawater and hot magma.

The infographic places the life at the zones where vent fluid and seawater mix. It labels the central jet as the hottest part and uninhabited, with microbial films on mixing interfaces, tubeworms in an oxygenated zone, mussels at diffuse flow, and shrimp and crabs near chemical gradients. Its pathway panel shows microbes using chemical energy, not sunlight. An accuracy note on the picture says field conditions vary, including temperature, mineralogy, flow, microbes, animals and chimney architecture.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A charring ablative heat shield protects a spacecraft during atmospheric entry by letting its own material be consumed. As it heats, the material decomposes, releases gases and leaves a layer of char, which limits the heat that reaches the spacecraft.
glance: A charring ablative thermal protection system for atmospheric entry
A char layer that re-radiates heat

sections.heading: Where the heat comes from
body: A NASA Ames Research Center presentation names two primary sources of reentry heating. One is convective heating, from the flow of hot gas past the vehicle's surface and from catalytic chemical recombination reactions at the surface. The other is radiation heating from the energetic shock layer in front of the vehicle. Heating depends on reentry speed, the vehicle's effective radius and atmospheric density.

The infographic shows a blunt capsule with a bow shock ahead of it, a shock layer of hot gas, and a stagnation region labeled as the place of maximum heating. Its heat-flux map, marked qualitative, puts the highest heat flux at the stagnation region, lower heat flux at the shoulder and the lowest on the backshell. A note says flow and heating depend on shape, trajectory and atmosphere.

sections.heading: How a charring ablator responds
body: The presentation describes ablative thermal protection as energy management through material consumption. Exposed to entry heating, the material pyrolyzes, or chars, and rejects heat in several ways. The polymer absorbs heat as it decomposes. Ablation products blown into the boundary layer reduce convective heating. A char layer forms and re-radiates heat. The surface can also recede. Together these changes limit the heat that reaches the spacecraft.

The infographic draws the shield as a stack. From the outside in, it labels hot gas, a receding surface, a porous char layer, a pyrolysis zone where decomposition takes place, polymer-rich virgin ablator, an adhesive bond layer and the carrier structure. A numbered sequence runs from untouched virgin material, to a warming surface, to the start of pyrolysis, to gases flowing outward through pores, to a thickening char layer, to surface reaction and recession in which mass is removed, and last to cooldown and a recovered shield. A recession gauge, marked exaggerated, shows the surface receding while the bond line remains intact.

sections.heading: Ablative and reusable systems
body: The presentation contrasts ablators with insulative, reusable thermal protection, which manages energy through storage and re-radiation and leaves the material unchanged. Among ablators, it says PICA was the enabling thermal protection material for the Stardust mission, where it was used as a single-piece heat shield, and that Avcoat, a material first used on Apollo, was chosen for Orion.

The infographic presents Avcoat and PICA as examples beside a reusable silica tile. Its mission panel, marked as selected examples, pairs Apollo and Orion with Avcoat, Stardust with PICA and the Space Shuttle with reusable tiles. It spells out PICA as phenolic impregnated carbon ablator.

sections.heading: What varies from shield to shield
body: The infographic's closing panel lists what varies: material, trajectory, chemistry, char structure, gas production, oxidation, recession and the heating map. A design panel names trade-offs that include entry speed, atmosphere, vehicle shape, ballistic loading, heating level, mass, bond-line temperature, manufacturability and uncertainty. A measurement panel shows embedded thermocouples, surface radiometry, pressure sensing and a post-flight thickness map.

2026-07-28-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The Lord Howe Island phasmid is a large, flightless stick insect that vanished from Lord Howe Island and survived on Ball's Pyramid, a rocky outcrop nearby. Its very restricted wild range is central to its listing as critically endangered.
glance: Males reach 120 mm and females 150 mm
A single site on Ball's Pyramid, 23 km south east of Lord Howe Island
Estimated at fewer than 50 mature individuals

sections.heading: A large, flightless stick insect
body: The Lord Howe Island phasmid, Dryococelus australis, is a large, flightless stick insect. The New South Wales listing document gives adult males as reaching 120 mm, more commonly 106 mm, and adult females as reaching 150 mm, more commonly 120 mm.

The infographic shows a female and a male side by side, with the label wingless, and a life cycle strip running from egg to hatchling, nymph, final molt and adult. A comparison panel titled body form varies sets the wingless phasmid beside a generic winged stick insect.

sections.heading: Lost from Lord Howe Island
body: The phasmid was once very common on Lord Howe Island, common enough to be used as bait for fishing. It became extinct there soon after a supply ship ran aground in 1918 and the ship rat came ashore with the cargo. The species was considered extinct until live individuals were discovered on Ball's Pyramid in 2001.
The infographic tells that history in three pictures: the former range on Lord Howe Island, a disappearance it attributes to introduced rats, and the rediscovery on Ball's Pyramid.

sections.heading: One site on Ball's Pyramid
body: In the wild the phasmid is known only from a single site on Ball's Pyramid, a rocky outcrop 23 km south east of Lord Howe Island. The insects have been reported only from within a foraging area considered to be 30 m x 6 m. Melaleuca howeana is likely the only host plant for the phasmid at that site.

The listing document estimates the wild population as extremely low, with fewer than 50 mature individuals. This very restricted range is central to the insect's conservation status. The infographic marks the refuge as a narrow band on the rock and labels the status critically endangered under the Australian EPBC Act, with the words exceptionally restricted wild range.
The infographic's night panels show a daily routine: day shelter in a humid crevice, dusk emergence, night foraging on leaves and a return to shelter.

sections.heading: Breeding as insurance
body: In 2003, two pairs of phasmids were collected from Ball's Pyramid and a captive breeding program was started. The listing document, citing a July 2011 communication, reports 800 adults in captivity producing viable eggs.

The infographic shows conservation breeding as an insurance population, with managed eggs, nymph rearing, adult pairing and record keeping. A neighboring panel lists habitat protection, genetic management, cautious re-establishment planning and ongoing monitoring. Its threats panel lists storms or landslip, habitat change, invasive species risk, disease or biosecurity risk and climate pressure, all under the heading vulnerabilities.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The Venus flytrap is a carnivorous plant that catches prey by closing its leaf blade. Sensory hairs on the leaf turn a touch into electrical and calcium signals, and the leaf moves only after two signals in succession.
glance: Six sensory hairs on the leaf blade
Two successive signals; the infographic gives two action potentials within about 15 to 20 seconds
DmMSL10, a stretch-activated chloride channel in cells at the hair base
Coastal North and South Carolina, according to the infographic

sections.heading: Six hairs that feel a touch
body: The Venus flytrap (Dionaea muscipula) senses mechanical stimuli through organs called sensory hairs, six of which form on the leaf blade. The infographic calls them trigger hairs and shows three on each lobe. A stimulated hair typically generates a single action potential, an electrical signal. In some cases it generates several, depending on the angle and angular speed of the stimulus.

The action potential and a long-range calcium signal travel from the hair to the leaf blade. A study in Nature Communications describes two steps inside the hair. First, sensing is limited to the stimulated cell. Then, depending on a threshold, an action potential fires and the calcium signal spreads. Weak stimuli generate only receptor potentials that stay below the threshold. Strong stimuli produce receptor potentials large enough to trigger action potentials.

sections.heading: Two signals to close
body: The leaf moves to catch prey after two successive calcium signals. The infographic states the rule as two action potentials within about 15 to 20 seconds: after a first touch the trap remains open, and a second touch in time brings rapid snap closure. It adds that no conscious counting is involved and that the timing threshold reduces wasted closure after one isolated contact. It draws the snap as the lobes going from an open, convex shape through an instability to a closed, concave one.

After closure, the infographic shows repeated contacts from continued movement producing more electrical signals. It states that more than three signals turn on digestive-enzyme genes and that the response rises with repeated stimulation. The trap seals to form a stomach, the glands secrete enzymes, and gland cells absorb nitrogen, phosphorus, sulfur, potassium and sodium from the digested prey.

sections.heading: A sensor for weak touches
body: The Nature Communications study examined a mechanosensitive channel called DmMSL10, a stretch-activated chloride channel concentrated in the outermost cells at the base of the hair. The channel contributes to detecting weak stimuli. In plants with the channel knocked out, no action potentials were observed at bending speeds below 0.1 rad/s, while unmodified plants kept generating them at reduced speeds.

The researchers also watched ants visit the traps. In the knockout traps, the probability of a calcium signal after an ant visit was significantly reduced, by 18.5%. Those traps also tended to close 13.3% less often, but that difference was not statistically significant.
The infographic's membrane inset labels sodium and calcium ions at the open channels. The study describes DmMSL10 as a chloride channel and follows calcium signals.

sections.heading: Where it grows
body: The infographic gives the native range as coastal North and South Carolina, in fire-maintained wet savanna with nutrient-poor soils. Its habitat panel shows pines over a ground fire.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The elongate bombardier beetle, Brachinus elongatulus, defends itself with an explosive discharge of hot chemical spray. When the beetle is challenged, chemical precursors held in a reservoir are sent into a reaction chamber, and the spray that results contains two major quinones.
glance: An explosive discharge of hot, noxious chemical spray
The reservoir and the reaction chamber

sections.heading: Two compartments, mixed when challenged
body: The beetle's defensive apparatus has two compartments, the reservoir and the reaction chamber. When the beetle is challenged, muscles around the reservoir contract and send chemical precursors into the reaction chamber, where they mix with enzymes. The result is an explosive discharge of hot, noxious spray containing two major quinones, 1,4-benzoquinone and 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone, also called toluquinone.

The infographic makes the same point in a callout: the beetle does not store a ready-made explosive mixture. Its chemistry panel is headed two-stage chemistry, with the note that the precursors are separate and mixed only when defense is triggered.

sections.heading: Where the two quinones come from
body: The study in The Science of Nature traced how these compounds are made in Brachinus elongatulus, which is a separate matter from how the spray is ejected. Untransformed fluid sampled from the reservoir held significant quantities of two precursors, 1,4-hydroquinone and 2-methyl-1,4-hydroquinone.

The researchers injected or fed beetles with precursors carrying stable-isotope labels. Labeled 1,4-hydroquinone was converted specifically to 1,4-benzoquinone. A different compound, m-cresol, was metabolized to 2-methyl-1,4-hydroquinone, which is then oxidized to 2-methyl-1,4-benzoquinone in the hot spray.

It had been speculated that all the benzoquinones originate from one core precursor, 1,4-hydroquinone. The results show instead that the two quinones are products of two independent pathways. The authors suggest this kind of pathway is not restricted to bombardier beetles and could well be a general pathway to benzoquinones.

sections.heading: The pulse cycle on the infographic
body: The infographic's cutaway labels the parts in a row: paired reservoirs, a one-way passage, a flexible expansion membrane, a rigid reaction chamber, a valve, an exit duct and an aimable nozzle. A five-step loop headed the passive pulse engine runs fill, react, pressure rises, valve closes and spray fires, pressure falls and valve reopens, with the line that mechanical feedback controls each burst.

That part of the picture draws on a different study, a 2015 paper in Science by Arndt and colleagues, which the infographic's source note cites for rapid discrete explosions, a hot pulsed quinone spray, synchrotron observation and passive mechanical-feedback control. The infographic also shows the bendable tip of the abdomen directing spray across a broad rear and side arc.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Hail grows inside thunderclouds, where strong updrafts keep hailstones suspended while layers of ice build up. The layers reflect changes in how the ice grew, but they are not a precise map of the stone's path.
glance: Solid precipitation in the form of balls or pieces of ice
Only in convective clouds, such as thunderclouds
5 mm to over 50 mm in diameter; most are smaller than 25 mm
It becomes too heavy for the updrafts to support

sections.heading: How hail forms in a thundercloud
body: Hail is solid precipitation in the form of balls or pieces of ice known as hailstones. The Met Office describes it developing in thunderclouds, where strong updrafts and downdrafts move water droplets up and down through the cloud. When the droplets reach the top of the cloud, they freeze in the cold temperatures.

Powerful updrafts can keep hailstones suspended for a long time, which lets them grow larger as more layers of ice accumulate. When they become too heavy for the updrafts to support, they fall to the ground as solid balls of ice. Unlike snow, hail forms only in these convective clouds.

sections.heading: What the layers record
body: The layers of a hailstone reflect changes in how the ice grew. They are not a precise map of the hailstone's path through the storm.

The infographic shows a cut hailstone with an embryo core, a zone of bubbly, opaque ice labeled dry growth, a zone of clear ice labeled wet growth, and a lobed outer shell. Its key reads clear bands as wet growth with high liquid water, and cloudy bands as dry growth with trapped air.

Its growth sequence runs: an embryo is captured in the updraft, it is carried upward in the rotating updraft, supercooled droplets freeze on contact, liquid water spreads and then freezes, uneven growth forms lobes and ridges, and the stone falls through downdraft and rain. The picture sets this inside a supercell storm, with a rotating updraft, a supercooled water zone and a freezing level.

sections.heading: What makes hail large or small
body: Hailstones are typically spherical or conical. They range from 5 mm to over 50 mm in diameter, though most are smaller than 25 mm. The Met Office says the largest hailstones form in multicell storms, which are more common in places like the United States. The infographic's subject is a supercell.

The infographic's cause-and-effect panel links a stronger updraft, supercooled droplets and a long residence time to larger hail, and melting below the freezing level to a smaller final size. Supercooled droplets, storm flow, residence time, wet and dry growth, and melting together build the layered anatomy of hail.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The Malaysian stalk-eyed fly, Teleopsis dalmanni, carries its eyes on stalks at the sides of its head. A study of contests between males linked the outcome to both eyespan and whether a fly already held the resource.
glance: Carried by both sexes, at the sides of the head
Linked to male eyespan and to resource ownership
Eyespan is not the only factor in a contest

sections.heading: What decides a contest between males
body: The study behind this infographic, published in Animal Behaviour, linked the outcome of contests in the stalk-eyed fly Teleopsis dalmanni to two things: male eyespan and whether the fly already held the resource. Eyespan is therefore not the only factor to consider when interpreting a contest.

Researchers connect the fly's exaggerated eyespan with mate choice, ritualized contests, resource ownership, development and reproductive quality. These findings are associations, and the outcomes depend on context.

sections.heading: What the infographic shows
body: The infographic shows that both sexes carry their eyes on sideways stalks. Its comparison panel says males have more exaggerated eyestalks relative to body size, and that females also have eyestalks, though less exaggerated. A cutaway of one eyestalk labels the head capsule, eyestalk, compound eye, antenna, optic nerve and cuticle.

The male contest panel runs in three steps, align, assess and retreat, and describes ritualized displays with no physical harm. Its caption says outcomes are influenced by eyespan and resource ownership, but are not guaranteed. A female choice panel, set at a dusk roost, says wider-eyespan males receive more approaches and calls this a documented mating preference, not conscious measurement.

Other panels say the eyestalks expand during the final molt, place the fly in streamside understory rainforest in Southeast Asia, and end with a loop headed evolution across generations, not individual intent.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The wood frog is a North American frog that survives whole-body freezing in winter. Frogs studied from Interior Alaska build up urea before freezing and release glucose from liver glycogen once freezing begins.
glance: North America, from the southern Appalachians to within the Arctic Circle
Urea, built up before freezing, and glucose, released after freezing begins
Tolerate freezing only to temperatures as low as -3 to -6°C

sections.heading: Tolerance depends on the population
body: The wood frog (Rana sylvatica) ranges from the southern Appalachians to within the Arctic Circle. Its freeze tolerance varies strongly among populations. Frogs native to the upper Midwestern United States and southern Canada tolerate freezing only to temperatures as low as -3 to -6°C. Frogs from Interior Alaska readily survived experimental freezing to -16°C. In Interior Alaska, the frogs' winter shelters reach minimum temperatures of -9 to -18°C.

The infographic sums this up as northern populations showing greater freeze tolerance, and it states that freeze tolerant does not mean indestructible. It lists population differences, acclimation state, cooling rate, minimum temperature, duration of freeze and thaw conditions as limits.

sections.heading: Urea before, glucose after
body: The study's authors hypothesize that the northern frogs' extreme tolerance comes in part from an enhanced set of protective solutes. Urea accumulates in autumn and early winter, before freezing occurs. Glucose is quickly mobilized from glycogen in the liver after freezing begins. Both reduce the amount of ice that forms in the body, and these solutes help protect tissues during freezing.

In the Alaskan frogs studied, plasma urea was near 10 micromoles per milliliter in late summer. During preparation for winter it rose to 85.5 micromoles per milliliter in frogs that remained fully hydrated.

Cycles of freezing and thawing, which winter-conditioned frogs readily survived, greatly increased the breakdown of liver glycogen and the delivery of glucose, but not urea, to skeletal muscle. The infographic shows this as freeze-thaw priming, with repeated mild cycles increasing glucose delivery.

sections.heading: What happens as ice forms
body: During experimental freezing, the frogs' organs shed water: up to one-half of the water in skeletal muscle and up to two-thirds of the water in the liver.

The infographic lays out a sequence. The frog winters in a shallow shelter beneath leaf litter. Ice starts outside the cells, with crystals forming at the body surface, and water moves out of the cells. Its protected cell holds glucose and urea, with the fluid inside labeled concentrated but stable, while its unprotected cell shrinks severely. It labels ice inside cells as dangerous and says that much of the body's water can freeze. It shows heartbeat, breathing, movement and energy use all falling in a reversible metabolic depression.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Xenos vesparum is a parasite of paper wasps whose two sexes grow up in very different ways. The male forms a pupa and goes through a conspicuous metamorphosis, while the adult female stays larva-like and remains mostly inside the host.
glance: Paper wasps; the study infected larvae of Polistes dominula
Forms a pupa that pushes out from the host's abdomen
Stays larva-like as an adult, mostly inside the host
The female's cephalothorax, pushed out through the host's cuticle
broad, raised in the last larval stage of males but not females

sections.heading: Getting into a paper wasp
body: Xenos vesparum is a twisted-wing parasite that develops inside the European paper wasp. Its first-stage larvae are free-living and seek a host within paper wasp nests. In the study behind this infographic, larvae of the paper wasp Polistes dominula were infected individually in the nest.
On entering a host, the first-stage larva molts into a legless second-stage larva with a soft cuticle that lives inside the wasp.

sections.heading: Two routes to adulthood
body: From there the sexes take different paths. A male larva in its 4th stage molts to form a pupa, which pushes out from the abdomen of the host. The male goes through a conspicuous metamorphosis and emerges as a winged adult.

The adult female keeps juvenile features and remains mostly inside the host. The paper says females remain larva-like and lists what they lack as adults: eyes, mouthparts, antennae, wings and external genitalia. A female develops a cephalothorax that is pushed out through the host's cuticle. It serves for mating and for releasing first-stage larvae, which leave through a brood canal.

sections.heading: The broad gene
body: The paper looks at a gene called broad. In insects in which both sexes go through metamorphosis, broad has been shown to be required for pupal development. In Xenos vesparum the researchers detected raised levels of broad in the last larval stage of males, but not of females.

The authors read this cautiously. They write that the data suggest the females' retained juvenile form could be linked to the suppression of pupal determination. The infographic keeps the same caution. Its panel calls the finding a reported association with Broad and adds that association is not proof of a sole cause.

sections.heading: What else the infographic shows
body: The infographic's close-up of the free male labels a branched antenna, a compound eye, a halterelike forewing and a fan-folded hindwing. A six-step life cycle strip runs from a mobile first-stage larva reaching a paper wasp nest to a free male mating at the female's opening. Smaller panels give a Mediterranean range and say, of stylopized wasps, that adult females gather away from the colony in large aggregations. That panel calls it a documented association whose mechanisms remain under study.
The infographic's drawing of the exposed female cephalothorax shows a face-like front with two dark, eye-like ovals. The paper states that adult females lack eyes.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Cuttlefish change their appearance with pigment sacs that muscles pull open in less than a second, working with cells that reflect and scatter light. They use the resulting body patterns for camouflage and for signaling.
glance: Chromatophores: a pigment sac with dozens of radial muscles
A pigment sac changes area in less than a second
Iridophores, which reflect by thin-film interference, and white leucophores

sections.heading: Pigment sacs pulled open by muscle
body: Cephalopod skin combines pigment-bearing chromatophores with cells that reflect light structurally. A chromatophore is a sac of pigment with dozens of radial muscles attached around its edge. The muscles are innervated directly by the brain. As they contract and relax, the sac increases or decreases in area in less than a second.

By selectively expanding and retracting distinct groups of chromatophores, cephalopods produce patterns such as bands, stripes and spots. The infographic shows the control path as eye and brain, motor nerve, radial muscle, then expanding pigment sac. It lists six patterns: uniform, mottled, disruptive, bands, spots and high-contrast edges.

sections.heading: Reflectors under the pigment
body: The infographic's skin cutaway puts chromatophores on top, iridophores beneath them and leucophores at the bottom, labeled absorb, reflect and scatter. Iridophores contain stacks of thin plates that reflect light by thin-film interference. The reflected color depends on the angle: the more oblique the angle, the shorter the peak wavelengths of the reflected light.

Cuttlefish and octopus also have leucophores, another type of structural reflector, which create bright white patterns, shapes and spots. In the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis, the leucophores have the optical properties of a perfect diffuser and appear equally bright from all angles of view.

The two mechanisms contribute different kinds of pattern and color, and the final appearance of the animal is frequently the result of optical interactions between iridophores and chromatophores. The infographic gives three cases: yellow pigment over a bright reflector, dark pigment masking the reflection, and a pale field of leucophores.

sections.heading: Camouflage, signals and limits
body: Cephalopods show a wide repertoire of body patterns for camouflage and signaling despite their apparent color blindness. The infographic shows a cuttlefish in a mottled pattern on fine sand and in a disruptive pattern on broken shell and rock. It also shows a pair of cuttlefish in a high-contrast display, labeled as communication.
The infographic ends with limits: appearance depends on species, light, viewing angle, background and behavior, and rapid color change is not perfect invisibility.

2026-08-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa, raises its young on a living American cockroach. Two stings leave the cockroach lethargic and compliant but not paralyzed, and the wasp leads it to a burrow and lays a single egg on it.
glance: One into the thorax, then one into the head cavity
A higher escape threshold and less spontaneous walking for 7 to 10 days
A single egg, hatching three days later
Three: two feeding from outside the cockroach, the third inside

sections.heading: Two stings
body: The attack has two stings. The first is a swift sting into the thorax, which briefly paralyzes the cockroach's front legs. The second goes into the head cavity. The wasp is able to sense the location of the head ganglia through mechanical sensing in its stinger.

The infographic numbers the two as the thoracic sting and the head sting, and labels the head sting's targets as the brain and the subesophageal ganglion. A panel headed stinger sensor array says sensors map tissue cues to locate neural targets.

sections.heading: A host that walks but does not flee
body: The venom in the head ganglia brings on behavioral changes that last 7 to 10 days: a higher threshold for escaping, a shorter escape distance and less spontaneous walking. The paper describes the stung cockroach as lethargic and compliant, but not paralyzed, a living food supply for the wasp's offspring. The wasp leads it into a burrow by grasping its shortened antennae.

The infographic shows this under the heading can walk, doesn't flee, with the summary that ability remains and drive is suppressed. Another panel reads not mind control, a precise change in locomotor motivation, and adds that the cockroach is not simply immobilized.
The cockroach is a living host for the wasp's young. It is subdued for reproduction, and the attack and the handling of the host are part of the wasp's life cycle, not simply a means of killing prey.

sections.heading: From egg to adult wasp
body: The wasp lays a single egg on one of the cockroach's mesothoracic legs, the middle pair, and the egg hatches three days later. The infographic's life cycle strip says a single egg is glued to a hind leg.

The larva develops through three stages. In the first two it feeds from outside the cockroach, and the third is spent only inside it. The cockroach remains alive through the first two stages and many hours into the third, as its organs are consumed selectively. The wasp then spins a cocoon and pupates inside the cockroach, where it develops into an adult after several weeks.

2026-08-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A brinicle is a hollow tube of ice that grows down from the underside of sea ice. Cold, dense brine draining from the ice freezes the seawater around it as it sinks.
glance: A tubular, finger-like ice formation under sea ice
A plume of cold, dense brine released from the sea ice
As low as −23 °C while remaining liquid
Both the Arctic and Antarctic oceans

sections.heading: Brine that freezes the sea around it
body: Ice brinicles are tubular, finger-like formations that grow downward from the underside of sea ice into the seawater below. They form when pockets of concentrated salt brine in the sea ice are released, sending a plume of cold, dense brine down from the bottom of the ice. Seawater around the flow freezes into a hollow tube, and brine can continue descending through it.

The cause is a temperature difference. Owing to freezing point depression, the brine may reach as low as −23 °C while remaining liquid, while the seawater is near its freezing point, about −1.8 °C. The infographic puts it this way: cold brine removes heat, freezing less-salty seawater around the plume.

sections.heading: Size, speed and where they occur
body: The tube can extend several meters down into the ocean, sometimes even reaching the seafloor. In McMurdo Sound, Antarctica, both small brinicles (10 to 100 cm long) and large ones (1 to 6 m long and 5 to 25 cm wide) have been observed. Natural growth speeds have been reported from about 0.2 to 2 cm per minute. Brinicles have been found in both the Arctic and Antarctic oceans.

The infographic adds cautions of its own. Its steps are a process sequence, not a fixed timetable, a brinicle may stop before the seabed, and not every sheet of sea ice makes brinicles.
