It lists the conditions that have to align: growing young sea ice, a connected drainage channel, very cold concentrated brine, cold surrounding seawater, sustained outflow and limited mixing.

sections.heading: Not an icicle
body: Earlier literature also called brinicles ice stalactites. The authors of the source study argue against that term, because an icicle is an ice stalactite with a different growth mechanism. The infographic sets the two side by side. It shows an ordinary freshwater icicle forming in air, driven by heat loss to the air, with liquid water freezing on the outside. It shows a brinicle forming underwater, driven by sinking cold, salty brine, with seawater freezing around the descending flow and the tube hollow during growth.

sections.heading: Brinicles grown in the laboratory
body: The source is a 2024 paper in The Cryosphere whose authors grew brinicles in the laboratory by injecting a flow of cold brine into a reservoir of less-salty water. They report that growth in a laboratory setting is highly dependent on the parameters of the experimental setup.

The infographic shows field observation and controlled experimental modeling as the ways brinicles are studied. Its flow panel shows a weak or intermittent flow, a window of stable tubular growth, and a vigorous, turbulent discharge with less orderly shapes. It says that in lab studies the form depends strongly on brine flow and ambient conditions. It also notes that contact with a moving freezing front can freeze slow animals on the seabed, though this is not inevitable.

2026-08-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Bertholdia trigona is a tiger moth that answers an approaching bat with bursts of ultrasonic clicks, a defense known as sonar jamming. A study found that the moths start clicking soon after a bat has detected and targeted them.
glance: Ultrasonic clicks used for sonar jamming, paired with diving
Bat calls that increase in intensity and come at slightly shorter intervals
Typically the early to middle approach phase of the bat's attack

sections.heading: A moth that answers back
body: Tiger moths respond to high-intensity bat calls with ultrasonic clicks. What the clicks do depends on the species. In some, they warn bats that the prey is toxic. Bertholdia trigona is a sonar-jamming moth. It emits bursts of ultrasound in response to an approaching bat, and its clicking is paired with diving.

The infographic shows where the sound comes from: paired tymbals on the thorax, drawn as striated plates controlled by muscles, with a four-step buckling sequence in which an ultrasonic click train is produced. Another panel says that not every tiger moth or click signal has the same function.

sections.heading: Timing the clicks to the attack
body: The researchers tested how the moth times its clicking to features of the bat's echolocation sequence. When a bat detects a prey echo, it gradually increases its call rate, which begins the approach phase.

The moths clicked soon after bats detected and targeted them, typically in the early to middle approach phase. Clicking was preceded by bat calls that increased in intensity and slightly decreased in pulse interval. This happened when bats were 1 to 3 m away.

The moths' clicking thresholds also closely matched the predicted optimal thresholds for telling a real threat from a false one. In the study a real threat was a bat attacking the moth itself, and a false threat was a bat attacking a nearby moth.

sections.heading: How the infographic explains jamming
body: The infographic's acoustic timeline lines up the bat's outgoing call, the returning echo from the moth and dense trains of moth clicks. It says dense clicks overlap the short interval before the prey echo arrives, creating interference that can disrupt distance estimates and target detection. A companion panel says jamming effectiveness rises continuously with duty cycle in experiments, with no universal threshold.

The encounter is drawn in five stages, from the bat searching to the bat missing or adjusting its attack, and the stated outcome is reduced bat capture success in experiments. A panel headed bat countermove says bats can compensate with a longer terminal attack buzz under high-duty-cycle playback, and calls the interaction an ongoing evolutionary contest.

2026-08-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Antarctic icefish are the only vertebrates that lack hemoglobin. They rely on oxygen dissolved in their blood, helped by cold, oxygen-rich water, larger hearts, greater blood volume, wider capillaries and very high mitochondrial density.
glance: Hemoglobin; the blood also has very few red blood cells
Greater blood volume, wider capillaries, larger hearts, dense mitochondria

sections.heading: The only vertebrates without hemoglobin
body: Antarctic fish of the family Channichthyidae are the only vertebrates that lack hemoglobin. They also have very few circulating red blood cells. British whalers sailing the Southern Ocean named them icefish for their translucent look, which is due to the absence of respiratory pigments and to scaleless skin. Without functional hemoglobin, an icefish relies on oxygen dissolved in its blood.

The infographic draws a pale icefish vessel beside the red vessel of a red-blooded relative, labeled dissolved in plasma and carried by hemoglobin. The fish in its main cutaway is labeled Chaenocephalus aceratus. The source study reports a draft genome of a different icefish, Chionodraco myersi, and examines cellular adaptations associated with this unusual physiology.

sections.heading: Cold water helps but is not enough
body: The Southern Ocean's extremely low water temperature, −1.8 °C, is considered the necessary condition for the evolutionary loss of hemoglobin. Oxygen solubility rises as water temperature falls, so the subzero Southern Ocean holds a substantially higher concentration of dissolved oxygen than temperate waters. That condition is not sufficient to compensate for the lack of hemoglobin.

Icefish also show cardiovascular modifications that offset the absence of oxygen carriers, such as greater blood volume, wider capillaries and larger hearts, and they show extraordinarily high mitochondrial density. The infographic adds a large, thin-walled heart, wide low-resistance vessels and dense capillaries. It gives the route in four steps: oxygen enters at the gills, dissolves in plasma, is pumped in high volume by the large heart and diffuses into the tissues.

sections.heading: How the hemoglobin was lost
body: Studies have asked whether losing hemoglobin was an adaptation to the extreme Antarctic environment or, conversely, a disaptation. The infographic presents the origin as debated: adaptation, tolerated disaptation or other selective pressures. From its genome comparison, the source study suggests the loss came through a series of deletion events, rapid sequence divergence, or both.

The infographic also shows a warming constraint. Warmer water holds less dissolved oxygen, and the panel describes a narrower physiological margin, not inevitable instant death. Its species panel is headed not all alike, and its notes say that some tissues may retain oxygen-related proteins depending on species.

2026-08-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The thorn bug, Umbonia crassicornis, is a treehopper whose young raise an alarm by vibrating the plant they live on. Their synchronized bursts of signals bring on the mother's defense against predators.
glance: South and Central America, Mexico and southern Florida
From 15 to 50 young, tended by the mother
Synchronized bursts of vibration through the plant
Kicks and wing-buzzes against invertebrate predators

sections.heading: An alarm sent through the twig
body: The study that described the alarm reports that the clustered nymphs of Umbonia crassicornis produce vibrational signals that travel through the plant, in synchronized bursts that bring on the mother's antipredator behavior. In the laboratory, nymphs were made to signal by a light touch imitating the approach of a predator. Signals from the nymphs at the site of the disturbance set off a rapid wave of signaling by many others in the group. When the vibrations were blocked from reaching the mother, her response was abolished. Only the study's published summary was read for this page.

The infographic lays this out as four stages: a predator-like touch reaches one nymph, that nymph vibrates the twig, its siblings answer with rapid, synchronized vibrations, and the mother turns to defend the brood. A cross-section of the twig is labeled substrate motion through twig, not airborne sound.

sections.heading: Why the timing matters
body: According to the summary, nymphs in an otherwise undisturbed group signaled only in response to signals coordinated into synchronized group displays, and not to signals in random patterns. After a period of simulated attack, the playback of one individual signal could set off a coordinated burst. It remains unknown whether siblings coordinate entirely cooperatively or compete to have the mother close by.

The infographic's signal timing panel says coordinated group bursts elicit a stronger maternal response, and random scattered signals a weaker one. In the summary, the comparison of synchronized and random signals is about how the nymphs respond; the mother's defensive behavior is described as associated with the coordinated signaling.

sections.heading: The mother's defense, and false alarms
body: A research paper on the closely related oak treehopper, Platycotis vittata, says female thornbug treehoppers, like female oak treehoppers, defend their offspring against invertebrate predators with kicks and wing-buzzes. It notes that thornbug juveniles often continue signaling after attacks end, which produces false alarms unless the mother's own signals inhibit them.
That paper's field experiment was on the oak treehopper. It showed that offspring signals evoke maternal defense and that maternal signals can inhibit offspring signaling.

sections.heading: The insect and its brood
body: The University of Florida's profile gives the thorn bug's range as South and Central America, Mexico and southern Florida. The adult is typically about 0.5 inch long and green or yellow with reddish lines and brownish markings, and the species varies in size, color and structure, particularly the males' horn. The female's horn is described as tall and essentially perpendicular.

Females lay their eggs in the tender bark of twigs, and the eggs hatch about 20 days later. The female actively tends her brood, which can number from 15 to 50, and lays only a single clutch. Young nymphs have three horns instead of the one seen on adults. The profile says a chemical passes between the parent and the nymphs, making them distasteful to potential predators.

The thorn bug feeds by piercing plant tissue and sucking the sap, and it cuts into the plant to lay its eggs. Hosts that have been severely damaged include hibiscus, powder-puff (Calliandra), woman's tongue tree and acacia. The infographic adds that development is gradual, with no pupa, and that the function of the nymph's three pronotal structures is not settled.

2026-08-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: In Arctic reindeer, the reflecting layer behind the retina, the tapetum lucidum, is golden in summer and deep blue in winter. The winter state is associated with greater visual sensitivity in dim light, at the cost of reduced acuity.
glance: The tapetum lucidum, a reflecting layer behind the retina
43.1 nm in summer, 26 nm in winter
Greater sensitivity in winter, reduced acuity

sections.heading: A mirror behind the retina
body: The tapetum lucidum is a reflecting layer behind the retina. It works as a mirror: by reflecting light back through the retina, it gives a second opportunity for photon capture, which enhances visual sensitivity. In Arctic reindeer this layer is golden in summer and deep blue in winter. The experiments were carried out at the University of Tromsø, Norway (70° N).

The infographic shows a summer eye and a winter eye side by side and states that what changes is the tapetum lucidum, not the iris or the rest of the eye. It also labels the pupil as permanently larger in winter.

sections.heading: Closer collagen, bluer reflection
body: The wavelength the tapetum reflects depends on the spacing of its collagen, and reduced spacing gives shorter wavelengths. The researchers measured a spacing between collagen fibers of 43.1 nm in summer eyes and 26 nm in winter eyes. More than 95% of the light was reflected directly back in summer eyes, compared with only 40% in winter eyes.

Winter animals had significantly increased pressure inside the eye, probably produced by permanent pupil dilation blocking the eye's drainage. When the researchers covered a summer tapetum with a cover slip and applied an 8 g weight, its reflection changed to blue immediately. The infographic marks higher eye pressure as a proposed mechanism, and the authors stress that they have not proved the functional relationships.

sections.heading: More sensitivity, less acuity
body: The shift to a blue reflection may scatter light through the photoreceptors instead of reflecting it directly, which would raise retinal sensitivity through increased photon capture. The winter state is associated with greater visual sensitivity under dim conditions. The increased sensitivity comes at the cost of reduced acuity, but the authors write that it may be an important adaptation for detecting moving predators in the dark Arctic winter.
The infographic illustrates this with a moving wolf silhouette and dark lichen on snow, and notes that the enhanced sensitivity does not provide perfect night vision.

2026-08-11-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The crypt-keeper wasp, Euderus set, is a parasitoid of a gall wasp that develops inside live oak stems. A parasitized gall wasp excavates an exit hole, plugs it with its own head and dies, and the parasitoid later emerges through the head.
glance: Bassettia pallida, the crypt gall wasp
Sand live oak and southern live oak in the southeastern USA
Excavates an emergence hole, plugs it with its head and dies
Parasitoids excavating their own hole were about three times more likely to die trapped
The precise mechanism behind the behavior

sections.heading: A gall wasp hidden in live oak
body: The host is the crypt gall wasp, Bassettia pallida, found on sand live oaks (Quercus geminata) and southern live oaks (Quercus virginiana) in the southeastern USA. Its stem galls are called crypts. They are tiny compartments in which the gall wasp develops before it excavates through the stem to emerge as an adult.
The researchers named its parasitoid the crypt-keeper wasp, Euderus set, after Set, the Ancient Egyptian god of evil and chaos.

sections.heading: The head-plugged exit
body: When Euderus set parasitizes a gall wasp, the adult gall wasp excavates an emergence hole in the crypt wall, plugs the hole with its head and dies. The parasitoid emerges through the host's head capsule when it reaches its adult stage.

The researchers never observed the egg stage of the parasitoid. They report that it appears to infect the adult stage of the host. The infographic's five-stage sequence says Euderus set lays its egg on the adult host, while its developmental panel marks egg placement as not directly observed.

sections.heading: Testing who benefits
body: The researchers tested whether the head-plugged hole benefits the parasitoid. Euderus set that had to excavate an emergence hole themselves were about three times more likely to die trapped in the crypt. The infographic shows the comparison as a pre-chewed route, where escape is easier, beside a hole resealed with bark, where success is reduced. Its summary runs: host excavates exit, shorter barrier to outside, improved escape success.

sections.heading: What is still unknown
body: The precise mechanism behind the behavior remains uncertain. The paper says that working out the specific induction methods, beyond the presence of Euderus set, is the next step. The authors also report an observation that suggests variability in the parasitoid's ability to manipulate its host.

The infographic splits a panel the same way. Under evidence it lists behavioral manipulation and an emergence benefit as supported. Under unknown it lists the exact biochemical or neurological mechanism. A closing note says later work found Euderus set associated with multiple oak gall wasp species.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A Tokay gecko clings to surfaces without glue or suction. Its toe pads carry microscopic branching hairs that make extensive close contact with a surface, and experiments support van der Waals forces as the primary source of the grip.
glance: Setae, each branching into much smaller pads called spatulae
Van der Waals forces, supported by experiments
Changing angle and peeling the toes away

sections.heading: Hairs that branch into smaller pads
body: The Tokay gecko, Gekko gecko, is native to Southeast Asia. Its toe pads carry microscopic hairs called setae, and each seta branches into much smaller end pads called spatulae. This branching, from toe pad to setae to spatulae, creates extensive close contact with a surface.

sections.heading: What holds the gecko on
body: Experiments support van der Waals forces as the primary mechanism of dry adhesion in Tokay gecko setae. The grip does not require secreted glue or suction, and it works without leaving a glue residue on the surface.

In those experiments, setae stuck similarly to strongly water-repelling and strongly water-attracting surfaces when both surfaces were polarizable. That result argues against capillary adhesion being necessary. The size and shape of the setal tips, not high surface polarity, are central to the measured mechanism.

sections.heading: Attaching and letting go
body: Simply touching a seta to a surface is not enough for strong attachment. Loading it toward the surface and slightly along the surface engages the adhesion. The directional geometry of the setae and spatulae makes attachment depend on the direction of loading.
Geckos detach rapidly by changing the angle of their toes and peeling them away. Peeling reduces contact progressively instead of breaking every contact at once.

sections.heading: Limits and design lessons
body: Natural surfaces can be more challenging than clean laboratory glass. Waxy coatings on leaves may hinder close contact between molecules.
Subdividing an adhesive surface into many small contacts increases contact density. This is a design principle for dry adhesives inspired by the gecko.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Issus coleoptratus is a jumping planthopper. Its nymphs have interlocking gear teeth on their hind legs that keep the two legs moving together in a jump, and the gears are lost at the final molt.
glance: Toothed strips on the two hind-leg trochantera of nymphs
About 400 micrometers long, with 10 to 12 teeth
Within about 30 microseconds of one another

sections.heading: Gears on the hind legs
body: Issus coleoptratus is a jumping planthopper. The nymph is a small six-legged insect with the standard insect body regions of head, thorax and abdomen. On its two hind legs, the segments called trochantera each carry a strip of teeth. The two strips face each other and interlock as working gears.
Each strip on a nymph is about 400 micrometers long and carries 10 to 12 teeth. The two strips have matching tooth counts, so the gearing ratio is 1:1.

sections.heading: How the gears steady a jump
body: The interlocking gears mechanically synchronize the two hind legs that drive a jump. High-speed video showed the legs beginning their propulsive movement within about 30 microseconds of one another. Synchronized propulsion limits unwanted yaw, which could spin the insect during takeoff.

The teeth are asymmetric and curved, because they pass on motion in the direction of the jump launch and not in both directions of rotation. The rounded bases of the teeth reduce the concentration of stress and help the teeth resist shearing.

sections.heading: Lost at the final molt
body: The working gears are found in juvenile nymphs and are lost at the final molt to adulthood. Adults synchronize their hind legs without the interlocking gear teeth. A damaged gear on a nymph may be replaced at a later molt. An adult has no later molt in which to repair its rigid cuticle.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Nacre is a biological composite made mostly of aragonite platelets with a small fraction of organic material between them. Its staggered structure sends cracks along winding paths and spreads damage, which makes it resistant to fracture.
glance: Thin organic interfaces, a small fraction of the whole

sections.heading: Platelets and thin organic layers
body: Nacre is a hierarchical biological composite. It is made mostly of aragonite platelets, separated by a small fraction of organic matrix. The platelets are staggered in an arrangement like bricks and mortar, with thin organic interfaces between them.

sections.heading: How a crack is slowed
body: In nacre, cracks are deflected and blunted, and microcracks form. These effects help create a tortuous, winding crack path and reduce catastrophic failure. Organic material can bridge platelets as they open apart, and it dissipates energy as cracks advance.
Platelet pull-out, and friction associated with nanoscale roughness on the interfaces (nanoasperities), also contribute to nacre's resistance to fracture.

sections.heading: Toughness across scales
body: At a larger scale, stacks of aragonite platelets that share the same orientation deform cooperatively, which adds another level of the hierarchy to nacre's toughening. Under indentation, monolithic aragonite tends to form a more direct major crack. Nacre spreads the damage and confines cracks near the loaded region. Nacre's toughness emerges from several mechanisms cooperating across scales, not from one feature of the interfaces alone.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The thistle tortoise beetle is a leaf beetle that feeds on thistles. Its green larva carries a shield of feces and cast skins on a forked tail process and can move the shield to block ant bites.

sections.heading: The shield on the larva's back
body: The larva is green and has spines along its margins. It has a forked tail process, which it holds over its back. On this fork it carries a packet of shield material made of feces and the cast skins it has retained.
The larva can maneuver the shield as a physical defense. Experiments found the shield effective at blocking ant bites.

Tortoise beetles of this subfamily build their shields using tail processes and deliberate handling of fecal material and cast skins. The architecture of the shield, and how it is retained, vary among tortoise beetle lineages.

sections.heading: Feeding on thistles
body: Cassida rubiginosa is a leaf beetle in the family Chrysomelidae and the subfamily Cassidinae. Adults and larvae both feed on thistle foliage, and Canada thistle is a primary host in North America. Young larvae window-feed on the undersides of leaves, while older larvae make irregular feeding holes.

sections.heading: Life cycle, size and range
body: The life cycle runs through egg, five larval instars, pupa and adult. In the North American setting described, there is one generation a year. Adults are oval and green, with a hard protective covering and a black underside. In the North American profile cited, larvae reach roughly 6 mm and adults up to roughly 7.5 mm.
The species is native to Europe. It has been used in North America and New Zealand as a biological-control herbivore of Canada thistle.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: An atmospheric river is a long, narrow band of water vapor carried by wind through the lower atmosphere. When it reaches land and rises over mountains, it can release that water as rain or snow.
glance: A relatively long, narrow region of enhanced water-vapor transport
Rain or snow, when moist air is forced up over mountains
Weaker events can bring rain and snowpack that support water supplies
Strong or slow-moving events can bring extreme precipitation, flooding, landslides and debris flows

sections.heading: A corridor of moving vapor
body: Atmospheric rivers are relatively long, narrow regions of the atmosphere where the transport of water vapor is enhanced. They carry much of the water vapor that moves outside the tropics, and they can carry moisture from lower latitudes toward higher latitudes. The name does not mean a river of liquid water in the sky. The water is vapor, concentrated primarily in the lower atmosphere.

Winds transport the vapor, so both the moisture content of the air and the wind contribute to how much is moved. A measure called integrated vapor transport is a useful way to represent the combined movement of atmospheric water vapor by the wind.

sections.heading: What happens at landfall
body: When the moist air reaches land and is forced upward over mountains, it cools and the vapor condenses. That can release the transported water as rain or snow.

sections.heading: Water supply and hazards
body: Atmospheric rivers vary greatly in size, strength, shape and impacts, and they are not all hazardous. Weaker ones can provide beneficial rain and snowpack that support water supplies. Strong or slow-moving ones can produce extreme precipitation, flooding, landslides and debris flows.
The effects of any one event depend on its intensity, how long it lasts, where it makes landfall, the terrain and how vulnerable the watershed is.

sections.heading: How they are studied
body: Observations from satellites, radar, aircraft and weather models are used to study atmospheric rivers and to forecast them.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A pyrocumulonimbus, or pyroCb, is a thunderstorm-like cloud produced by an intense fire. A strong one acts as a chimney that can carry smoke into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere.
glance: A thunderstorm-like cloud produced by an intense fire
Heat, smoke and moisture lofted by the fire
The upper troposphere and lower stratosphere
A dark, smoke-fed lower column with a brighter ice-cloud tower or anvil above

sections.heading: How the cloud builds
body: A pyrocumulonimbus is produced when an intense fire lofts enough heat, smoke and moisture to drive deep convection. The result is a thunderstorm-like cloud. It can grow from an earlier stage, pyrocumulus convection above a wildfire, but not every pyrocumulus becomes a large pyrocumulonimbus.
The visible cloud may show a dark lower column fed by smoke, with a brighter tower or anvil of ice cloud above it.

sections.heading: A chimney for smoke
body: A strong pyroCb acts as a vertical chimney. It carries smoke through the troposphere and can inject it into the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere. Smoke that reaches the stratosphere can spread over very large distances and stay aloft longer than smoke confined to the lower troposphere.

sections.heading: Not every large fire makes one
body: Whether a pyroCb occurs, and how high it injects smoke, depends on the fire and the surrounding atmosphere acting together. A large wildfire does not automatically produce a smoke plume in the stratosphere.

sections.heading: What researchers are still investigating
body: Researchers are investigating which fires produce pyroCbs, what controls direct injection into the stratosphere and the size of the plume, and how the injected smoke changes the composition of the upper atmosphere and its radiation.
Smoke injection by pyroCbs is studied with remote sensing from aircraft, in-situ instruments, ground-based sensors, satellites and atmospheric models.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The green orchid bee is a metallic green bee about the size of a honey bee. Males gather fragrant compounds from their surroundings, store them in their hind legs and release the perfume in courtship displays.
glance: Central America; naturalized in South Florida

sections.heading: What it looks like
body: The green orchid bee, Euglossa dilemma, is an orchid bee in the family Apidae and the tribe Euglossini. Adults are metallic green and roughly the size of a honey bee, with dark transparent wings and a long tongue.

The sexes differ in their legs. Males have brush-like front tarsi and enlarged hind tibiae. Females do not have the fragrance-storing tibiae. They have pollen-carrying structures called corbiculae on their hind legs instead.

sections.heading: Collecting and storing perfume
body: Male orchid bees collect fragrant volatile compounds from sources in their environment, including flowers, fungi and decaying vegetation. A male gathers the material with the mop-like or brush-like structures on his front tarsi and transfers it into his enlarged hind tibiae. A hole in each hind tibia opens into a spongy compartment inside, which stores the collected compounds.
Males release the resulting blend of perfume during courtship displays at perching sites, fanning their wings as they display.

Perfume chemistry and collecting behavior can differ between closely related orchid bee species, and they contribute to sexual signals that are characteristic of each species. That does not mean perfume guarantees a mating.

sections.heading: Where it lives and nests
body: Euglossa dilemma belongs to a lineage of tropical orchid bees of the New World. It occurs in Central America and is established as a naturalized species in South Florida. Females build nest cells of resin in enclosed cavities and supply their developing young with nectar and pollen.

Orchid bees are important pollinators in the Neotropics. The green orchid bee can collect fragrance from sources other than orchids, and it does not need a matching orchid to persist in Florida, where it is naturalized.

2026-08-18-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Onymacris unguicularis is a darkling beetle of the Namib Desert. In fog it climbs to a dune crest, tips head-down into the wind and drinks the water that collects on its back.
glance: Head-down on a dune crest, in fog-laden wind

sections.heading: Fog in a very dry desert
body: Onymacris unguicularis is a darkling beetle in the family Tenebrionidae that lives in the Namib Desert. The Namib is extremely arid, and fog is an important source of water for the organisms there. During fog at night, the beetle can emerge from the sand and fog-bask outside its usual daytime period of activity.

sections.heading: The head-down stance
body: During fog the beetle climbs to the crest of a dune and positions itself in the fog-laden wind. There it takes up a characteristic head-down stance. Fog water collects on its upper surface and runs toward the mouth, where the beetle drinks it.

sections.heading: A steady runoff
body: Experimental observations found a steady flow of water from the beetle's wing covers (elytra), not occasional cascades. A steady runoff can provide water during short fog-basking periods. It also lets the beetle, which is exposed on the dune ridge, leave if it is disturbed.

sections.heading: What the evidence does not show
body: The evidence does not show that this beetle is the most efficient fog collector possible. It also does not show that every desert beetle collects fog in this way.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Lightning is often observed during explosive volcanic eruptions. Collisions among ash particles, and among water and ice particles that form higher in the plume, can generate and concentrate electrical charge.
glance: Often during explosive eruptions, commonly with ash-plume formation
Near the vent, in the rising column and in the spreading umbrella region
Size-dependent triboelectrification of colliding ash particles
Collisions among water and ice particles when they form aloft
Lightning patterns and rates can give information about plume activity that is otherwise obscured

sections.heading: Where the lightning occurs
body: Lightning is often observed during explosive volcanic eruptions and is commonly associated with the formation of an ash plume. It can occur in three parts of the plume: the gas-thrust region near the vent, the rising, convecting column, and the umbrella region where the plume spreads.

sections.heading: How ash builds charge
body: Collisions and clustering among ash particles can generate and concentrate electrical charge in a volcanic plume. A principal charging pathway is triboelectrification, in which colliding ash particles become charged in a way that depends on their size.
Turbulence can concentrate particles into denser patches. That increases the opportunities for collisions and creates favorable conditions for charge to concentrate.

sections.heading: More than one mechanism
body: Several processes can contribute to the electrification of a plume: the fragmentation of magma, the convection and buoyancy of particles, and the formation of hydrometeors, the particles of water and ice in the plume. When water and ice form aloft, collisions among those particles can add an ice-related charging pathway.

sections.heading: What lightning can tell observers
body: The patterns and rates of volcanic lightning can provide monitoring information about plume activity that is otherwise obscured. The relationship is not fixed. It depends on conditions in the plume and on the charging mechanisms at work.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The diabolical ironclad beetle is a flightless beetle of western North America whose wing covers form a solid shield. Layered material and a jigsaw-shaped seam help it resist crushing, and in compression tests it withstood about 39,000 times its body weight.

Beneath rocks, or squeezed between tree bark and trunk

sections.heading: A beetle that cannot fly
body: The diabolical ironclad beetle, Phloeodes diabolicus, is flightless. Its elytra, the wing covers that derive from the forewings, have evolved into a solid protective shield. The adult is about one inch long.

Adults occur in western North America, including the U.S. Southwest and the foothills of the Sierra Nevada. They can live beneath rocks or squeezed between the bark and trunk of a tree. The beetle feeds on fungi associated with tree bark.

sections.heading: How the armor is built
body: The elytra consist of layers of chitin in a protein matrix. The two halves meet along a seam down the middle, the medial suture, which is shaped like interlocking jigsaw-puzzle pieces. Rodlike microtrichia on the surfaces of the interlocking blades are interpreted as friction pads that resist slipping.

sections.heading: What happens under load
body: Under compression, the layered material inside the interlocking blades separates progressively, layer from layer, instead of failing through a sudden, catastrophic neck fracture.

Compression testing found that the beetle can withstand a force of about 39,000 times its body weight. X-ray microtomography at the Advanced Light Source made the internal architecture and the interlocking regions visible during compression. Researchers also built composite joints inspired by the beetle to test the engineering value of the geometry and the layering.

sections.heading: The larva
body: A larval stage of Phloeodes diabolicus has been formally described. The infographic gives no exact length of development and no seasonal schedule for the species.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Red sprites are short-lived red electrical discharges high above thunderstorms. They are connected to lightning, but not every lightning flash produces one.
glance: Short-lived red electrical discharges above thunderstorms
Typically roughly 70 to 80 kilometers above thunderstorms
Long vertical tendrils, jellyfish-like forms and grouped events
The International Space Station, aircraft, spacecraft and distant ground viewpoints

sections.heading: Where sprites appear
body: Sprites typically begin roughly 70 to 80 kilometers above thunderstorms and can develop downward over tens of kilometers. The thunderstorm sits in the troposphere. The sprite is high above it, in the stratospheric and mesospheric region. Sprites are upper-atmosphere events, distinct in location and form from the ordinary lightning that occurs in or below the thunderstorm.
Sprites can show long vertical tendrils and jellyfish-like forms, and they can occur as grouped events. Each one lasts only milliseconds.

sections.heading: How lightning sets them off
body: Sprites are connected to lightning. In a conventional explanation, some positive cloud-to-ground lightning strokes are followed by brief thunderstorm electric fields, and those fields produce a streamer-like breakdown of the air in the middle atmosphere. The link is conditional. Not every lightning flash produces a sprite.

sections.heading: Why they are hard to see
body: Sprites are difficult to see from the ground because the parent thunderstorm often blocks the view. They have been recorded from the International Space Station, aircraft, spacecraft and distant ground viewpoints, with low-light or high-speed cameras.
Airborne sprite research has used high-speed imaging and slitless spectroscopy to study their spatial, temporal and spectral structure.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The New Zealand glow-worm, or titiwai, is the larva of a fungus gnat, not a worm. It hangs sticky silk lines from a ceiling or overhang and glows blue-green to lure small insects into them.

sections.heading: A gnat larva, not a worm
body: The New Zealand glow-worm is the insect species Arachnocampa luminosa. The glowing animal is the larva of a fungus gnat, not a worm. It is found only in New Zealand, in still, dark, damp caves and forest habitats that have suitable prey. Larvae can reach about 30 millimeters before they pupate.
The life cycle runs through egg, larva, pupa and winged adult fungus gnat. The larva is the luminous, predatory stage and the main feeding stage.

sections.heading: Building the fishing lines
body: The larva lives suspended in a horizontal tube of mucus attached to a ceiling or overhang. It secretes silk through labial glands associated with its mouthparts and lowers multiple vertical fishing lines from the tube. The lines carry regularly spaced droplets of sticky mucus that trap small insects.
The droplets are mostly water. They are hygroscopic and contain dissolved elements and peptide material. They differ from the glue droplets of orb spiders.
The length of the lines varies with habitat and exposure to wind. Longer lines are favored in still, moist cave conditions and shorter lines in forest habitat that is prone to wind.

sections.heading: Lure, catch and haul
body: A light organ near the larva's rear end gives off blue-green light. The organ is associated with the Malpighian-tubule system. The glow works as a lure for prey, and the hanging sticky lines do the catching. After prey sticks to a line, the larva can use its mouthparts to haul the line up and reach the prey.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A sea star moves on many soft tube feet connected to its water vascular system. Each foot extends or retracts as fluid volume changes, and separate secretions let it stick to a surface and release again.

In rows along the oral underside of each arm

sections.heading: The water vascular system
body: Sea stars are echinoderms. The adult body typically has a five-part radial plan around a central axis. The water vascular system includes a central ring canal and radial canals that extend along the arms. A structure called the madreporite lies on the aboral surface, the side away from the mouth, and connects to the ring canal through a stone canal.

sections.heading: How a tube foot extends
body: Rows of tube feet project along the oral underside of each arm and connect to the radial canals. Each tube foot is controlled by a bulb-like ampulla, and the foot extends or retracts as the volume of fluid changes. The water vascular system provides the hydrostatic force used in moving and in handling prey.

sections.heading: Sticking and letting go
body: Tube feet use specialized adhesive cells to attach temporarily to underwater surfaces. Attachment and release use different secretions. That allows a foot to stick and detach rapidly, again and again, as the animal moves.

sections.heading: Many feet, several jobs
body: A sea star does not walk on a small set of jointed legs. It coordinates many tube feet to move across the seabed. Tube feet also contribute to feeding, attachment, and sensing by touch and by chemistry.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Acanthaspis petax is an assassin bug whose nymphs carry a backpack of ant carcasses. In an experiment, jumping spiders responded as predators less often to bugs wearing the backpack than to bugs with it removed.
glance: Carcasses of its preferred ant prey
From the Lake Victoria region of East Africa

sections.heading: A backpack of ant carcasses
body: Acanthaspis petax is a species of assassin bug, in the family Reduviidae and the true-bug order Hemiptera. It covers itself with a mask, or backpack, made from the carcasses of the ants it prefers as prey. The bug shown in the infographic is a juvenile nymph carrying this camouflage.

sections.heading: The jumping-spider experiment
body: The experiment used bugs and jumping spiders from the Lake Victoria region of East Africa. Researchers compared bugs with the carcass mask intact against bugs with the mask removed, using live bugs or lures. Jumping spiders made predatory responses significantly more often to the naked bugs than to the masked ones.

Jumping spiders are predators guided by vision. The experiment supports a cautious reading: the carried mask can hinder recognition by these spiders. It does not show that the mask gives perfect protection against every predator.

sections.heading: Backpacks in related bugs
body: A separate refereed study in the journal Animal Behaviour documents backpack camouflage in the nymphs of West African Acanthaspis and Paredocla assassin bugs. It gives wider context for the behavior. It is not proof about every Acanthaspis species.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The reddish-pink flash on a male Anna's hummingbird comes from structure, not from pigment alone. Stacked layers of melanosomes, keratin and air inside the feather's barbules reflect selected wavelengths, and the color and brightness change with the angle of light and view.
glance: Within the barbules, small branches off the feather's barbs
Structural, and strongly dependent on angle

sections.heading: From feather to barbule
body: The male Anna's hummingbird, Calypte anna, has bright reddish-pink iridescent feathers on its crown and its gorget, the throat patch. A feather branches from a central shaft, the rachis, to barbs and then to smaller barbules. The structures that produce the iridescence are located within the barbules.

sections.heading: Layers that reflect light
body: The iridescent barbules contain stacks of melanosomes, which carry the pigment melanin, embedded in keratin and separated by it. Internal air spaces create strong contrasts in refractive index.

These repeating layers of melanosome, keratin and air act as an optical multilayer. Its reflections reinforce selected wavelengths and produce structural color. The infographic's comparison between absorption by pigment alone and structural reflection is qualitative. Melanin contributes to the optical system, but the nanoscale organization is essential to the iridescent effect.

sections.heading: Why the color flashes
body: The reflected color and brightness depend strongly on the angle of the light and the angle of view. A feather can flash brightly at the right angle and become much darker when it is rotated away from it. In measured Anna's hummingbird feathers, changing the angle of incidence shifted the reflected color toward shorter wavelengths, which is characteristic of an optical multilayer.
The far end (distal portion) of a gorget feather carries the strongest reddish-pink reflection. The reflecting barbules are oriented to produce a directional, roughly mirror-like glint.

sections.heading: Differences among hummingbirds
body: Hummingbirds vary in melanosome shape, stacking and air content, and in the dimensions of the feather layers. This variation helps produce diverse iridescent colors. Not every hummingbird feather has bright structural color.

2026-08-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The globe skimmer is a dragonfly found nearly worldwide. Its aquatic nymph catches small prey by shooting out a jointed lower lip, closing a pair of palpi around the prey and pulling it back toward the mouth.
glance: Fresh water, including temporary rain pools

sections.heading: A dragonfly found nearly worldwide
body: Pantala flavescens is commonly called the globe skimmer or wandering glider. Its distribution is nearly global and primarily circumtropical. Globe skimmers need fresh water to reproduce. Their larvae can develop in temporary rain pools before emerging as migratory adults. The enlarged base of the adult's hindwing contributes to efficient gliding during long-distance migration.

sections.heading: The nymph and its mask
body: The nymphs are aquatic predators. They catch small aquatic prey with a modified labium, or lower lip, that moves rapidly. This extendable labium has a postmentum, a prementum and a pair of labial palpi, connected by joints.
The palpi carry setae and sensilla. These are visible sensory structures, but exactly what they do should not be overstated.
Globe skimmer nymphs have been collected from natural and artificial ponds. Mosquito larvae can be among the small aquatic prey they capture.

sections.heading: How a strike unfolds
body: During a strike the jointed labium unfolds and extends forward. The paired palpi open and then close around the prey. The labium then pulls back, bringing the captured prey toward the mouth. High-speed video documents this rapid extension and retraction underwater.

2026-09-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Coral fluorescent proteins absorb higher-energy light and emit lower-energy light at a longer wavelength. The pigments differ among species and individuals, and their precise biological roles are not fully resolved.
glance: Host pigments like green fluorescent protein

sections.heading: Proteins that shift light
body: Many coral host pigments are similar to green fluorescent protein. The fluorescent forms span cyan, green and red emission colors. A fluorescent protein absorbs higher-energy light and emits lower-energy light at a longer wavelength.

Non-fluorescent chromoproteins can absorb visible light strongly while producing little or no fluorescence. They commonly contribute purple-blue coloration. The pigment types and their expression can differ among coral species and among individuals of the same species.

sections.heading: Pigments inside coral tissue
body: Coral tissue can contain photosynthetic symbionts, dinoflagellates that live inside cells of the endodermis. The host's fluorescent pigments occupy tissue locations that depend on the species, and they modify the light environment around the symbionts.

Host pigments can alter the local light field inside coral tissue. Proposed effects include protection from light or enhancement of light, depending on species and environment. Their precise biological roles are not fully resolved.

sections.heading: A study of deep Hawaiian corals
body: One study examined four Hawaiian mesophotic Leptoseris species at 65 to 125 m. Cyan and green fluorescence was located mainly in the coenosarc, the oral disc, or both. Fluorescent and non-fluorescent colonies occurred together across the depths investigated. Cyan fluorescent protein was more common at the shallower sampled depths, green fluorescent protein at the deeper ones, and both occurred at intermediate sampled depths.

Fluorescent and non-fluorescent corals in the study had similar symbiont genotypes, abundance and pigments, and similar photosynthetic efficiency, photosynthetic rates and chlorophyll excitation spectra. Those fluorescent proteins were therefore unlikely to significantly enhance symbiont photosynthesis in the corals studied.

2026-09-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Colobopsis explodens is a Southeast Asian ant. In close fights, a minor worker can rupture its own body wall and cover an opponent with sticky yellow secretion, an irreversible act of self-sacrifice.
glance: Colobopsis cylindrica species group, Southeast Asia
Bright yellow and sticky, from mandibular-gland reservoirs

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: Colobopsis explodens is an ant in the Southeast Asian Colobopsis cylindrica species group. It was described from material associated with Borneo, Thailand and Malaysia. Field observations were made in lowland dipterocarp rainforest in Brunei, where colonies occupied trees and wooden nest cavities.

sections.heading: Minor and major workers
body: Minor workers are reddish-brown and about 4 to 7 mm long. They carry enlarged mandibular-gland reservoirs that extend through much of the body. Major workers have enlarged, plug-shaped heads and can block the entrances to wooden nests. This defensive behavior is known as phragmosis.

sections.heading: How the rupture works
body: During close territorial conflict, a minor worker can rupture the outer wall of its gaster. The behavior is called autothysis. It is irreversible and self-sacrificial. The rupture releases the bright yellow, sticky contents of the mandibular-gland reservoirs onto an arthropod opponent, which helps restrain, repel or kill the opponent.

The defense works at close contact. It is not a fireball or a pressure explosion: the gaster ruptures and transfers sticky secretion to the opponent. The rupture belongs to minor workers. It should not be read as something every caste does or as the outcome of every encounter.

sections.heading: What the secretion contains
body: Chemical analyses found a complex mixture of volatile compounds in the reservoir contents of minor workers, including alkanes, carboxylic acids and phenolic compounds. Researchers proposed that phenolic constituents, which are likely irritant and antibiotic, may contribute to defense against arthropod opponents or microbes. The functions of many individual compounds remain unresolved.

2026-09-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Frost heave is the lifting of the ground as layers of ice, called ice lenses, grow in freezing soil. The lenses are fed by liquid water that moves toward the freezing zone, and they can lift and crack pavement.
glance: Large vertical ground displacement produced by growing ice lenses
Horizontal layers of solid ice in the soil
Liquid water migrating toward a freezing zone
Freezing conditions, an available water supply and frost-susceptible soil

sections.heading: How ice lenses grow
body: Frost heave is driven chiefly by liquid water moving toward a freezing zone, and by the formation and thickening of segregated ice lenses. It is not merely a matter of water freezing in place in the pores of the soil.

Frozen soil can contain both frozen and unfrozen water. The proportions depend on how far the temperature is depressed, on the specific surface area of the soil and on its salt content. During freezing, the unfrozen liquid water can migrate vertically and feed the growth of horizontal layers of solid ice, the ice lenses. The lenses can separate the soil above from the soil below and produce large vertical displacements of the ground.

sections.heading: Which soils heave
body: Three conditions govern damaging frost action: freezing conditions, an available supply of water and frost-susceptible soil. Not every wet or frozen soil heaves equally. Soil type and mineralogy, groundwater and flow properties, moisture content, temperature, salinity and material properties all influence how a soil freezes and how severe the heave is.

Fine-grained, frost-susceptible soils can support more damaging frost action than many coarser soils. Texture alone does not settle the matter. Susceptibility depends on the complete system of soil, water and freezing.

sections.heading: Damage to pavement and the thaw
body: Frost heave can lift and damage pavement, producing roughness, displacement and cracking above the zone where ice lenses are growing. During thaw the lenses melt, and ground that had heaved may lose support or settle unevenly. The exact outcome varies with the soil, drainage, loading and the history of freezing and thawing.

sections.heading: How freezing is tracked
body: The freeze-thaw state of pavement layers can be investigated with subsurface temperature measurements, with moisture measurements such as time-domain reflectometry, and with models that couple heat and moisture.

2026-09-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Pseudacteon tricuspis is a small South American fly whose larva develops alone inside a fire-ant worker. The larva moves into the ant's head, the head detaches, and the larva uses the head capsule as the chamber for its puparium.
glance: Phorid fly; its larva is a solitary parasitoid
Imported fire-ant workers, including the red imported fire ant, Solenopsis invicta

sections.heading: A fly much smaller than its host
body: Pseudacteon tricuspis is a phorid fly. Its larvae are solitary parasitoids of imported fire-ant workers, including the red imported fire ant, Solenopsis invicta. The adult female is a small, hump-backed fly with reduced wing venation and a specialized external ovipositor. Pseudacteon flies are much smaller than the fire ants they attack.

sections.heading: From egg to head capsule
body: A female can hover several millimeters above a fire-ant worker and make a rapid strike from the air that inserts an egg into the worker's thorax. After hatching, the first instar develops in the thorax. A later instar migrates into the ant's head. The third instar consumes tissue in the head capsule before pupariation, killing the worker.

Near pupariation, the late larva appears to release a substance, likely an enzyme, that breaks down the membranes holding the ant's exoskeleton together. This allows the head to detach. The larva uses the detached head capsule as a protective chamber for pupariation. Its hardened front plate fills the mouth opening, and paired breathing structures can extend from the puparium. The adult fly eventually emerges through the detached head capsule.

sections.heading: Use against imported fire ants
body: Pseudacteon tricuspis is native to South America. It was introduced in the United States as a biological-control agent against imported fire ants. The presence of attacking flies can interrupt fire-ant foraging by triggering defensive or evasive behavior. That does not mean the flies control colonies everywhere or completely.

2026-09-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: When provoked or attacked, a hagfish releases a slime exudate from glands along its sides. In seawater, coiled protein threads and mucus combine into a fibrous gel that traps water and can interfere with the mouth and gills of an attacking fish.
glance: Rows of glands or pores along the sides of the body
The hagfish is provoked or attacked
Coiled protein thread skeins and mucin-containing vesicles
A coherent fibrous hydrogel that traps seawater

sections.heading: Where the slime comes from
body: Hagfish release a defensive slime exudate from rows of glands or pores along the sides of the body when they are provoked or attacked. The exudate has two major functional components: coiled skeins of protein thread, and vesicles that contain mucin.

The infographic steps down in scale from the body to a pore, a gland, and then the skeins and vesicles. That sequence represents where the stored slime components originate and how they enter seawater.

sections.heading: How it deploys in seawater
body: On contact with water, the mucin vesicles swell, rupture and release mucus. Adding water alone does not fully explain how the slime deploys. Agitation and mixing stretch the mucin strands and help transmit the forces that rapidly unravel the coiled thread skeins.

sections.heading: A gel for defense
body: The hydrated mucus and the network of unraveled protein threads together form a coherent fibrous hydrogel that traps seawater. The slime functions in defense. It can interfere with the mouth and gills of attacking fish.

2026-09-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Epomis circumscriptus is a ground beetle whose larva preys on amphibians much larger than itself. The larva lures an amphibian with movements of its antennae and mandibles, evades the tongue strike and attaches with double-hooked mandibles.
glance: Moist places, with shelters such as stones and wood debris

sections.heading: The larva
body: Epomis circumscriptus is a ground beetle in the family Carabidae, and the animal featured is its larva. The species has three larval instars. Later larvae vary in color, from pale yellow-brown or whitish with black and orange markings to nearly black with orange markings. The legs and the urogomphi at the tail end are yellow, and the dark mandibles have reddish tips.

Epomis larvae and amphibians occur together in moist habitat and can share shelters such as stones and wood debris. The adults are more generalist, but the larvae are specialist predators of amphibians.

sections.heading: Luring, evading and attaching
body: The larva lures an amphibian while staying in place. It waves its antennae and makes alternating sideways movements of its antennae and mandibles. An amphibian may approach, pounce and extend its tongue toward the moving larva as if the larva were prey.

The larva can evade the tongue strike, counter toward the amphibian and attach before it begins to feed. Specialized double-hooked mandibles help it attach firmly to the amphibian's skin. The larva is much smaller than the amphibian it attacks, so the roles of predator and prey are reversed.

sections.heading: Molting between hosts
body: At the end of each larval instar, an Epomis larva leaves the amphibian and molts in a concealed place. It then seeks another amphibian host.

2026-09-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The chambered nautilus lives in the outermost chamber of a spiral shell. A tube of living tissue, the siphuncle, regulates how much liquid and gas the shell chambers hold, which changes the animal's overall density and buoyancy.
glance: The siphuncle, a tube of living tissue connecting the older chambers
Jet propulsion through a siphon near the head

sections.heading: A shell of chambers
body: Among living cephalopods, the nautilus has an external chambered shell. The animal occupies the outermost chamber, the living chamber. As it grows, it adds a new, larger living chamber and leaves the older chambers behind within the spiral shell. A tube of living tissue called the siphuncle connects the older chambers.

sections.heading: How the siphuncle changes buoyancy
body: The siphuncle regulates the relative volumes of liquid and gas in the shell chambers. That changes the animal's overall density and its buoyancy. Active transport of ions creates osmotic gradients, and these move water between the chamber liquid and the siphuncle's tissue.

When ions, and then water, leave a chamber, its gas space expands. Dissolved gases diffuse into the lower-pressure chamber and come out of solution. Overall density falls and buoyancy increases. The reverse process increases the chamber liquid, increases overall density and reduces buoyancy.

sections.heading: Buoyancy is separate from swimming
body: Buoyancy regulation sets the animal's lift or trim. Directional swimming is produced separately, by jet propulsion through a siphon near the head.
A simplified comparison with a submarine's ballast is useful, but it has a limit. The nautilus moves chamber liquid through living siphuncular tissue. It does not open a flood valve.

2026-09-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Meloe franciscanus is a blister beetle whose first-stage larvae climb vegetation and cluster together to imitate a female bee. The larvae attach to male bees drawn to the cluster, can transfer to a female bee, and are carried by her to her nest.
glance: First-instar larvae called triungulins, approximately two millimeters long
Desert sand dunes in the southwestern United States
Vegetation, male bee, female bee, host nest

sections.heading: Larvae in the dunes
body: Meloe franciscanus is a blister beetle. Its first-instar larvae are called triungulins. They are six-legged insect larvae approximately two millimeters long. In the study system in the southwestern United States, the beetle and its host, the solitary bee Habropoda pallida, live in desert sand dunes where Astragalus plants form scattered patches of resources.

sections.heading: A decoy made of larvae
body: Newly emerged triungulins climb vegetation and cooperate, forming a tight, dark cluster positioned like a perched female host bee. The cluster mimics visual features of a female bee, including her approximate size, color and perching place.

The cluster also produces a volatile chemical cue that mimics components of the female bee's sex pheromone and attracts male bees. In field tests, visual mimicry alone was not sufficient. Chemical cues were the primary means of attracting males.

sections.heading: By way of two bees
body: When a male Habropoda pallida contacts the cluster in an attempt to mate, the triungulins attach to his body as a group. They can transfer from the male to a female bee during mating or attempted mating. The female carries them to her nest, where they dismount. The complete route runs from the cluster on vegetation to a male bee, then to a female bee, then to the host nest.
Inside the nest the beetle larvae develop as nest parasites. They consume the stored pollen and nectar and the host bee's egg before completing their development.

2026-09-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Opal is hydrated silica with no definite crystal structure. In precious opal, an orderly array of tiny silica spheres and voids separates white light into colors that change with the angle of the light, an effect called play-of-color.
glance: A regular three-dimensional array of similarly sized silica spheres separated by tiny voids
White, black, crystal, fire and boulder opal
Sudden or extreme changes in temperature or humidity

sections.heading: What opal is
body: Opal is hydrated silica. It is amorphous, which means it does not have a definite crystal structure. Opal can form when water that carries silica deposits it in cracks and spaces in rock as the water is lost.
Opal contains water. Because of that, sudden or extreme changes in temperature or humidity can cause the stone to crack.

sections.heading: Why precious opal shows color
body: Precious opal contains a regular three-dimensional array of submicroscopic hydrated-silica spheres of similar size, separated by tiny voids. This ordered structure of spheres and voids acts as a three-dimensional diffraction grating that separates white light into spectral colors. Interference among the diffracted wavelengths reinforces some colors and cancels others, and that produces play-of-color. The size and spacing of the spheres influence which visible wavelengths are reinforced.
Small dislocations in the ordered stacking create bounded color domains. Their appearance changes with the angle of the incoming light.
Common opal lacks play-of-color because its silica-sphere structure is not regular enough and its spheres vary in size.

sections.heading: Types of opal
body: The names white, black, crystal, fire and boulder opal describe different combinations of body color, transparency, matrix and play-of-color. Fire opal does not necessarily show play-of-color.

2026-09-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Regimbartia attenuata is a small aquatic beetle that can survive being swallowed by a frog. In laboratory trials, most swallowed beetles were excreted alive and active within six hours.
glance: 3.8 to 5.0 mm in the laboratory study
93.3% of swallowed beetles, within six hours

sections.heading: A beetle of paddy fields
body: Regimbartia attenuata is an aquatic water scavenger beetle in the family Hydrophilidae and the tribe Berosini. The adults used in the laboratory study were 3.8 to 5.0 mm long. The beetle and the frog Pelophylax nigromaculatus frequently occur together in Japanese paddy fields, where the frog can attack aquatic insects.

sections.heading: Swallowed and still alive
body: In laboratory feeding trials, frogs readily swallowed adult beetles. Even so, 93.3% of the swallowed beetles were excreted alive and active within six hours. The passage times observed were 0.1 to 3.5 hours. In the comparison the study describes, the undigested remains of other prey took more than 24 hours to be excreted.

The study's observations indicate that swallowed beetles actively moved through the esophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine toward the frog's cloacal opening. They did not pass through only as lifeless remains.

sections.heading: How it gets out is not settled
body: A frog's sphincter normally keeps its vent closed. For that reason the authors cautiously proposed that the beetle may stimulate the frog's gut to promote excretion. This is an inference. The mechanism has not been shown directly.

sections.heading: The larvae
body: All three larval instars of Regimbartia attenuata have been described, from Japanese material that was reared and collected in the field. The escape through a frog was observed in adult beetles. The description of the larvae does not show that larvae do the same.

2026-09-13-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Astraphobia, also called brontophobia, is an intense fear of thunder and lightning. It can affect children and persist into adulthood, and the anxiety can start while a person is preparing for a storm.
glance: Children, and it can persist into adulthood
Severe anxiety, dizziness, palpitations, chest tightness, nausea, trembling
Cognitive behavioral therapy, including exposure therapy

sections.heading: What astraphobia is
body: Astraphobia is an intense fear of thunder and lightning. It is also called brontophobia. It can affect children and can persist into adulthood.

The National Institute of Mental Health describes a specific phobia as intense fear or anxiety about an object or situation that is out of proportion to the actual danger. The infographic draws the same line between perceived danger and actual danger.

sections.heading: Before and during a storm
body: People with astraphobia may feel extreme anxiety while preparing for a thunderstorm. They may check weather reports again and again, or have panic attacks during a storm. Encountering a phobic trigger can produce immediate, intense anxiety.
Phobia symptoms can include severe anxiety, dizziness, palpitations, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, and a fear of fainting or losing control.

sections.heading: What avoidance takes away
body: People may take active steps to avoid the feared situation. Avoidance can keep them from activities and situations associated with the feared trigger.

sections.heading: Treatment and professional help
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment for phobias. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that confronts feared situations to help people re-engage with activities they have avoided. It may be paired with relaxation exercises. It is a supported treatment pathway, not a high-intensity challenge for a person to take on alone.
The National Institute of Mental Health and the National Health Service both point to professional help when phobia symptoms are affecting daily life.

2026-09-13-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Agoraphobia is a fear of situations where escape might be difficult or help might not be available if something goes wrong. It can involve public transport, open or enclosed spaces, lines, crowds and being outside the home alone.
glance: Escape might be difficult, or help might not be available
Public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, lines or crowds, being outside the home alone
Rapid heartbeat, rapid breathing, sweating, feeling hot, nausea
Avoiding the situations, or leaving home only with a trusted companion
Cognitive behavioral therapy, with gradual, supported exposure

sections.heading: Situations that set it off
body: Agoraphobia involves fear of situations where escape might be difficult, or where help might not be available if something goes wrong. Triggering situations can include public transport, open spaces, enclosed spaces, standing in line or in crowds, and being outside the home alone.
The infographic maps how concerns about escape or help can connect these different settings. It does not diagnose the viewer.

sections.heading: The body's alarm
body: A stressful triggering situation can produce immediate, intense anxiety and panic-like symptoms, such as a rapid heartbeat, rapid breathing, sweating, feeling hot or nausea. Phobic fear may be out of proportion to the actual danger the situation presents.

sections.heading: Avoidance and panic attacks
body: People may actively avoid triggering situations, or leave home only with a trusted companion. Avoidance may follow an association between panic attacks and the places where they occurred. Not everyone with agoraphobia has a history of panic attacks.

sections.heading: Therapy and assessment
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to help reduce anxiety and fear. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that gradually addresses feared situations and activities that have been avoided. It is a supported treatment pathway, not an abrupt challenge for a person to attempt alone.
A primary care provider or a qualified mental health professional can assess symptoms and help identify appropriate treatment options.

2026-09-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Nepenthes pitcher plants trap insects with a slippery rim. When the ridged rim is wet, a film of water lubricates it, visiting insects lose their footing, and prey can slide into the pitcher.
glance: A pitcher, a specialized leaf that works as a pitfall trap
The peristome, with radial ridges at macroscopic and microscopic scales
Nutrients from captured prey, in nutrient-poor habitats

sections.heading: A leaf that works as a pitfall
body: Nepenthes pitchers are specialized leaves that function as pitfall traps for arthropod prey. The rim of the pitcher, called the peristome, carries a hierarchy of radial ridges at both macroscopic and microscopic scales.

sections.heading: Why a wet rim is slippery
body: Rainwater and nectar can wet the peristome and create a continuous lubricating film of liquid. A wet peristome is slippery to visiting insects. A dry peristome gives them substantially better footing.

The water film disrupts the contact made by an insect's soft adhesive pads. The stepped surface, which differs with direction, reduces the effective purchase of the claws toward the inside of the pitcher.

sections.heading: What the ridges do
body: The macroscopic radial ridges help water spread radially and help form continuous slippery tracks even when little water is available. The microscopic ridges help stabilize the water film between an insect's adhesive pad and the peristome, which enables the insect to aquaplane.

sections.heading: From the rim into the pitcher
body: Once its footing fails at the rim, prey can slide inward and fall into the pitcher fluid. Captured prey contributes nutrients that the plant uses in nutrient-poor habitats.

2026-09-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Bocydium globulare is a small treehopper. An enlarged plate on its thorax, the pronotum, carries slender horns with inflated globes, and the function of the structure remains unknown.
glance: Miconia, feeding from the undersides of leaves
Tropical parts of Central and South America

sections.heading: The helmet and its globes
body: Bocydium globulare is a recognized species of the treehopper genus Bocydium, in the insect family Membracidae. In treehoppers, the pronotum is the upper plate of the first segment of the thorax. It can become enlarged into elaborate forms that differ from species to species.

In Bocydium the pronotum bears slender horns with inflated bulbs and a simple, spine-like process at the rear, arising from a central stalk. Bocydium globulare is told apart in the key to adults by the wide separation between its side globes relative to the humeral angles.
The surface of the pronotum is pitted. Each pit bears a long, narrow bristle, and the surface between the pits is covered with fine bumps.

sections.heading: The insect underneath
body: Adult Bocydium are 4.6 to 7.5 mm long. Beneath the enlarged pronotum is a small, dark, delicate body. The head has compound eyes that are not on stalks, and ocelli. The legs are ordinary walking legs, and the hind tibia carries rows of cucullate setae.

sections.heading: Where it has been found
body: Bocydium globulare has been recorded on Miconia, feeding from the undersides of leaves a few feet above the ground. The genus Bocydium is recorded across tropical parts of Central and South America, including Costa Rica, Trinidad, Venezuela, the Guianas, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil and Paraguay.

sections.heading: Growth and an open question
body: Treehoppers develop through nymphal instars before the adult stage, with no pupal stage. The shape of the pronotum begins to differentiate during nymphal development, and the final molt is associated with a major expansion of the pronotum and wings.
The biological function of the globe-bearing structure remains unknown. A resemblance to seeds or spiny fruit has been proposed, but that is a hypothesis, not an established explanation.

2026-09-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Male Maratus volans peacock spiders court females with a display that combines visual signals and vibrations carried through the surface beneath them. Mating trials found that male mating success depended on the combination.
glance: Visual signals combined with substrate-borne vibrations
Brightly colored abdominal flaps and an ornamented third pair of legs
Video for movement, laser vibrometry for vibration
Depended on visual and vibratory displays together, in experimental trials

sections.heading: Flaps, legs and vibration
body: Males of Maratus volans use a multi-modal courtship display. It combines visual signals with vibrations carried through the surface the spider stands on. During courtship, a male can unfurl brightly colored flaps around his abdomen and display them toward a female. The expanded abdominal display is coordinated with movements of his ornamented third pair of legs.
The male's abdominal bobbing is associated with vibratory signaling. Visible motion and vibration in the surface are therefore linked parts of the display.

sections.heading: A set of distinct moves
body: The documented courtship repertoire contains distinct, stereotyped behavioral elements. It is not one continuous, undifferentiated dance. Flickering of the pedipalps can appear during courtship but was also observed in other contexts, so it is not necessarily specific to courtship.

sections.heading: What the studies measured
body: Researchers characterized the courtship movements with video and measured vibration in the surface with laser vibrometry. Experimental mating trials found that male mating success depended on a combination of visual and vibratory displays.
This evidence comes from controlled observations and mating trials. It does not show that every female responds in the same way, or that any one element of the display guarantees mating.

2026-09-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Stenus comma is a small, dark rove beetle of the water's edge, with orange spots on its wing covers. Stenus beetles catch prey with a long lower lip that is shot out by hemolymph pressure and tipped with sticky pads.
glance: Mainly dark, with black legs and conspicuous orange spots on the elytra

sections.heading: A rove beetle of the water's edge
body: Stenus comma is an accepted species of rove beetle in the family Staphylinidae. No English common name is given for it here. The adult is approximately 5.5 to 6 mm long. It is mainly dark, with black legs and conspicuous orange spots on its wing covers (elytra). The species is associated with the edges of water bodies and is fairly widespread in England and Wales.

sections.heading: Hunters of springtails
body: Stenus species are obligate predators. They hunt in ground-based microhabitats and in vegetation, and prey particularly on springtails. All Stenus share large, globular, protruding compound eyes, which are associated with active predation.

sections.heading: The sticky lip
body: The prey-capture apparatus of Stenus is an elongated labium, or lower lip, that is projected toward prey by hemolymph pressure. At its tip, structures called paraglossae are modified into sticky pads that produce an adhesive secretion.

The sequence the infographic follows is a cautious one: the beetle detects prey, projects the labium, the sticky pads make contact, and the prey is drawn back toward the mouth. No exact speed is given for the strike.

sections.heading: Life history
body: Published work describes variation in the life histories of predatory Stenus beetles living in waterside environments. How long a generation of Stenus comma lasts is not established here.

2026-09-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A resting glassfrog becomes more transparent by removing about 89 percent of its red blood cells from circulation and packing them in its liver. The shift makes the frog roughly two to three times more transparent.
glance: About 89 percent, taken out of circulation
Transparency increases roughly two- to threefold

sections.heading: Why blood gets in the way
body: Transparency can function as camouflage, by reducing the scattering and absorption of light as it passes through an animal's body. Red blood cells strongly attenuate light. A circulatory system filled with blood is therefore a major obstacle to transparency in a vertebrate.

sections.heading: Packing blood into the liver
body: While resting, glassfrogs remove about 89 percent of their red blood cells from circulation and pack them within the liver. This redistribution increases a resting glassfrog's transparency by roughly two to three times. Glassfrog transparency combines see-through tissues with an active mechanism that clears respiratory pigments from those tissues.

sections.heading: Tracking the cells, and the clotting question
body: Photoacoustic imaging was used to track red blood cells in living glassfrogs. Glassfrogs can regulate the location, density and packing of their red blood cells without clotting. That capability is relevant to research on blood flow and on blood clots.

2026-09-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The long-tailed mayfly, Palingenia longicauda, spends three years as a larva in the clay banks of lowland rivers. Its winged emergence is highly synchronized and lasts only a few hours.
glance: Can reach about 10 centimeters in total size
Three years, in eroding clay riverbanks
Highly synchronized, lasting only a few hours
Include the Tisza and Raba river systems in Hungary

sections.heading: A mayfly of lowland rivers
