body: Palingenia longicauda, the long-tailed mayfly, is an insect in the order Ephemeroptera and the family Palingeniidae. It is a lowland river species, historically associated with medium-to-large European rivers. Documented surviving populations include those of the Tisza and Raba river systems in Hungary. The species can reach about 10 centimeters in total size.

sections.heading: Three years in a clay bank
body: The larvae develop for three years. They do so almost exclusively in steep outer riverbanks that are continuously eroding and made mostly of clay. Reinforcing eroding riverbanks with riprap or concrete destroys this clay-bank habitat.

Burrowing mayfly nymphs use legs adapted for digging, and tusks, in materials that include clay, and their gills help move water through the burrow. Mayfly nymphs in general are aquatic. They usually have three terminal filaments, prominent forewing pads, ten abdominal segments, and paired jointed gills on at most abdominal segments one through seven.

sections.heading: A few hours on the wing
body: After the long larval development comes a mass emergence as subimagos and imagos. It is highly synchronized and lasts only a few hours. The species is known for its synchronized reproductive swarms.

Mayfly development has no pupal stage. An aquatic nymph gives rise to a winged subimago, and the subimago may molt into the adult, or imago. Adult mayflies have two pairs of wings, with the hind wings smaller than the forewings, and two or three terminal filaments depending on the kind of mayfly.

sections.heading: Mayflies and other animals
body: Mayflies as a group transfer nutrients between aquatic ecosystems and terrestrial ones, and they provide food for many other animals. This is a statement about mayflies in general.

2026-09-17-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is brief, intense vertigo that comes with particular head movements. It arises when loose calcium-carbonate particles in the ear, called otoconia, enter one of the semicircular canals and produce incorrect position signals.
glance: Loose otoconia enter a semicircular canal and produce incorrect positional signals
Brief, intense vertigo with particular head movements
Rolling over in bed, bending down, looking up or over a shoulder
Maneuvers such as the Epley maneuver move particles back toward the utricle

sections.heading: How the balance organs signal movement
body: The semicircular canals are three fluid-filled ducts arranged roughly at right angles to one another. Fluid motion in a canal bends the cupula and the sensory stereocilia, and that signals head rotation.
The utricle and saccule contain calcium-carbonate particles called otoconia. These help signal head position and linear movement relative to gravity.

sections.heading: When otoconia enter a canal
body: In BPPV, loose otoconia can enter a semicircular canal. There they produce incorrect positional signals, which cause brief, intense vertigo with particular head movements. Common movements that provoke it include rolling over in bed, bending down, and looking up or over a shoulder.
Posterior-canal BPPV is the most common canal form. Diagnosis typically uses a head-hanging positional test that looks for characteristic positional nystagmus.

sections.heading: Moving the particles back
body: Canalith-repositioning maneuvers, such as the Epley maneuver, use a sequence of head and body positions to move the displaced particles out of the canal and back toward the utricle. Therapeutic repositioning maneuvers have better outcomes than no treatment or sham maneuvers. Symptoms may still persist or recur, and some people need repeat treatment.

sections.heading: Other causes, falls and stroke warnings
body: Dizziness has many causes, so an evaluation distinguishes BPPV from other inner-ear, medication-related, cardiovascular and brain causes. The infographic is general education, not a diagnosis.

Sudden dizziness or loss of balance together with trouble walking, a vision change, one-sided weakness or numbness, confusion, speech difficulty or a sudden severe headache can be a stroke warning and requires immediate emergency help.
Fall-risk precautions and individualized clinical guidance are appropriate when dizziness makes walking, stairs, bathing, driving or exercise unsafe.

2026-09-17-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when the upper airway becomes repeatedly narrowed or blocked during sleep, reducing or stopping airflow. A sleep study can identify the type and severity of apnea, and the appropriate treatment depends on the person.
glance: The upper airway is repeatedly narrowed or blocked during sleep
Breathing that starts and stops, frequent loud snoring, gasping for air
Sleepiness and tiredness that can impair learning, focus and reaction
A sleep study can identify the apnea type and severity
Individualized lifestyle changes, PAP, custom oral appliances, selected surgical procedures

sections.heading: How the airway is blocked
body: Obstructive sleep apnea occurs when the upper airway becomes repeatedly narrowed or blocked during sleep, which reduces or stops airflow. The tongue and soft palate can move backward during sleep and contribute to the obstruction.
This differs from central sleep apnea. Obstructive apnea involves a blockage of the airway, whereas central sleep apnea results from missing brain signals that are needed to breathe.

sections.heading: Clues by night and by day
body: Common clues during sleep include breathing that starts and stops, frequent loud snoring and gasping for air. Daytime sleepiness and tiredness can impair learning, focus and reaction.

Risk factors and associations include older age, obesity, a large tongue or tonsils, family history, some endocrine disorders, smoking and alcohol use. These factors do not by themselves diagnose obstructive sleep apnea.

sections.heading: Evaluation and sleep testing
body: A clinical evaluation considers symptoms, risk factors and family history, and a sleep study can identify the type of apnea and its severity. The guidance for people with possible symptoms is to discuss them with a healthcare provider. A sleep study may be needed, especially when daytime sleepiness affects attention or reaction.

sections.heading: Treatment and follow-up
body: CPAP provides continuous air pressure through the nose, the mouth or both to help keep the airway open during sleep. A clinical practice guideline from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine says positive airway pressure (PAP) treatment should follow a diagnosis established with objective sleep apnea testing. PAP therapy requires education, troubleshooting, monitoring and follow-up, not a one-size-fits-all setup.
Treatment options can include individualized lifestyle changes, PAP, custom oral appliances and selected surgical procedures. The appropriate choice depends on the person and on clinical assessment.
Untreated sleep apnea can impair concentration, decision-making, memory and behavior. It is associated with an increased risk of stroke, heart attack and other serious problems.

2026-09-17-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Kidney stones are solid build-ups of crystals formed from substances present in urine. A stone can move from a kidney into a ureter and obstruct the flow of urine, and treatment is chosen according to the stone and its effects.
glance: Solid crystal build-ups formed from substances present in urine
High urinary levels of calcium, oxalate and phosphorus
Back, side, lower abdomen or groin; it may come in waves
Shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy
Adequate fluid intake helps prevent many stones; the amount is individualized

sections.heading: How a stone forms and moves
body: Kidney stones are solid crystal build-ups formed from substances present in urine. High levels of calcium, oxalate and phosphorus in the urine can contribute to their formation. A stone can move from a kidney into a ureter and obstruct the flow of urine.

sections.heading: Pain and other symptoms
body: Kidney-stone pain may be felt in the back, side, lower abdomen or groin, and it may come and go in waves. Blood in the urine, painful or urgent urination, nausea, vomiting, fever, chills and an inability to urinate can also occur with kidney stones. These require healthcare assessment.

sections.heading: Laboratory tests and imaging
body: Urinalysis can detect blood, stone-forming minerals, white blood cells or bacteria, and blood tests can identify elevated mineral levels. CT can show a stone's size and location and whether it blocks the urinary tract. Ultrasound can help identify stones and blocked urinary flow.

sections.heading: How treatment is chosen
body: Treatment is selected according to the stone's size, location and composition, the symptoms, and whether urine flow is blocked. Some small stones pass without a procedure. Larger, painful or obstructing stones may require urgent treatment.
The categories of procedure include shock-wave lithotripsy, ureteroscopy and percutaneous nephrolithotomy. When flow is blocked, a ureteral stent or a nephrostomy may restore drainage.

sections.heading: Preventing more stones
body: Analyzing a recovered stone and, when indicated, testing urine can help guide prevention according to the type of stone and the individual's risk. Adequate fluid intake helps prevent many kidney stones. The appropriate amount, and any dietary changes, are individualized for a person's health conditions and stone type.

2026-09-17-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when pressure inside a narrow, rigid passage in the wrist squeezes the median nerve. It produces numbness, tingling, pain or weakness, and symptoms commonly begin gradually.
glance: The median nerve, inside the carpal tunnel at the wrist
Thumb, index finger, middle finger and thumb-side half of the ring finger
May be worse at night or during prolonged activities with the wrist bent
A neutral-position night wrist splint and modification of aggravating activities
Carpal tunnel release divides the transverse carpal ligament

sections.heading: A narrow passage in the wrist
body: The carpal tunnel is a narrow, rigid passage in the wrist, bounded by the carpal bones and the transverse carpal ligament. The median nerve and the tendons that flex the fingers pass through it. Carpal tunnel syndrome occurs when pressure within this confined passage squeezes the median nerve, producing numbness, tingling, pain or weakness.

Sensation carried by the median nerve in the hand includes the thumb, index finger, middle finger and the thumb-side half of the ring finger. The nerve also controls muscles around the base of the thumb.

sections.heading: How symptoms develop
body: Symptoms commonly begin gradually. They may be worse at night or during prolonged activities with the wrist bent, and shaking or moving the hand may ease them temporarily. As nerve dysfunction becomes more severe or prolonged, hand clumsiness, dropping objects, persistent numbness, and weakness or wasting at the base of the thumb can occur.
Persistent numbness, worsening weakness or visible wasting of muscle at the base of the thumb warrants timely clinical assessment, because prolonged compression can cause lasting nerve dysfunction.

sections.heading: Associated factors
body: Carpal tunnel syndrome usually reflects a combination of factors. Associated factors include wrist anatomy or injury, pregnancy-related swelling, diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, thyroid disease, repeated hand motions, and prolonged extreme flexion or extension of the wrist. Long-term typing or computer use alone has not been established as a definite cause.

sections.heading: Evaluation and testing
body: Clinical evaluation begins with the symptom history and medical history, plus an examination of sensation and of strength at the base of the thumb. Provocative wrist maneuvers may reproduce tingling, but they do not replace the full evaluation.
When needed, nerve-conduction studies and electromyography can assess nerve and muscle function. Ultrasound can show the median nerve, and X-rays can help assess other wrist causes.

sections.heading: Splints, injections and surgery
body: Common nonsurgical options are a night wrist splint that holds the wrist in a neutral position and modification of aggravating activities. Clinician-guided nerve-gliding exercises or a corticosteroid injection may be considered for selected patients. An injection may provide temporary relief of symptoms but is not guaranteed to provide long-term benefit.

Carpal tunnel release surgery divides the transverse carpal ligament to enlarge the tunnel and reduce pressure on the median nerve. It may be considered when symptoms are severe, when testing shows significant nerve changes, or when nonsurgical care is insufficient.

2026-09-19-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Trypanophobia refers to severe fear of needles. Needle fear ranges from mild to a severe blood-injection-injury phobia, and it can lead people to avoid vaccinations or other medical care.
glance: From mild fear to severe blood-injection-injury phobia
Visible needle imagery and anticipated procedure pain
A vasovagal response that can cause dizziness or fainting
Avoiding vaccinations or other medical care
Exposure-based therapy and applied muscle tension

sections.heading: From mild fear to phobia
body: A phobia is an intense fear or aversion that is out of proportion to the actual danger. Receiving injections is a recognized example of a specific phobia. Needle fear ranges from mild fear to severe blood-injection-injury phobia, and it can lead people to avoid vaccinations or other medical care.

People with phobias may anticipate the feared situation, avoid it, feel immediate intense anxiety when they encounter it, or endure it with intense anxiety. Visible needle imagery and the pain a person anticipates from a procedure can both trigger fear.

sections.heading: The fainting response
body: Blood-injection-injury phobia can include a vasovagal response. An initial rise in heart rate and blood pressure may be followed by a drop that reduces blood flow to the brain and can cause dizziness or fainting.

Applied muscle tension is designed to raise blood pressure when the warning signs of vasovagal fainting occur. A systematic review found evidence that it reduces fainting compared with exposure alone.

sections.heading: Support during necessary care
body: Guidance for healthcare providers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists things that can reduce distress during necessary care: calm, private surroundings, preparation, support, distraction and pain-management options. Patient-centered preparation can include explaining the procedure, agreeing on coping strategies, and allowing a support person the patient has chosen when that is feasible.

sections.heading: Treatment for severe needle fear
body: Exposure-based therapy presents feared needle-related cues in a planned hierarchy. It has evidence of benefit for reducing high needle fear. It is guided by a qualified professional, not improvised during a procedure. Severe needle fear warrants referral to a mental health provider.

2026-09-19-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Nyctophobia is an intense fear of darkness and night. Within the framework of specific phobias, the fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, and it can bring physical symptoms and avoidance.
glance: Severe anxiety, dizziness, noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, nausea, trembling

sections.heading: Darkness as a feared situation
body: A phobia is an intense fear or aversion focused on a particular object or situation, and the fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger. Specific phobias can center on particular situations. The infographic applies that framework to darkness and night, the feared situation in nyctophobia.

sections.heading: Worry, alarm and avoidance
body: People with a phobia may worry excessively about encountering the trigger, avoid it, feel immediate intense anxiety when they encounter it, or endure it with intense anxiety. Avoidance is a common response to phobic fear.
Phobia symptoms can include severe anxiety, dizziness, a noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, and an intense fear of fainting or losing control.

sections.heading: What CBT involves
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment approach for phobias. It teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to reduce anxiety and fear. A university anxiety clinic, the University of Pennsylvania Center for the Treatment and Study of Anxiety, describes CBT for specific phobias as education about phobias, exposure to feared sensations and situations, and techniques that challenge unhelpful thoughts and beliefs.
Exposure therapy focuses on safely confronting feared situations so a person can re-engage with activities they have avoided. It is supported care, not an unsafe challenge for a person to try alone.

sections.heading: When professional help is relevant
body: Breathing exercises may help with relaxation. The National Health Service points to professional help when phobia symptoms affect daily life. A qualified health professional can assess symptoms and recommend appropriate treatment.

2026-09-19-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Ophidiophobia is an animal-type specific phobia in which snake-related cues can evoke fear or anxiety out of proportion to the actual danger. Noticing snakes quickly is not the same as having the phobia.
glance: Snake-related cues, which can include harmless images
Snake images drew stronger early visual responses in non-phobic adults

sections.heading: Fear out of proportion
body: Ophidiophobia is an animal-type specific phobia. Snake-related cues can evoke fear or anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger. People with a specific phobia may worry about encountering the feared object, actively avoid it, feel immediate intense anxiety when they encounter it, or endure an unavoidable encounter with intense anxiety.
Specific phobias can arise through genetic and environmental factors that interact. A traumatic encounter is one possible risk factor. It is not a required cause.

sections.heading: Snakes and early visual attention
body: In laboratory studies of adults without a phobia, pictures of snakes produced stronger early posterior visual responses than comparison pictures of other reptiles, spiders or slugs. That supports the idea that snake images capture attention rapidly. It does not show that every person is phobic.

sections.heading: Real snakes and phobic alarm
body: Real-world snake safety and phobic alarm are separate questions. Keeping distance from an unidentified wild snake is prudent. A phobic response can also be triggered by harmless images or by ambiguous snake-like shapes.

sections.heading: Avoidance and treatment
body: Avoiding feared cues can provide immediate escape, while leaving daily activities restricted and the fear untested. Psychotherapy is the primary treatment approach for phobias. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches new ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to reduce anxiety and fear.
Exposure therapy is a CBT method that confronts the underlying fear and helps people re-engage in activities they have avoided. It is planned professional care, not a forced surprise encounter.

2026-09-20-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Aviophobia is an intense fear of flying, an example of a specific phobia. Anxiety can begin with thinking about a flight, before the person encounters the situation, and the fear may be out of proportion to the actual danger.
glance: Thinking about or anticipating it can produce anxiety
Rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, sweating, trembling, nausea, dizziness, muscle tension

sections.heading: Fear and anxiety about flying
body: Fear of flying is an example of a specific phobia, an intense fear or anxiety focused on a particular situation. In a phobia, the fear may be out of proportion to the actual danger the situation poses.

The American Psychiatric Association separates fear from anxiety. Fear responds to an immediate perceived threat, while anxiety can involve anticipation of a future concern. Thinking about or anticipating a feared situation can produce anxiety before the person encounters it.

sections.heading: Alarm in the body
body: Encountering a phobic trigger can produce immediate, intense anxiety and physical alarm symptoms. These can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, sweating, trembling, nausea, dizziness, muscle tension or feeling on edge.

sections.heading: Avoiding or enduring
body: People may actively avoid a feared situation, or endure it with intense anxiety. Avoidance can interfere with daily life and activities.

sections.heading: Therapy and referral
body: Psychotherapy is the primary treatment approach for phobias. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches ways of thinking, behaving and reacting that can reduce fear and anxiety. Exposure therapy is a CBT method for phobias that focuses on confronting feared situations so people can re-engage with activities they have avoided. It is gradual and professionally guided, not forced.
A primary care provider can refer someone with mental health concerns to a qualified mental health professional for assessment and next steps.

2026-09-20-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Cynophobia is an intense fear of dogs, an example of a specific phobia. The fear is out of proportion to the actual danger, and anxiety can come on at an encounter with a dog or in anticipation of one.
glance: Rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, restlessness, difficulty concentrating

sections.heading: A fear larger than the danger
body: Fear of dogs is an example of a specific phobia. A phobia involves intense fear or aversion that is out of proportion to the actual danger the object or situation presents.
Encountering a feared object can bring immediate, intense anxiety. Anticipation can also produce anxiety before any encounter takes place.

sections.heading: How anxiety shows up
body: Anxiety can include a rapid heartbeat, shortness of breath, muscle tension, restlessness and difficulty concentrating. Symptoms vary between people.

sections.heading: Effects on daily life
body: People with phobias may actively avoid the feared object, or endure unavoidable encounters with intense anxiety. Anxiety disorders can interfere with daily activities, work, school, relationships or overall well-being.

sections.heading: Treatment tailored to the person
body: Psychotherapy is the primary treatment approach for phobias, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a well-established treatment. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that gradually addresses feared situations and can help people re-engage with activities they have avoided.
Assessment and treatment planning are matters for a qualified health professional, and they are tailored to the individual.

2026-09-22-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A snow crystal forms in a cloud that is below freezing, around a tiny airborne particle, and grows as water vapor joins it. Its shape is influenced by the temperature and moisture it meets as it falls.
glance: In below-freezing clouds, around tiny airborne particles
Water vapor joins the crystal as it falls through the cloud
Plates, columns, prisms, needles or branched forms
One ice crystal, or several fused together

sections.heading: How a crystal starts and grows
body: Snow crystals form in clouds that are below freezing, around tiny airborne particles. As a crystal falls through the cloud, water vapor joins the growing ice. The way water molecules are organized in ice gives the crystal its six-sided structure.

sections.heading: Why the shapes differ
body: Temperature and atmospheric moisture influence whether a snow crystal grows as a plate, a column, a prism, a needle or a branched form. Changes in temperature or moisture along a crystal's path can change how its arms grow and branch, while the sixfold organization is preserved.

The arms of one crystal can resemble one another because they experience the same local atmospheric conditions as the crystal grows. Different paths through a cloud expose crystals to different growth histories, so their detailed forms vary.

sections.heading: Crystals and snowflakes
body: A snowflake may be a single ice crystal, or it may be an aggregate of several ice crystals fused together.

2026-09-22-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Myrmeleon immaculatus is an antlion whose larva digs a funnel-shaped pit in dry, loose soil and waits buried at the bottom for ants and other small arthropods.
glance: North and Central America; most often encountered in the United States east of the Mississippi River
Roughly three-quarters to two inches wide, about one-half inch deep
About one inch long, active at night

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: Myrmeleon immaculatus is a species in the antlion family, Myrmeleontidae, and the insect order Neuroptera. It is native to North America and Central America and is most often encountered in the United States east of the Mississippi River.
Females place their eggs in dry, powdery or sandy soil. Often this is sheltered loose soil near foundations or the bases of trees, where an overhang or the tree canopy reduces flooding.

sections.heading: Digging the pit
body: The larva is gray-brown and slightly hairy, with armor-like plating, six legs and enlarged, sickle-shaped mandibles. It moves backward through loose soil in a spiral and flips soil away with its head and mandibles to dig a funnel-shaped pit. Observed pits are roughly three-quarters to two inches wide and about one-half inch deep. Wet soil impedes construction, and rain can destroy pits.

sections.heading: How the trap works
body: The larva waits buried at the bottom of the pit with its mandibles exposed. The loose, dry grains give small arthropods poor traction. When prey tries to climb out, the larva flicks its head and mandibles rapidly, throwing sand onto the slope. This can create small landslides toward the larva.

The larva seizes the prey with its mandibles, injects digestive secretions and extracts the liquefied tissues. It discards the remains outside the pit. It is a carnivorous sit-and-wait predator of ants and other small arthropods. It is part of forest and landscape food webs, and it does not harm nearby plants.

sections.heading: From larva to adult
body: The species passes through three larval instars. Before it pupates, the final instar spins silk that binds soil particles into a cocoon. The adult is a slender-bodied insect about one inch long, active at night, with net-veined, unspotted wings.

2026-09-22-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Biological soil crust is a living community on the surface of dryland soil. Its organisms bind soil particles into a continuous crust that helps resist erosion, and it can be broken by foot traffic, bicycles and vehicles.
glance: A living surface community on dryland soil
Cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses, green algae, microfungi and other bacteria
Binds soil particles, which helps resist erosion by wind and rain
Foot traffic, bicycles and vehicle tracks
Climate, soil conditions, disturbance severity and timing

sections.heading: A community that binds soil
body: Biological soil crust is a living surface community that can include cyanobacteria, lichens, mosses, green algae, microfungi and other bacteria. In the crusts described for southeast Utah, the cyanobacteria are dormant while dry. When wet, they move through the soil and leave sticky fibers that bind soil particles. Binding the particles into a continuous crust helps resist erosion by wind and rain.

In the southeast Utah example, young crusts can appear flat and brown. More mature crusts may be bumpy and dark, and may include visible lichens or mosses. As biocrusts mature they can trap fine soil particles, and the nutrient and organic-matter contents of the soil can increase.

sections.heading: Crust and water
body: In one study on sandy soils of the Colorado Plateau, intact, well-developed dark biocrusts had lower runoff, low sediment loss and the highest aggregate stability. Disturbance altered those responses.

That is one study on one kind of soil. How a biocrust affects water depends on context: its stage of development, the structure of the soil and the type of disturbance can all change runoff, infiltration and sediment loss.

sections.heading: Damage and recovery
body: Foot traffic, bicycles and vehicle tracks can break biological soil crust. Once it is fragmented, the pieces can be scattered by wind or rain.

Natural recovery after disturbance depends on climate, soil conditions, how severe the disturbance was and its timing. Recovery is often dynamic, not linear. A common sequence begins with cyanobacteria and algae, followed later by lichens and bryophytes, but local conditions can alter that sequence.

2026-09-22-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Bittacus strigosus is a hangingfly, a long-legged predatory insect that hangs from plants instead of standing on them and captures insect prey with grasping feet.
glance: Clear, with heavily margined crossveins and a yellow pterostigma
Varied habitats, especially moist forests with patches of nettles

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: Bittacus strigosus is an insect in the order Mecoptera and the family Bittacidae. Members of this family have long legs and long wings and look superficially like crane flies, but they have a single grasping claw on the foot.
Bittacus strigosus is identified by its clear wings with heavily margined crossveins, a yellow pterostigma, and legs and abdomen that are dark yellow to light brown.

sections.heading: Hunting while hanging
body: Bittacus species are predators that hang from plants instead of standing on the vegetation. What is unusual is the combination: the insect hangs from foliage and captures prey with specialized grasping feet. The capture is made by the feet, not by a mantis-like strike of the front legs.

sections.heading: The grasping foot
body: Adult Bittacus hangingflies have three pairs of raptorial legs, all similar in structure. The grasping apparatus is formed by the fourth and fifth segments of the foot (tarsomeres). The foot includes a strong, modified flexor system in the pretarsus that is associated with the action of closing the claw.

sections.heading: Where it is found in Ontario
body: In Ontario, Bittacus hangingflies occur in varied habitats, especially moist forests with patches of nettles. Ontario has three species, and B. strigosus is the more common and widespread of them.

2026-09-22-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Leafcutter ants harvest fresh plant material and use it to grow a fungus, which is their primary food. Partly broken-down material is removed to refuse dumps that are separate from the garden.
glance: The fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus, in the studied system
Gongylidia, swollen tips of fungal threads
Refuse dumps, distinct from the gardens

sections.heading: From leaf to garden
body: Leafcutter ants harvest fresh plant material and use it as the growing material for a fungus they cultivate. The fungus lives in a mutualism with the ants and is their primary food source.

Workers prepare incoming plant material by chewing it, applying fecal droplets and inoculating it with fungal mycelium. Then they incorporate it into the garden. Workers also protect and maintain the fungus, supply it with nutrients and spread fungal material within the colony.

sections.heading: What the fungus does
body: In the garden system that was studied, the cultivated fungus Leucoagaricus gongylophorus is the primary degrader of the plant material. The fungus forms swollen tips on its threads (hyphae) called gongylidia, which are clustered in staphylae. In the higher-attine system that was studied, these provide food to the larvae and most of the food of adult workers.
Some of the fungal enzymes eaten with the gongylidia remain active through the ant's gut. They are deposited in fecal fluid onto freshly prepared plant material.

Resident bacteria take part in the garden ecosystem as well. In the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory study, they transformed digested plant polymers into metabolites used as amino acids and vitamins, which support the growth of the fungus and its breakdown of plant material.

sections.heading: Garden and refuse kept apart
body: Fungus gardens and refuse dumps are distinct environments within the colony. They differ in location and in chemistry, and each has its own community of microbes. Refuse consists largely of partly degraded plant material that has been removed from the productive garden. This creates a gradient across the colony system in how far the plant material has been broken down.

2026-09-22-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The Philippine leaf insect, Phyllium philippinicum, masquerades as a leaf, and its two sexes are built very differently. Females are large, flat and sedentary, while the much lighter males fly in search of them.
glance: A phylliid phasmid, or leaf insect
Large, sedentary, a strong leaf mimic; no hindwings, cannot flap
About nine times lighter, almost twice as slender, capable of flapping flight
Stick with a water-soluble glue that water activates

sections.heading: Built to look like a leaf
body: Phyllium philippinicum is a phylliid phasmid commonly called the Philippine leaf insect. Leaf insects are flattened from top to bottom and masquerade as plants. Across the family Phylliidae, leaf-like vein patterns and lobe-like extensions on the abdomen and legs contribute to the masquerade. In this species the large, sedentary adult females are strong leaf mimics because of leaf-like expansions on the sides of the abdomen and legs.

The insect is a solitary canopy-dweller and feeds on plants. Females in the laboratory culture cited moved to adjacent leaves to feed. Much of the species' natural history in the field remains incompletely known.

sections.heading: Two sexes, two bodies
body: Adult males are about nine times lighter than adult females and almost twice as slender, and they have relatively longer antennae. Adult females lack hindwings. Their extended forewings lie flat over the back, where they aid camouflage and may contribute to parachuting, but they cannot flap. Adult males have rudimentary forewings and long, fully developed, transparent hindwings that permit flapping flight.

Male leaf insects use their long antennae to detect pheromones, and they fly through the canopy searching for the comparatively sedentary females. In experiments, smaller males were more agile in the air and ascended faster than larger males. Greater body size impaired the flight performance that was measured.

sections.heading: Feet for holding on
body: Both sexes have five-segmented tarsi. The tarsal segments carry heel pads called euplantulae, and the pretarsus has a toe pad called the arolium and two claws. Female euplantulae are smooth. Male euplantulae carry maze-like ridges of cuticle, which the study interprets as suited to the broader range of surfaces a male meets while actively searching.

A landing model predicted that heavier males experience larger impact forces and a higher risk of slipping, especially on small, stiff leaves. This remains a prediction from a model, not an outcome shown in the field or one that holds everywhere.

sections.heading: Eggs that stick when wet
body: The eggs have densely packed, fiber-like structures on their surface and a water-soluble glue. Contact with water spreads the fibers and the glue, so that they conform to the surface beneath and adhesion is activated. In laboratory tests the eggs could be detached, reactivated with water and attached again, repeatedly.

2026-09-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Migraine is a neurologic health condition with recurrent episodes and symptoms that go beyond head pain. An episode can pass through several phases, but the phases and their order vary, and not every person has every phase.
glance: A neurologic health condition with recurrent episodes
Prodrome, aura in some people, headache and postdrome
Often throbbing and one-sided, but it can vary
Nausea and sensitivity to light, sound and smell
Mainly from history and physical or neurologic examination

sections.heading: Phases of an attack
body: A typical episode can include a prodrome, an aura in some people, a headache and a postdrome. The phases and their order vary, and not every person has every phase.

The prodrome may feature yawning, mood change, fatigue or food cravings before head pain. Aura occurs only in some people and may include evolving zigzags or bright spots, tingling or language difficulty. Aura is not required for migraine.

Migraine head pain is often throbbing and one-sided, but it can vary. Nausea and sensitivity to light, sound and smell can accompany it. After the headache subsides, the postdrome can include fatigue, dizziness and difficulty concentrating.

sections.heading: Pain signaling and triggers
body: Migraine-related head pain involves nerve signaling, brain chemicals and blood vessels interacting with one another. CGRP is a protein involved in pain signaling.
Possible triggers vary by person. They may include menstrual hormone changes, disrupted sleep or changes in routine. A trigger is not a universal cause.

sections.heading: How migraine is diagnosed
body: Clinicians diagnose migraine mainly from the history and a physical or neurologic examination. Imaging may be used if another condition is suspected, but it is not used routinely to prove migraine. A headache diary that records onset, duration, associated symptoms, sleep and medicines can help a clinician recognize patterns and guide care.

sections.heading: Acute and preventive care
body: Acute care may include resting in a quiet, dark room and medicines selected by a clinician, such as triptans or CGRP-targeting agents. The choice of treatment is individual. Preventive care can involve regular sleep and meals, hydration, exercise, and preventive medication selected by a clinician for suitable patients.

sections.heading: Symptoms that need prompt evaluation
body: New aura-like symptoms that come on suddenly or persist, one-sided weakness, or altered alertness warrant prompt medical evaluation. They are not to be assumed to be migraine.

2026-09-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Knee osteoarthritis involves changes that develop over time in the tissues of the knee joint, and it can affect several of them. It has no cure, but symptoms can be managed, and severity varies by person.
glance: Cartilage, bone, synovium, meniscus, and supporting ligaments and tendons
May include cartilage damage and bony edge growths called osteophytes
Movement-related pain, stiffness after rest, swelling, a sense of instability, reduced movement
Older age, previous joint injury or repetitive stress, obesity, family history
No cure, but symptoms can be managed

sections.heading: The whole joint is involved
body: The knee joint includes cartilage covering the ends of the bones, bone, synovium, meniscus, and supporting ligaments and tendons. Osteoarthritis can affect multiple joint tissues. The tissue changes develop over time and may include cartilage damage and bony growths at the edges, called osteophytes.

sections.heading: Symptoms and risk
body: Knee osteoarthritis may cause movement-related pain, stiffness after rest, swelling, a sense of instability and reduced movement. Severity varies by person.
Older age, previous joint injury or repetitive stress, obesity and family history are associated with a greater risk of osteoarthritis. Age alone does not make it inevitable.

sections.heading: Movement and self-management
body: Joint pain can reduce activity. Inactivity may weaken muscles, which could add stress on the joint. Physical activity can reduce arthritis pain and improve function, and appropriately paced movement is part of self-management. For people with overweight or obesity, weight management can reduce arthritis-related pain and disability.

sections.heading: Care with a clinician
body: A clinician can assess symptoms and discuss physical therapy, medicines, supportive devices and, if other treatments have not worked, joint replacement surgery. Osteoarthritis has no cure, but its symptoms can be managed. An educational diagram is not a personal diagnosis.

2026-09-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways of the lungs can become inflamed and narrowed, making exhaling harder. Symptoms often vary over time, and triggers vary by person.
glance: Airways can become inflamed and narrowed, making exhalation harder
Wheeze, cough, shortness of breath and chest tightness
Cold air, pollen, exercise and viral infections, varying by person
Spirometry measures how much and how fast a person exhales
No cure, but treatment and an action plan can help manage it

sections.heading: What happens in the airway
body: Asthma is a long-term condition affecting the airways of the lungs. The airways can become inflamed and narrowed, which makes exhaling harder. An asthma flare can narrow the airway through swelling or tightening. The infographic compares a wide airway with a narrowed, inflamed one.

sections.heading: Symptoms and triggers
body: Symptoms can include wheeze, cough, shortness of breath and chest tightness, and they often vary over time. Cold air, pollen, exercise and viral infections may trigger symptoms. Secondhand smoke, dust mites, air pollution and mold are possible triggers for some people. Triggers vary from person to person.

sections.heading: Measuring airflow
body: Spirometry measures how much and how fast a person exhales. A test of bronchodilator responsiveness compares airflow before and after a medicine that opens the airways.

sections.heading: The asthma action plan
body: A personalized asthma action plan, made with a clinician, guides monitoring and the response to worsening symptoms. Daily controller medicine is continued in the green and yellow zones of the plan. Reliever medicine is added for worsening symptoms, according to the personal plan.
Severe breathing difficulty, or symptoms that medicines do not relieve during an attack, need emergency help. There is no cure for asthma, but treatment and an action plan can help manage it.

2026-09-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) can develop when the lower esophageal sphincter, a barrier where the esophagus meets the stomach, is weak or relaxes inappropriately. Stomach contents can then flow into the esophagus.
glance: Stomach contents flow up into the esophagus
The lower esophageal sphincter and the diaphragm
Heartburn behind the breastbone; regurgitation into the throat or mouth
Upper GI endoscopy and esophageal pH monitoring
Antacids, H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors

sections.heading: The barrier above the stomach
body: The lower esophageal sphincter and the diaphragm form barriers at the junction of the esophagus and the stomach. They usually limit the backflow of stomach contents. GERD can develop when the lower esophageal sphincter is weak or relaxes inappropriately, which permits stomach contents to flow into the esophagus.
Reflux is the movement of stomach contents upward. It does not necessarily mean that the stomach is producing excess acid.

sections.heading: Symptoms and associated factors
body: Common symptoms include heartburn behind the breastbone and regurgitation into the throat or mouth. Not everyone has both. GERD can also present with difficulty or pain in swallowing, a chronic cough or hoarseness, but these symptoms are not specific to GERD.
Obesity, pregnancy, smoking and hiatal hernia can increase the likelihood of GERD or its symptoms. Not every person with these factors develops GERD.

sections.heading: How it is evaluated
body: Clinicians often evaluate symptoms and history first. Tests may be used for possible complications, alternative causes or persistent symptoms. Upper GI endoscopy uses a flexible camera to inspect the esophagus and upper digestive tract, and it can check for complications or other problems. Esophageal pH monitoring measures reflux-related acid exposure in the esophagus, using a catheter or a wireless capsule.

sections.heading: Lifestyle steps and medicines
body: Selected lifestyle steps may include weight loss when appropriate, avoiding an individual trigger, changing meal timing, elevating the head for nighttime symptoms and stopping smoking. Antacids may relieve mild symptoms, while H2 blockers and proton pump inhibitors reduce the production of stomach acid. Medication choices require clinical context.

sections.heading: Signs that warrant medical evaluation
body: Persistent vomiting, swallowing difficulty, signs of bleeding, unexplained weight loss or chest pain warrant medical evaluation. Chest pain should not be assumed to be reflux.

2026-09-26-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Acrophobia is a fear of heights, an example of a specific phobia. The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, though actual height hazards still require safety precautions.
glance: May bring short-term relief yet make the situation harder to face later

sections.heading: Fear at a height
body: Fear of heights is an example of a specific phobia. Phobic fear can be disproportionate to the actual danger. A height situation can trigger severe anxiety and worry, and a phobia can prompt immediate anxiety at the feared situation. Possible phobia symptoms include dizziness, a noticeable heartbeat, nausea and shaking. Symptoms vary.

sections.heading: Felt danger and actual danger
body: The fight-or-flight response can be heightened in situations that are not actually dangerous. The infographic sets its example on a guarded public skywalk. Actual height hazards require safety precautions, and protection features matter in assessing how much danger is actually present.

sections.heading: What avoidance does
body: A phobia can prompt avoidance. Avoidance may bring short-term relief yet make a feared situation harder to face later.

sections.heading: Help for a height phobia
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment for phobias. Exposure therapy can involve planned, gradual confrontation of feared situations. Someone whose phobia symptoms affect their life can seek help from a GP or a qualified mental health professional.

2026-09-26-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Claustrophobia is an intense fear of confined or enclosed spaces, such as elevators, tunnels and enclosed rooms. The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, and even thinking about a confined situation can trigger anxiety.
glance: Elevators, tunnels, enclosed rooms, or thinking about a confined situation
Sweating, trembling, shortness of breath, rapid heartbeat
Feeling dizzy, confused or afraid of losing control
Can reinforce fear and restrict daily activities
Cognitive behavioral therapy, including gradual exposure

sections.heading: Spaces that trigger it
body: Claustrophobia is an intense fear of confined or enclosed spaces. Elevators, tunnels and enclosed rooms can trigger it. Even thinking about a confined situation can trigger anxiety, and a person may anticipate a feared encounter before entering a confined space.

The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger. The same enclosed space can be physically ordinary while the danger a person feels is intense. Perceived alarm and the assessed danger of the situation are different things.

sections.heading: Physical and emotional reactions
body: Claustrophobia may produce sweating, trembling, shortness of breath and a rapid heartbeat. During an intense reaction, a person may feel dizzy, confused or afraid of losing control.

sections.heading: Avoidance, therapy and care
body: Avoiding enclosed spaces can reinforce the fear and restrict daily activities. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) explores thoughts, feelings and behavior, and develops ways of responding to the phobia. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that gradually approaches feared situations, sometimes with professional help.
A GP or a qualified mental health professional can help a person plan care when fear affects daily life.

2026-09-26-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Hemophobia is a fear of blood, a recognized example of a specific phobia. Seeing blood, or anticipating it, can trigger severe worry or immediate anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger.
glance: Dizziness, noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, nausea, trembling
Cognitive behavioral therapy and exposure therapy

sections.heading: Blood as a phobia trigger
body: Fear of blood is a recognized example of a specific phobia. A phobia involves intense fear or anxiety that is out of proportion to the actual danger. Seeing the feared object, or anticipating it, can trigger severe worry or immediate anxiety. The infographic sets its example in a supervised blood-test setting.

sections.heading: Symptoms and avoidance
body: A phobia can cause dizziness, a noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, nausea or trembling. Responses vary. People may actively avoid a feared object or situation, and avoidance can interfere with daily life.

sections.heading: Support from professionals
body: Professional support can include cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and exposure therapy. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that helps people engage with situations they have been avoiding. Treatment is planned with a qualified professional. Someone whose phobia affects their life can seek help from a GP or another health care provider.

2026-09-27-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Mysophobia, also called germophobia, is an extreme fear of germs and contamination. A public surface of uncertain cleanliness, such as a shared door handle, can be a trigger.
glance: A public surface of uncertain cleanliness
Intense anxiety, noticeable heartbeat, dizziness, trembling

sections.heading: The fear and its trigger
body: Mysophobia, also called germophobia, is an extreme fear of germs and contamination. A public surface whose cleanliness is uncertain can be a trigger. The infographic centers on an ordinary shared door handle.

A phobia can produce fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger. That does not imply that all public surfaces are germ-free, and the infographic makes no statement about contamination on any surface.

sections.heading: Symptoms and avoidance
body: Phobia symptoms can include intense anxiety, a noticeable heartbeat, dizziness and trembling. People with specific phobias may avoid feared objects or situations, and avoidance can interfere with daily life.

sections.heading: Treatment and next steps
body: Phobia treatment can help. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment for phobias. Exposure therapy is a CBT approach that helps people engage with situations they have been avoiding, and it can be planned with a qualified professional. A healthcare professional can evaluate phobia symptoms and discuss next steps if fear affects daily life.

2026-09-27-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Emetophobia is a marked fear or anxiety about vomiting, or about seeing others vomit. It may involve monitoring of body sensations and avoidance of restaurants or certain foods.
glance: Vomiting oneself, or seeing others vomit
Unfamiliar restaurant food, nausea or stomach sensations, possible illness in others
Increased heart rate, altered breathing, nausea, light-headedness
Avoiding restaurants or certain foods, date-checking, excessive cleaning, reassurance seeking
CBT, including clinician-guided exposure approaches adapted to emetophobia

sections.heading: What the fear centers on
body: Emetophobia is a marked fear or anxiety about vomiting oneself or seeing others vomit. The fear may involve uncertainty about being sick, losing control, or being unable to leave a situation.

Triggers can include unfamiliar restaurant food, nausea or stomach sensations, and noticing possible illness in other people. The restaurant scene in the infographic is illustrative. It does not show a dangerous incident.

sections.heading: Sensations and checking
body: Anxiety may bring an increased heart rate, altered breathing, nausea and light-headedness. These sensations do not by themselves prove that vomiting is imminent.
People may monitor their own internal sensations, or watch others for signs of illness. They may interpret ambiguous sensations as evidence that vomiting is near.

sections.heading: Avoidance and its effects
body: Avoidance of restaurants or certain foods, date-checking, excessive cleaning and reassurance seeking may occur. These behaviors may narrow daily life. Avoidance can bring short-term relief, yet maintain the fear and interfere with daily activities.
A phobia response can be out of proportion to the actual danger. Ordinary caution about food safety remains reasonable all the same.

sections.heading: Treatment with a professional
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), including clinician-guided exposure approaches adapted to emetophobia, is an evidence-based treatment. A qualified professional can help individualize care.
The infographic offers education. It is not a diagnosis, and it is not an instruction to induce vomiting, eat unsafe food or abandon hygiene.

2026-09-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Limacina helicina is a sea butterfly, a planktonic marine snail that swims with wings formed from its foot and collects food in a mucus web. Its delicate aragonite shell shows dissolution in seawater with low aragonite saturation.
glance: A shelled pteropod, a planktonic marine snail
Delicate aragonite calcium carbonate with an outer periostracum
Collects suspended food in a mucus web
Dissolution is favored when aragonite saturation is below one

sections.heading: A snail that swims
body: Shelled pteropods are marine snails that live as plankton. The swimming wings of a sea butterfly are a modified gastropod foot. Limacina helicina has a delicate shell of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate, with an outer layer called the periostracum.

Limacina helicina uses a mucus web to collect suspended food, and shelled pteropods can capture plankton particles in this web. Pteropods are prey in marine food webs, including for fish in the North Pacific.

sections.heading: What carbon dioxide does to seawater
body: Carbon dioxide absorbed by seawater changes its carbonate chemistry. It reduces the availability of carbonate ions and lowers aragonite saturation. When aragonite saturation is below one, the dissolution of calcium carbonate is favored. Shell building may still occur while exposure damages existing shell.
In the northeastern Pacific, coastal upwelling can bring water that is rich in carbon dioxide and low in saturation toward the surface.

sections.heading: What shell studies found
body: Puget Sound experiments with L. helicina found greater shell dissolution under conditions undersaturated in aragonite than in oversaturated treatments. Field sampling in the California Current found that severe damage to pteropod shells was correlated with the extent of aragonite-undersaturated habitat.
Observed shell damage does not establish that all exposed animals die. In the Puget Sound experiment, effects on survival varied by treatment.

2026-09-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Belostoma flumineum is a freshwater giant water bug of North America. Females of its genus glue their eggs to the backs of males, and the males carry the clutch.
glance: At least 20 mm and under 30 mm
Southern Canada and New England into parts of the southern United States
Glued to the male's back and carried by him
Aquatic predator that seizes prey with strong front legs

sections.heading: What kind of insect it is
body: Belostoma flumineum is a valid species of insect in the order Hemiptera and the family Belostomatidae. Giant water bug is the common name for that family. This species is a relatively narrow, dark giant water bug that lives in fresh water. The University of Florida identification key places it at 20 mm or more and under 30 mm.

The adult has a head, thorax and abdomen, six legs, and the folded forewings of a true bug. Its North American range extends from southern Canada and New England into parts of the southern United States.

sections.heading: Eggs carried on the father's back
body: Females of Belostoma glue their eggs to the backs of males, and an egg-bearing male carries the clutch on his back. The eggs develop and hatch into aquatic nymphs, which grow toward winged adults.
Not every giant water bug does this. Belostoma and Abedus carry eggs on the males' backs. Lethocerus deposits its eggs above the water, on vegetation or other objects.

sections.heading: Breathing and hunting
body: Giant water bugs live in freshwater ponds and ditches. They hang below the surface to breathe through a pair of appendages on the abdomen. They are aquatic predators that seize prey with strong front legs and use a piercing beak.

2026-09-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Giant kelp is a brown alga that anchors to rocky seafloor and rises on gas-filled floats to form a canopy at the surface. The forest it builds is layered from canopy to seafloor and supplies marine animals with food, shelter and nursery habitat.
glance: A brown alga, not a land plant
A branching holdfast on rocky seafloor
Cool, sunlit, nutrient-rich nearshore water with rocky substrate
Marine heatwaves, warming water, sediment runoff and unchecked grazing

sections.heading: How giant kelp is built
body: Giant kelp is a brown alga, not a land plant. It has no true roots, stems or leaves. A branching holdfast anchors it to rocky seafloor, but the holdfast is not a root system that absorbs nutrients. Flexible stipes carry leaf-like blades upward through moving water toward sunlight. Gas-filled floats called pneumatocysts buoy the blades and help form a canopy at the surface.
Kelp grows in cool, sunlit, nutrient-rich water near shore, where the bottom is rocky. Currents deliver the nutrients.

sections.heading: A forest in layers
body: Kelp forest habitat is layered vertically into the canopy, the midwater and the rocky seafloor. The canopy shelters animals, including sea otters. Fish shelter among the fronds in midwater. Holdfasts and the rocky seafloor shelter invertebrates such as sea stars, anemones and urchins.
The structure of the forest supplies food, shelter and nursery habitat to marine animals. Detached kelp fronds can become food for grazers and decomposers in the forest food web.

sections.heading: Grazing, heat and sediment
body: Sea urchins graze on kelp. Sea otters eat urchins and can help limit overgrazing. In some places, unchecked grazing can create urchin barrens. Marine heatwaves and warming water can stress kelp, and sediment runoff can reduce light or smother young kelp.

2026-09-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The orchid mantis is a white and pink predatory insect with a flowerlike outline, reported from tropical Southeast Asia. Juvenile females on leaves have been observed catching honeybees that approached as though to land on a flower.
glance: Tropical Southeast Asian habitats, including Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia

sections.heading: A flowerlike outline
body: The orchid mantis, Hymenopus coronatus, is a predatory insect in the order Mantodea and the family Hymenopodidae. It has six legs, and its forelegs are built for seizing prey.

The white and pink mantis has a broad abdomen and petal-like lobes on the femora of its middle and hind legs. Together they give it a generalized flowerlike silhouette. It does not copy one particular orchid species. In juvenile and adult females, the shape patterns of the petal-like lobes are symmetric between the left and right sides.

sections.heading: How it looks in ultraviolet
body: The white of the orchid mantis's body mainly absorbs ultraviolet light. A visual comparison found low color contrast among its body parts, which can make the insect resemble UV-absorbing flowers to hymenopteran insects such as bees. In field observations, a juvenile mantis on foliage contrasted with the nearby leaves in ultraviolet-sensitive imaging.

sections.heading: Bees that approach and are caught
body: The species is reported from tropical Southeast Asian habitats, including Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia. The juvenile mantises that were observed rested or hunted on leaves. Field observations found juvenile females on leaves and, in some cases, adult females on flowers.

Oriental honeybees were observed approaching juvenile female mantises as though to land on a flower, and the juveniles captured visiting bees with their forelegs. The infographic shows the sequence as an approach to the flowerlike visual signal, a hover near the juvenile mantis, then capture with the forelegs. This is a record of observed behavior. It is not nectar exchange, and the mantis is not pollinating anything.

sections.heading: Juveniles and adults
body: Juvenile and adult females differ in wing development and posture. Juveniles bend the abdomen upward, while an adult's wings limit that posture. The infographic's small comparison of the juvenile and the adult is qualitative and is not a timed life-cycle chart.

2026-09-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A salt marsh can gain height as flood tides bring in sediment and root material accumulates below ground. Its water-saturated, oxygen-poor soil slows decay, so some of the carbon the plants take in can stay stored underground for long periods.
glance: Marsh plants take up atmospheric carbon dioxide through photosynthesis
Sediment from flood tides plus accumulated root material
Some carbon returns to the air through plant or microbial respiration

sections.heading: How carbon enters the marsh
body: Salt marsh plants take up carbon dioxide from the atmosphere through photosynthesis and use the carbon to grow leaves, stems and roots. Dead leaves and roots can become incorporated into the marsh soil and buried there.

The carbon in salt marsh sediment may come both from marsh plants and from organic material transported in from elsewhere. A U.S. Geological Survey comparison found that the mixture of sources differed between a restoring marsh and a reference marsh.

sections.heading: Why some carbon stays buried
body: Wetland soil that is saturated with water is largely oxygen-poor, because oxygen diffuses slowly through water. Organic material decomposes more slowly in oxygen-poor soil, and that allows some carbon to remain stored underground for long periods.
Not all of the carbon is kept permanently. Some captured carbon returns to the air through the respiration of plants or microbes.

sections.heading: How the marsh gains height
body: Flood tides carry sediment into a marsh, where some of it is trapped and added to the marsh surface. Below ground, root growth and accumulated root material add material that can raise the elevation of the surface.

Whether a marsh persists as sea level rises depends on that gain in surface elevation, including the buildup of root material and the sediment left by flood tides. The ability to keep pace varies with conditions.

2026-09-29-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The giraffe weevil is a small leaf-rolling beetle from the forests of Madagascar. Males have much longer necks than females, and each female rolls a leaf into a nursery for a single egg.
glance: Forest in Madagascar, and nowhere else
Leaves of the trees it lives on
One egg in each rolled leaf

sections.heading: What it looks like
body: The adult has a black head, neck, body, legs and antennae, with red-orange hardened wing covers on its back. It is a small beetle beside the broad leaf it stands on, and the infographic shows it magnified, not life-size.

Males have much longer necks than females. The San Francisco Zoo reports a male's neck as about two to three times as long. The long neck likely helps males compete, but no single purpose has been proven.

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: The giraffe weevil is found only in forest in Madagascar. It lives on trees and feeds on their leaves, and the same leaves become the nursery for its young.

sections.heading: The rolled-leaf nursery
body: A female rolls a leaf into a tube around one egg. When the packet is finished she separates it from the tree, and it falls to the forest floor. The rolled leaf is food for the newly hatched larva in its first days.
The infographic follows that order: the adult female, the single egg inside the rolled leaf, and the larva feeding in the packet.

2026-10-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Gallstones are hard, pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder. Most are silent and cause no symptoms, but a stone that obstructs a bile duct can cause severe pain and, in some cases, complications.
glance: In the gallbladder, below the liver in the upper right abdomen
Cholesterol stones, typically yellow-green; pigment stones, dark and made of bilirubin
Can be severe and constant, upper right or middle abdomen, lasting several hours
Gallbladder removal for symptomatic gallstones, often laparoscopic

sections.heading: The gallbladder and the path of bile
body: The gallbladder is pear-shaped and lies below the liver in the upper right abdomen. It stores bile, which the liver produces. Bile passes through the hepatic, cystic and common bile ducts into the duodenum, and the pancreas also delivers digestive juices to the duodenum. Eating signals the gallbladder to release stored bile into the duodenum to mix with food.

sections.heading: How stones form
body: Gallstones are hard, pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder. Cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green. Pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin. Stones may form when bile has too much cholesterol or bilirubin or not enough bile salts, or when the gallbladder empties incompletely or too infrequently. The reasons for these changes in bile are not fully understood.
Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity and rapid weight loss, and in women. Risk factors do not establish a diagnosis in an individual.

sections.heading: Silent stones and blocked ducts
body: Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms, and gallbladder stones without symptoms usually need no treatment. A stone that obstructs a bile duct can cause bile to build up and bring on biliary colic. Attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends.

The pain can be severe and constant, in the upper right or middle abdomen. It can last several hours and come with nausea or vomiting. Attacks often follow heavy meals. A blockage that persists can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection or gallstone pancreatitis. These are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.

sections.heading: Evaluation, treatment and risk reduction
body: Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests. Similar symptoms may have other causes that require clinical assessment. The main treatment for gallstones that cause symptoms is removal of the gallbladder, often laparoscopic, and ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances. After the gallbladder is removed, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum instead of being stored.

Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce the risk of gallstones. They do not guarantee prevention, and they do not dissolve existing stones.

sections.heading: When urgent care is needed
body: The guidance is to seek urgent medical care for sudden severe abdominal pain, pain lasting several hours, fever or chills, jaundice, or pain spreading to the back with vomiting. Dark urine and pale stools may accompany complications.

2026-10-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Iron deficiency can impair the production of healthy red blood cells, and in the anemia that results, low hemoglobin reduces the oxygen carried from the lungs to other organs. Treatment depends on the cause and the severity.
glance: Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen carriage from the lungs to other organs
Small red blood cells with pale centers can appear
Heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding
There may be none when the anemia is mild or moderate
Complete blood count, ferritin and other iron studies
Clinician-guided oral iron, paired with treating the underlying cause

sections.heading: Iron, hemoglobin and oxygen
body: Iron deficiency can impair the production of healthy red blood cells. In anemia, low hemoglobin reduces the carriage of oxygen from the lungs to other organs. On a blood smear, iron-deficiency anemia can show small red blood cells with pale centers. A low mean cellular volume is a common laboratory finding.

sections.heading: Blood loss, intake and absorption
body: Blood loss removes iron. Heavy menstrual bleeding and gastrointestinal bleeding are causes that require evaluation. A low intake of iron-containing foods can contribute, and celiac disease and stomach or intestinal surgery can impair the absorption of iron.

sections.heading: Symptoms and testing
body: Mild or moderate iron-deficiency anemia may have no symptoms. More serious disease can cause fatigue, dizziness, pale skin, cold hands and feet, shortness of breath or chest pain.

Evaluation includes a medical and diet history, a complete blood count with hemoglobin and cell size, ferritin, and other iron studies. Further testing depends on the suspected cause. Low ferritin indicates reduced iron stores. Iron deficiency can occur without anemia, so hemoglobin alone does not establish the status of iron stores.

sections.heading: Treatment and its limits
body: Treatment depends on cause and severity. Clinician-guided oral iron is common, and intravenous iron may be used for poor absorption, intolerance, severe deficiency or chronic blood loss. Oral iron may cause an upset stomach or constipation, and significant symptoms are a matter to discuss with the treating clinician.

Iron replacement must be paired with finding and treating the underlying cause. Transfusion is reserved for selected severe cases and does not completely correct iron deficiency. Untreated iron-deficiency anemia may lead to heart problems, pregnancy complications or developmental delays in children.

sections.heading: Food and prevention
body: Beans, tofu, lean red meat, fortified cereals and dark leafy greens provide iron. Foods rich in vitamin C, such as oranges, can support absorption. Treating blood loss or absorption problems may help prevent iron-deficiency anemia. Diet supports iron intake but is not a universal substitute for treatment.

2026-10-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A cataract is a clouding of the eye's natural lens, which is normally clear and bends incoming light to help vision. Most age-related cataracts develop gradually, and only surgery removes a cataract.
glance: Clouding of the natural lens of the eye
Most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates
One or both; cataracts do not spread between eyes
Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night
Only surgery, which replaces the lens with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL)

sections.heading: The lens and how it clouds
body: A cataract is a clouding of the natural lens. The lens is normally clear and bends incoming light to help vision. The cornea, iris and lens are structures at the front of the eye. The retina, the light-sensitive layer of tissue, is at the back.

Age-related changes cause proteins in the lens to break down and clump, which creates cloudy areas. Most age-related cataracts develop gradually, at variable rates. Cataracts can affect one or both eyes, but they do not spread between eyes.

sections.heading: Symptoms and risk factors
body: Cloudy or blurry vision, faded or yellowish colors, glare or halos, difficulty seeing at night, and ghosted or double images in the affected eye can occur. These symptoms can also reflect other eye problems.
Older age, smoking, diabetes, sun exposure, steroid use, family history and previous eye injury are risk factors for cataract. They do not establish a diagnosis in an individual.

sections.heading: The eye examination
body: Evaluation includes visual acuity or refraction, a slit-lamp examination of the structures at the front of the eye, and a dilated examination. Dilation widens the pupil, and the eye is checked, including the retina and optic nerve at the back.

sections.heading: Aids, surgery and protection
body: For mild symptoms, updated glasses, brighter reading light and magnification can help a person function, but they do not remove the cataract. Only surgery removes a cataract. The cloudy natural lens is taken out and replaced by an artificial intraocular lens (IOL).

Surgery is considered when cataracts interfere with everyday activities. Immediate surgery is not always needed, and its benefits and risks are a matter to discuss with an ophthalmologist. UV-protective sunglasses and a brimmed hat, stopping smoking, and protective eyewear can help reduce avoidable risks to the eyes. These measures do not guarantee that cataracts are prevented.

sections.heading: Sudden changes point elsewhere
body: Sudden new floaters, flashes, or a curtain or shadow across vision can signal retinal detachment, not the gradual change of a cataract. The National Eye Institute guidance for these signs is to see an eye doctor or go to an emergency room immediately.

2026-10-01-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Atopic dermatitis, also called atopic eczema, is a chronic inflammatory skin disease that is not contagious. Changes in the skin barrier let moisture escape, inflammation can trigger itch, and scratching causes further damage and inflammation.
glance: A chronic inflammatory skin disease; not contagious
Often in childhood, but possible at any age
Intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin
Elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have it on the face
Treatment can control symptoms; there is currently no cure

sections.heading: A barrier that lets moisture out
body: Skin has a protective outer layer. In atopic dermatitis, changes in this barrier allow moisture to escape and expose the skin's immune system to the environment. Genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause. The infographic's comparison of an intact and a disrupted surface is schematic. It illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin.
Inflammation can trigger itch. Scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation, and it increases the risk of bacterial infection.

sections.heading: How it looks and feels
body: Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin. Scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid. Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement, and itch can disturb sleep.

The appearance of eczema varies with skin tone. It can appear red, purple, gray, or lighter or darker than the surrounding skin, and inflammation may leave changes in color. Common sites include the bends of the elbows and knees and the hands, and babies often have eczema on the face. The distribution varies by age, and eczema can occur elsewhere.

sections.heading: Family history, triggers and diagnosis
body: Atopic dermatitis often starts in childhood but is possible at any age. A family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with an increased likelihood, which is not proof of one cause. Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms, and triggers vary by person.
Diagnosis involves a clinical examination of the skin and a medical, family and trigger history. Clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes.

sections.heading: Daily care and treatment
body: Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps the skin retain water and supports the skin barrier. Gentle cleansing with unscented or non-soap products and lukewarm water can help. The care guidance is to avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce damage from scratching, and not to change diet unless a clinician advises it.

Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation. Clinicians may consider other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines depending on severity, age and response. These are not universal treatments. Treatment can control symptoms, but there is currently no cure. The guidance is to seek care for symptoms, or for treatments that are not helping.

sections.heading: Infection signs and a fire warning
body: Painful, warm, swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking or crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum. These warrant urgent medical advice.
Emollients that transfer onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make the fabrics catch fire more easily. The NHS guidance is to avoid smoking and naked flames.

2026-10-03-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Arachnophobia is a fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia. The fear can be intense and out of proportion to the actual danger, and some people cannot look at a picture of a spider.
glance: Palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness, nausea
Not always clear; frightening experiences and learned fear can be involved
CBT; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias

sections.heading: How the fear shows itself
body: Arachnophobia is fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia. Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to the actual danger. Seeing the feared object can cause immediate anxiety. Anticipating it, or even thinking about it, can also cause anxiety.

Some people with arachnophobia avoid touching a spider. Some cannot look at a picture of a spider. Physical symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea, and experiences vary.

sections.heading: Avoidance in daily life
body: People may actively avoid feared objects and organize their lives around avoidance, which limits daily activities. A repeated encounter can provoke anxiety again. Avoidance and intense anxiety are common features of a phobia. They are not proof of actual danger.

sections.heading: Why a phobia develops
body: It is not always clear why a phobia develops. Frightening experiences can be involved, and so can learned fear.

sections.heading: Treatment and support
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an effective treatment. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that is particularly effective for phobias. Exposure treatment can involve gradually becoming exposed to the feared object. Plans differ, and a specialist can help.

Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms. Images of the trigger may be distressing. The sources point to a primary care provider or a qualified mental health professional when symptoms interfere with life.

2026-10-03-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Dentophobia is intense dental fear. Anxiety can occur before a visit, and severe, persistent fear can lead a person to avoid dental care. Ordinary nervousness does not by itself establish a phobia.
