glance: Sight of instruments, drilling sounds and vibrations, clinical smells, the reclined chair
Feared pain, difficult previous experiences, unfamiliar procedures, perceived lack of control
Noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension, sweaty palms
CBT and professionally guided exposure-based approaches

sections.heading: Nervousness, fear and phobia
body: Dental anxiety can occur before a visit. Severe, persistent dental fear can lead to avoidance. Ordinary nervousness does not by itself establish a phobia.

Dental fear can be associated with feared pain, previous difficult experiences, unfamiliar procedures or a perceived lack of control. Uncertainty about what will happen can also contribute to anxiety.

sections.heading: Triggers and body responses
body: For some people, anxiety can be triggered by the sight of dental instruments, the sounds and vibrations of drilling, clinical smells and the reclined position of the dental chair.
Possible anxiety responses include a noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension and sweaty palms. Symptoms vary.

sections.heading: The avoidance cycle and pain
body: Avoiding dental care can increase the risk of dental problems and make later visits more difficult, which reinforces the fear. This is a possible cycle, not an inevitable outcome.

Fear can concern perceived danger, but concerns about pain are not to be dismissed. The sources advise patients to discuss pain management, and to tell the dentist if pain occurs even with local anesthetic.

sections.heading: Coping at a visit
body: The American Dental Association's guidance for patients is to tell the dental team about anxiety and previous experiences, to ask what will happen, and to agree on a raised-hand signal to pause. Asking questions about the procedure can help reduce fear of the unknown.
The same guidance lists things that can help manage dental anxiety: headphones for bothersome drilling sounds, a handheld stress ball, slow breathing and relaxing tense muscles.

sections.heading: Professional help
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and professionally guided exposure-based approaches can help with dental phobia. Management is tailored to the person and the clinical situation. The sources point to professional help when phobia symptoms affect life, and a dentist and a mental health professional may work together on care.

2026-10-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Aquaphobia is an intense fear of water or drowning. It is a separate matter from the genuine hazards of water, which are not to be dismissed as anxiety.
glance: Severe worry, noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, trembling, nausea, dizziness
Learning to swim, and daily life
Currents, waves, hidden rocks or vegetation, limited visibility

sections.heading: Fear of water
body: Aquaphobia is an intense fear of water or drowning. A specific phobia involves fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger in a particular situation. Fear of water can come with exposure to water, with thoughts of water, and with reluctance to enter water or to immerse the face or body. Individual experiences vary. Fear of water can interfere with learning to swim, and it can persist into adulthood.

Unfamiliar things a person perceives in the water can accompany anxiety. A small exploratory study described concerns about depth, about locating the surface and about finding solid support. These are illustrative concerns. They are not universal symptoms, and they are not a safety assessment.

sections.heading: Symptoms and avoidance
body: Phobia symptoms can include severe worry, a noticeable heartbeat, chest tightness, trembling, nausea and dizziness. Not everyone has every symptom.

Anticipating or encountering a feared situation can bring intense anxiety and active avoidance, and phobias may interfere with daily life. The infographic shows a sequence of repeated encounters and avoidance. The sequence is an illustration, not a universal account of cause or a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Genuine hazards and precautions
body: Natural water may have currents, waves, hidden rocks or vegetation, and limited visibility. Genuine hazards are not to be dismissed as anxiety.

Drowning prevention guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says swimming lessons can reduce drowning risk, and that swimming with a buddy and choosing lifeguarded sites when possible remain important precautions. Life jackets reduce drowning risk while boating and can help weaker swimmers around natural water and pools. Inflatable or foam toys are not safety devices.

sections.heading: Treatment and support
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is an established treatment for phobias, and exposure therapy is a particularly effective CBT method. Healthcare professionals can help determine next steps. The infographic gives no treatment protocol for entering water. Its scenes are illustrative, not a diagnosis or an instruction to enter water.
The sources point to a healthcare professional if symptoms affect life. Breathing exercises and talking to someone trusted can help manage symptoms. Managing anxiety does not replace water safety.

2026-10-04-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Pyrophobia is an intense fear of fire. Within the framework of specific phobias, the fear is out of proportion to the actual danger, while ordinary fire precautions remain necessary.
glance: Palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness, nausea
CBT; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias
At least 12 inches from anything that burns

sections.heading: Fire as a phobia trigger
body: Specific phobias involve intense fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger. The infographic applies that framework to fear of fire. Anticipating a feared object or situation can cause excessive worry, and encountering it can cause immediate, intense anxiety.

Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea. People may actively avoid feared objects and situations, or endure them with intense anxiety. Avoidance can restrict activities.

sections.heading: Actual fire risk from candles
body: Open flames are dangerous if candles tip over or are too close to combustible objects, and ordinary fire precautions remain necessary.

The U.S. Fire Administration's candle guidance suggests considering battery-operated flameless candles. Lit candles need stable holders, need to be at least 12 inches from anything that burns, and are extinguished when a person leaves the room or before bed. For a power outage, the guidance is to use flashlights, not candles.

sections.heading: Therapy and support
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting. Exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias. Exposure-based CBT helps people engage in activities and situations they have avoided, and relaxation exercises may accompany it.

Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms. The sources point to a primary care provider when symptoms affect life. A provider can refer a person to a qualified mental health professional.

2026-10-06-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: An aurora is light released by oxygen and nitrogen in the upper atmosphere after electrons accelerated in Earth's magnetosphere collide with them. The energy enters the magnetosphere from the solar wind.
glance: The solar wind, which transfers energy into Earth's magnetosphere

sections.heading: Energy from the solar wind
body: The solar wind transfers energy into Earth's magnetosphere, and the pressure of the solar wind stretches a magnetotail away from the Sun. Energy transfer through magnetic reconnection is favored when the magnetic field of the solar wind and the magnetic field of Earth point in opposite directions.

Auroral electrons are accelerated within the magnetosphere. The electrons of a nighttime aurora can come from the magnetotail, rather than arriving directly as solar-wind electrons. The accelerated electrons follow magnetic field lines into the upper atmosphere near the magnetic poles.

sections.heading: How the light and colors arise
body: Collisions transfer energy from the electrons to atoms and molecules in the atmosphere, exciting them. When they relax, they release photons. Excited atomic oxygen produces green and red light. Nitrogen can produce blue and pink-purple light.

Red oxygen light is favored higher up, where the atmosphere is thinner. Green oxygen light and the pink-purple nitrogen lower borders can occur below it. These are tendencies, not rigid altitude boundaries. The excited state of oxygen that produces red light lasts longer than the state that produces green. In the denser air lower down, collisions can quench the red emission before a photon is emitted.

sections.heading: Ovals, arcs and curls
body: Auroral emissions form ovals around the magnetic poles, not a single spot over the geographic pole. Quiet displays can be simple arcs. Greater geomagnetic activity can yield brighter multiple arcs, rays, waves and curls, and can expand the oval toward lower latitudes.

sections.heading: What eyes and cameras see
body: Cameras can detect auroral colors that are too dim for human eyes. A faint aurora may look pale to a person because night vision favors brightness over color.

2026-10-06-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Nicrophorus vespilloides is a burying beetle that turns the carcass of a small vertebrate into an underground nursery. Parents strip, roll and bury it, smear it with fluids that inhibit microbial growth, and can feed their larvae.
glance: Orange markings across dark, shortened wing covers
By both parents or by a single parent

sections.heading: Recognizing the adult
body: Nicrophorus vespilloides is a burying beetle in the genus Nicrophorus and the family Silphidae. The adult specimen in the reference photograph has a black head and pronotum, black clubbed antennae and six jointed legs. Its wing covers are dark and shortened, with orange markings running across them, and the tip of the abdomen is exposed.
The species occurs in woodland populations west of Cambridge, England. The leaf litter and soil in the infographic stand for that kind of woodland. They are not a map of the full range.

sections.heading: Finding and burying a carcass
body: Adults locate the carrion of small vertebrates, and flight is part of how they find it. The carcass serves as both the breeding resource and the food for their offspring. Parents remove the fur or feathers, roll the flesh into a ball and bury the prepared carcass in an underground chamber.
Carrion is a scarce resource, and beetles compete over it. They use their mandibles in contests. Larger individuals often have the advantage, but they are not guaranteed to win.

sections.heading: Keeping microbes in check
body: Parents smear the carcass with exudates that inhibit microbial growth. This is known as social immunity. It does not sterilize the carcass completely.

Lysozymes, which are antimicrobial enzymes, are implicated in social immunity. In females, the antimicrobial properties of the anal exudate correlate with the expression of one particular lysozyme gene. The infographic does not illustrate a specific molecular reaction.

sections.heading: Feeding and raising the larvae
body: After hatching, the larvae feed on the prepared carcass and can also receive regurgitated meat from their parents. The mouth-to-mouth contact in the infographic is feeding, not an attack. Care by both parents and care by a single parent both occur in this species, so the pair shown is one possible family arrangement, not an obligation.

Larvae disperse from the carrion to pupate and later emerge as adults. The life-history strip is schematic and not to scale, and it gives no fixed timing or brood size. In this way the beetles turn vertebrate carrion into food for growing offspring. The infographic makes no broader, quantified statement about recycling.

2026-10-06-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A tsunami moves through the whole depth of the ocean. In deep water it has a long wavelength and often a small height. As it enters shallow coastal water it slows, its wavelength shortens and it can grow much taller.
glance: Long wavelength and often small surface height
Depends on water depth: faster in deeper water, slower in shallower water
Shorter wavelength, larger amplitude and stronger currents
The increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water
Maximum height reached inland above normal sea level

sections.heading: A wave through the whole water column
body: A tsunami propagates through the entire depth of the water. Wind waves are different: their motion is concentrated near the surface. In the deep ocean a tsunami has a long wavelength and often a small surface height, and it may be barely noticeable.

sections.heading: Speed, depth and wavelength
body: The speed at which a tsunami propagates depends on the depth of the water. Deeper water permits faster propagation, and shallower water slows it. For a long wave, the propagation speed c is approximated by the square root of g times h, where g is gravitational acceleration and h is the water depth.
As a tsunami enters shallower water, its wavelength decreases. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength. Slowing down does not in itself change the frequency, so the wavelength becomes shorter.

sections.heading: Shoaling near the coast
body: Shoaling is the increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water. Tsunami waves can grow much taller near the coast, and currents intensify as a tsunami approaches shallow coastal water.

Even after shoaling, the wavelength of a tsunami remains relatively long, and water can continue flowing inland for many minutes. Run-up is the maximum height reached inland above normal sea level. It is distinct from inundation, the horizontal extent of the flooding.

2026-10-06-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The giant salmonfly is a stonefly of western North American rivers. Its large nymph spends multiple years on the river bottom, with gill tufts under its thorax, shredding leaves before it climbs out of the water and molts into a winged adult.
glance: Western North American rivers, including the Coast, Cascade, Rocky and Sierra Nevada ranges
River bottom among cobbles, in swift, well-oxygenated water
Leaves and other large organic material
Orange or red band behind the head and under the abdomen

sections.heading: Gills under the thorax
body: The nymph's tracheal gill tufts sit on the underside of its thoracic segments. The filaments of these tufts are part of the respiratory system that takes up and delivers oxygen. Nymphs live on the river bottom among cobbles, in swift, well-oxygenated water.
Warming and low oxygen can interact to affect the nymph's physiology. The responses vary with the population and the conditions, and no universal threshold is given.

sections.heading: A shredder on the river bottom
body: Nymphs are shredders. They feed on leaves and other large organic material collected among rocks or debris, and this feeding processes organic material. Salmonflies are in turn food for aquatic and terrestrial consumers, including trout and insect-eating birds.
The species occurs in western North American rivers, including those of the Coast, Cascade, Rocky and Sierra Nevada mountain ranges.

sections.heading: From the water to the air
body: The aquatic nymph is a large-bodied insect, and the adult is winged and lives on land. The infographic shows both enlarged, not life-size. Nymphs spend multiple years in the water and grow through repeated molts. The length of this stage varies, so no single duration is given.

Mature nymphs crawl to shore and climb out of the water before the final molt into adults. Adults have an orange or red band behind the head, an orange or red underside to the abdomen, and broad wings with dark veins. Females lay their eggs on or above the water. The eggs separate and sink to the bottom, where the next generation begins.

2026-10-06-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Coccolithophores are single-celled marine algae that form microscopic calcite plates inside the cell and push them out to make an overlapping outer covering. Carbonate from their plates contributes to seafloor sediment.
glance: Inside the cell, in the coccolith vesicle
The coccosphere, made of overlapping coccoliths
Dense clouds of coccoliths can make water look opaque turquoise

sections.heading: Algae with a covering of plates
body: Coccolithophores are single-celled algae that live as plankton in the upper ocean. Their photosynthesis produces organic carbon, and their calcification produces inorganic carbon. The plates they make, called coccoliths, are microscopic plates of calcium carbonate in the form of calcite, CaCO3.

sections.heading: How a plate is built
body: Coccoliths are formed inside the cell, generally one at a time, in a compartment called the coccolith vesicle. Formation begins with a ring, the protococcolith ring, at the edge of an organic base-plate scale. Completed coccoliths are pushed out of the cell and form an overlapping external covering called a coccosphere.

Coccoliths of the Noelaerhabdaceae have multiple calcite crystal segments distributed radially around a central grid, and they have proximal and distal shields. Coccolith size and mass vary among species and even within a single coccosphere. The study behind these details used three-dimensional X-ray imaging to separate the plates and measure their geometry.

sections.heading: Plates in the water and on the seafloor
body: Additional coccoliths enter the surrounding seawater when cells multiply, die or produce excess plates. Dense clouds of coccoliths can give the water of a bloom an opaque turquoise appearance.
Coccolith carbonate contributes to seafloor sediment. This does not mean that every plate reaches the bottom, and it does not imply a net benefit for the climate.
The cells and plates are microscopic. The infographic shows them strongly enlarged and not to a common scale.

2026-10-06-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Chrysis ignita is a cuckoo wasp 5 to 10 mm long, with a shiny blue, green and golden red body. Cuckoo wasps have tough, heavily sculptured exoskeletons, and most of the Chrysidinae can curl into a defensive ball.
glance: Western Europe to central Asia and China
Uncertain; Ancistrocerus parietum is only a probable host

sections.heading: Colors and surface sculpture
body: Chrysis ignita has a body length of 5 to 10 mm, so every close-up view in the infographic is enlarged. The head and the mesosoma, the middle section of the body, are shiny blue or violet, with green reflections on the pronotum and mesoscutellum. The tergites, the upper plates of the abdomen, are golden red. The sternites, the lower plates, are green or blue.

The pits on the mesoscutum are the same color as the surface between them. Tergites T2 and T3 have coarse, regular pitting and sharply produced teeth at the tip. The ridge across the front of the head, the frontal carina, is shallowly M-shaped or arched. It does not take the form of four tooth-like bumps.

Chrysis ignita has close lookalikes, which complicate identification. The infographic shows the frontal ridge, the sculptured body and the wings as anatomical views, not as proof that the species can be identified from color alone.

sections.heading: Where it is found
body: The species occurs from western Europe to central Asia and China. Distribution records can be confused by identifications that have not been revised. Its habitats include gardens, parks and forest margins. Adults occur on old wooden or stone walls, dead tree trunks, poles and log piles.

sections.heading: Armor and the defensive curl
body: Cuckoo wasps have an abdomen that is hollowed on the underside. Most Chrysidinae can curl into a defensive ball, a behavior called conglobulation. Females that are disturbed or attacked fold into a compact ball, which shields vulnerable body parts. The curl is described at the level of the family, not for this species alone.
The exoskeletons of cuckoo wasps are heavily sculptured and very tough, and they serve as armor against the stings of hosts. This is protection, not invulnerability.

sections.heading: Uncertain hosts and family-level development
body: At the level of the family, the stages of a cuckoo wasp include egg, larva, cocoon or pupa, and adult. Many cuckoo wasps develop in the nests of solitary wasps or bees, as parasitoids or as consumers of the food the host stored. Exact feeding habits differ among species.

For Chrysis ignita itself, the hosts are uncertain. Ancistrocerus parietum is only a probable host. Numerous earlier host records are unreliable because the taxonomy was inconsistent, and the close lookalikes complicate older host records.

2026-10-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Retinal detachment separates the light-sensitive retina from its normal position at the back wall of the eye and from the blood supply beneath it. It is a medical emergency that risks permanent vision loss.
glance: The retina, the light-sensitive tissue lining the back of the eye
Sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, a dark curtain or shadow
Dilated eye exam; OCT or ultrasound when more information is needed
Laser or freezing, scleral buckle, vitrectomy, pneumatic retinopexy

sections.heading: What the retina does
body: The retina is light-sensitive tissue that lines the back of the eye. It converts the light entering the eye into electrical signals, which are sent to the brain through the optic nerve. A detachment separates the retina from its normal position at the back wall and from the underlying blood supply. That impairs its function and risks permanent vision loss.

sections.heading: How a retina detaches
body: The most common type is tear-related, or rhegmatogenous. Fluid passes through a hole or tear in the retina and collects beneath it, lifting it away. Aging-related separation of the vitreous gel from the retina can cause a retinal tear. Thinning of the peripheral retina and trauma can also lead to tears.

A tractional detachment occurs when scar tissue pulls the retina away. Diabetes or other conditions can cause it. An exudative detachment occurs when leaking vessels allow fluid to accumulate beneath the retina. Inflammation or abnormal vessels can be involved.

sections.heading: Warning signs and risk factors
body: Warning signs include a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, and a dark curtain or shadow in the field of vision. Some small detachments cause no symptoms. Retinal detachment is a medical emergency. Symptoms require an eye doctor or an emergency room right away, and prompt treatment can help protect vision.

Risk factors include extreme nearsightedness, advancing age, previous eye surgery, serious eye injury, a previous detachment and family history. Risk factors do not mean that a detachment is inevitable.

sections.heading: Diagnosis and repair
body: Diagnosis uses a dilated eye exam to inspect the retina, including its periphery. OCT or ultrasound may help when more information is needed. Laser or freezing treatment can seal retinal tears, and a larger detachment may require surgery to put the retina back into place.

A scleral buckle is a silicone band outside the wall of the eye that pushes the wall closer to a retinal tear, while freezing treatment seals the tear. Vitrectomy removes the vitreous gel and drains fluid from beneath the retina. Laser or freezing seals the tears, and a gas bubble can hold the retina while it heals. Pneumatic retinopexy uses a gas bubble and a specific head posture to position the bubble over a tear, with laser or freezing to seal it.

A retina specialist selects the treatment based on the detachment. More than one procedure may be needed, and reattachment does not guarantee complete visual recovery. The macula is the center of the retina, and involvement of this central area affects the outlook for vision.

sections.heading: Limits of prevention
body: Many aging-related detachments cannot be prevented. Protective eyewear during risky activities reduces the risk of injury, and regular dilated eye exams can find small tears or detachments early.

2026-10-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the lower leg, thigh or pelvis. A clot may restrict the return of blood to the heart, and a clot that detaches can travel to the lungs.
glance: A blood clot in a deep vein
Lower leg, thigh or pelvis; it can also occur in the arm
Swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, redness or discoloration
A detached clot travels through the heart and blocks blood flow in the lungs
Prevent a clot from growing or spreading and prevent new clots

sections.heading: A clot in a deep vein
body: DVT is a blood clot in a deep vein, usually in the lower leg, thigh or pelvis. It can also occur in the arm. Veins return blood from the limbs and organs to the heart, and a clot in a vein may restrict that return and cause pain and swelling.
Platelets and plasma proteins cooperate in forming clots. Dangerous clots may form inside vessels without an obvious injury, or may fail to dissolve naturally.

sections.heading: What raises the risk
body: Slow blood flow from limited movement, and injury to veins, can increase the risk of DVT. Surgery and major injury are associated with a higher risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE), and increased estrogen and family history can raise it as well. Risk factors do not establish a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Symptoms and diagnosis
body: Symptoms of DVT can include swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, and redness or discoloration in the affected leg or arm. DVT can also occur without symptoms. Possible symptoms require prompt medical evaluation, and special medical tests are needed to diagnose DVT or pulmonary embolism (PE).

sections.heading: When a clot reaches the lungs
body: A clot that detaches from a vein can travel through the heart to the lungs and block pulmonary blood flow. This is a pulmonary embolism. Difficulty breathing, chest pain that worsens with breathing or coughing, coughing blood, or fainting can be signs of PE and require immediate medical help. PE can occur without symptoms of DVT.

sections.heading: Treatment, risk reduction and later effects
body: Anticoagulants prevent a clot from growing or spreading and prevent new clots. Clot-dissolving medicines or clot removal are used in selected situations, not for everyone. Movement after confinement and leg exercises during long sitting can help reduce risk. Preventive medicines or compression stockings are individualized and are a matter to discuss with a clinician.
Damage to vein valves after DVT can cause post-thrombotic syndrome, with persistent swelling, pain, skin discoloration or, in severe cases, ulcers.

2026-10-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Shingles, or herpes zoster, is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox. The reactivated virus travels in a specific nerve and commonly produces a band of rash on one side of the trunk.
glance: Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, which also causes chickenpox
A band on one side of the trunk; the face can also be affected
Pain that persists in the affected area after the rash has gone
CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for certain adults

sections.heading: A virus that stays in nerve cells
body: Shingles is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus (VZV), the same virus that causes chickenpox. After recovery from chickenpox, the virus remains inactive in some nerve cells and may reactivate later. Why reactivation occurs in some people is not fully understood. The reactivated virus travels in a specific nerve, commonly producing a band of rash on one side of the trunk. The face can also be affected. Risk increases with older age and with weakened immunity, including from certain diseases and immune-suppressing medicines.

sections.heading: How the rash develops
body: Burning or tingling pain, itching or numbness may come before a red rash. Fluid-filled blisters then dry and crust, and the scabs later clear. The timing varies. Shingles may be painful or itchy, and in some people a light touch can provoke intense pain.

Postherpetic neuralgia is pain that persists in the affected area after the rash has gone. Older people have a greater chance of developing it. Blisters on the face require prompt medical attention. Blisters near or in the eye can cause lasting eye damage and blindness.

sections.heading: Treatment and comfort
body: The guidance when shingles is suspected is to contact a clinician as soon as possible. Early antiviral treatment can shorten the illness and reduce its severity, and pain relief may help. Cool washcloths, loose clothing, keeping the area clean and avoiding scratching can help with comfort and skin care.

sections.heading: How the virus spreads
body: A person cannot catch shingles from another person with shingles. VZV can spread from shingles blisters to susceptible people and cause chickenpox. Spread can occur by direct contact with blister fluid or by breathing virus particles from the blisters. The virus is not spread before blisters appear or after the rash scabs over.

The CDC guidance is to cover the rash, avoid touching or scratching it, and wash hands. It also says to avoid contact with susceptible pregnant people, premature or low-birth-weight infants and immunocompromised people until the rash scabs over.

sections.heading: Vaccination
body: CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults age 50 and older, and for adults age 19 and older with immune systems weakened by disease or therapy. The aim is to prevent shingles and related complications.

2026-10-08-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve at the back of the eye. Reducing eye pressure aims to limit further nerve damage, and vision that has been lost cannot be restored by glaucoma treatment.
glance: A group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve
Develops gradually; painless, often with no obvious early symptoms
The iris can block the drainage angle; sudden complete blockage is an emergency
Peripheral vision loss and blind spots
Older age, a family history of glaucoma and high eye pressure
Cannot be restored by glaucoma treatment

sections.heading: Fluid, pressure and the optic nerve
body: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve at the back of the eye. The optic nerve contains many nerve fibers, and loss of these fibers causes blind spots. Aqueous fluid in the front of the eye normally leaves through the drainage angle. Impaired drainage can increase eye pressure.

High eye pressure increases risk, but some people with high pressure do not develop glaucoma, and some have glaucoma at normal pressure. Older age, a family history of glaucoma and high eye pressure are risk factors, not guarantees of disease.

sections.heading: Open-angle and angle-closure glaucoma
body: Open-angle glaucoma develops gradually when the eye does not drain fluid well even though the angle is open. It is painless and often has no obvious early symptoms. Later glaucoma can cause loss of peripheral vision and blind spots. The field loss pictured in the infographic is illustrative and variable, not a diagnostic simulation.

In angle-closure glaucoma, the iris can block the drainage angle. A sudden complete blockage can raise eye pressure rapidly and is an emergency. Sudden intense eye pain, a red eye, blurred vision or nausea can signal angle closure, and halos, headache and vomiting can occur. The guidance for these signs is to seek urgent eye care or emergency care immediately.

sections.heading: How glaucoma is found
body: Diagnosis needs a comprehensive eye examination. Pressure alone is insufficient. The examination includes assessment of the optic nerve, visual field testing and inspection of the drainage angle, and corneal thickness may be measured.

sections.heading: Lowering eye pressure
body: Prescription drops lower pressure by reducing the production of aqueous fluid or improving its outflow. The choice of treatment depends on the person and the type of disease. Laser trabeculoplasty improves drainage in open-angle glaucoma, and laser iridotomy makes a small opening in the iris for angle-closure glaucoma. Glaucoma surgery can create a new drainage route or use a drainage tube. Reducing pressure aims to limit further nerve damage, not to restore lost vision.
The care guidance is to follow the prescribed treatment, report side effects, attend regular follow-up, and not stop glaucoma medicines without discussing it with the ophthalmologist.

2026-10-10-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Insects can be the focus of a specific animal phobia. The fear is intense and out of proportion to the actual danger, which makes it more than ordinary dislike.
glance: Palpitations, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, dizziness, severe worry
CBT; exposure therapy is particularly effective for phobias

sections.heading: More than ordinary dislike
body: Insects can be the focus of a specific animal phobia. Phobic fear is intense and out of proportion to the actual danger. It is more than ordinary dislike.

Anticipating or thinking about the feared object can provoke intense anxiety, and encountering it can also trigger anxiety. The infographic uses a moth of ordinary size on the far side of glass as a fictional example. The scene is illustrative, not diagnostic.

sections.heading: Symptoms and avoidance
body: Symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, nausea, trembling, dizziness and severe worry. Symptoms vary. People with phobias may actively avoid feared objects and situations, or endure them with intense anxiety. Avoiding the feared object can limit daily activities and lead people to organize their lives around avoiding their fear.

sections.heading: Treatment and support
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) teaches different ways of thinking, behaving and reacting to reduce fear and anxiety. Exposure therapy is a CBT method that is particularly effective for phobias. Treatment for a simple phobia can involve gradually becoming exposed to the feared object. Treatment is individualized, and a qualified mental health professional can help plan next steps.
Breathing exercises, talking with a trusted person and support groups can help manage symptoms. The NHS sources point to professional help when phobia symptoms interfere with everyday life.

2026-10-10-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Ornithophobia is a phobia of birds, an animal-type specific phobia. The fear is intense and out of proportion to the actual danger, and the avoidance and distress can interfere with life.
glance: Fast heartbeat, sweating, trembling, tense muscles, dizziness, chest tightness, nausea
Not always identifiable; a frightening event or learned responses may contribute
CBT, and graded exposure in small, manageable steps

sections.heading: Fear of birds
body: Ornithophobia means phobia of birds. It is an animal-type specific phobia. Specific phobias involve intense fear that is out of proportion to the actual danger, and the avoidance and distress can interfere with life.

Encountering, anticipating or thinking about a feared object can produce anxiety. Pictures can also trigger fear in some people. The bird pictures and the courtyard encounter in the infographic are illustrative examples, not universal triggers.
A frightening event or learned responses may contribute to phobias, but a clear cause is not always identifiable.

sections.heading: Predictions and the body's alarm
body: People may overestimate the danger and underestimate their ability to cope. Uncertainty about a feared encounter may fuel anxious predictions.

Possible physical symptoms include a fast heartbeat, sweating, trembling, tense muscles, dizziness, chest tightness and nausea. Symptoms vary between people. Physical alarm prepares the body for possible danger, the fight-or-flight response. Alarm does not by itself prove that the feared situation is dangerous.

sections.heading: How avoidance maintains the fear
body: Avoidance can reduce anxiety quickly. It also prevents opportunities to revise feared predictions, and it can maintain the phobia. Repeated avoidance can restrict everyday activities. In the infographic, skipping the courtyard is a fictional example of that effect.

sections.heading: Therapy and support
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) examines unhelpful thoughts and habits. Graded exposure uses small, manageable steps, and therapist-assisted exposure can treat specific phobias. The steps are chosen for the individual. They are not a universal exposure prescription.

Talking to someone trusted and practicing relaxing breathing may help. The sources point to professional help if fear affects daily life. The scenes in the infographic are fictional educational illustrations, not a diagnosis and not instructions to approach or handle birds.

2026-10-10-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Ailurophobia is a fear of cats, an animal-focused specific phobia. The fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger, and its symptoms can interfere with daily life.
glance: Encountering or thinking about a cat; examples, not universal triggers
Pounding heart, shaking, sweating, tight muscles, dizziness, nausea; not the same for everyone
CBT and gradual exposure under controlled circumstances, at an individual pace

sections.heading: What ailurophobia means
body: Ailurophobia means fear of cats. It is an animal-focused specific phobia. Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger, and the symptoms can interfere with daily life.

Feeling afraid is not itself a measure of actual danger. The infographic illustrates the fear with a fictional encounter with a cat on a stair landing. That scene is made up, and it does not prove that any animal is safe.

sections.heading: Triggers, thoughts and body alarm
body: Encountering a feared animal, or thinking about one, can trigger anxiety. Meeting a cat and anticipating a meeting are the examples illustrated. They are not triggers that every person has.
Phobic thinking can overestimate harm, or how likely it is that the feared object will be encountered, and can underestimate a person's ability to cope. The next event may be imagined as threatening.
Body alarm may include a pounding heart, shaking, sweating, tight muscles, dizziness and nausea. Not everyone experiences the same symptoms.

sections.heading: How avoidance keeps the fear going
body: Avoidance can quickly reduce anxiety. It can also prevent a person from learning that a situation can be manageable, and that maintains the phobic fear. Avoidance can change the routes a person takes and interfere with social activities and everyday life.

sections.heading: Support and treatment
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and gradual exposure, under controlled circumstances and at an individual pace, can help specific phobias. Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person can help manage anxiety. Professional support is relevant when fear affects daily life.
The treatment scene on the infographic is conceptual. It is not an instruction to approach, touch, restrain or provoke an animal, and care planning is individualized.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Appendicitis is an infected, swollen appendix, a small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen. Symptoms and the location of pain vary, and suspected appendicitis requires immediate medical assessment.
glance: A small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen

Surgical removal of the appendix (appendectomy), with antibiotics

sections.heading: The appendix and possible causes
body: The appendix is a small pouch attached to the bowel in the lower right abdomen. Appendicitis means an infected, swollen appendix. Possible causes are blockage by hardened stool or enlarged tissue in the wall of the appendix. In many cases the cause is unclear.

sections.heading: How the pain changes
body: Abdominal pain may start around the belly button and move to the lower right. It may worsen over hours and worsen with movement or coughing. Loss of appetite, nausea or vomiting, and fever may occur. Not everyone has the typical symptoms or the typical location of pain.

sections.heading: Urgent assessment and diagnosis
body: Suspected appendicitis requires immediate medical assessment. Severe abdominal pain, confusion or difficulty breathing require emergency care. Untreated appendicitis can lead to a burst appendix, peritonitis, an abscess or sepsis. These are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.
Diagnosis uses clinical assessment and may include blood and urine tests, ultrasound or CT. No single test always identifies appendicitis, and other conditions can cause similar pain.

sections.heading: Surgery and antibiotics
body: The usual treatment is surgical removal of the appendix, called an appendectomy, with antibiotics. Selected mild cases may be treated with antibiotics alone under medical supervision, but surgery remains standard care.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease in which immune activity destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. With little or no insulin, blood glucose rises, and insulin treatment is essential.
glance: Insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas
Frequent urination, thirst, fatigue, unexplained weight loss and blurred vision

sections.heading: The missing insulin signal
body: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease. Immune activity destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas, which causes little or no insulin. Insulin helps glucose enter the body's cells for energy, and insufficient insulin causes blood glucose to rise. The tissue and glucose symbols in the infographic are schematic and not to scale. Type 1 diabetes can develop at any age, and a family history raises the risk.

sections.heading: Symptoms and diagnosis
body: Common symptoms include frequent urination, thirst, fatigue, unexplained weight loss and blurred vision. Suspected type 1 diabetes needs urgent medical assessment. Diagnosis uses blood glucose tests, and autoantibody tests help establish the type.

sections.heading: Insulin and monitoring
body: Insulin treatment is essential. Insulin pens or pumps and regular glucose monitoring support individualized care with a diabetes team. Healthy eating and activity support management, but they do not replace insulin. Too much insulin can cause low blood glucose, so treatment and monitoring require an individualized care plan.

sections.heading: Diabetic ketoacidosis
body: Without enough insulin, the breakdown of fat produces ketones. These can accumulate and cause diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency. Vomiting or abdominal pain, fast deep breathing, fruity breath, sleepiness or confusion may signal DKA. The guidance for these signs is to seek emergency care immediately, especially when they come with thirst and frequent urination.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs in which the alveoli, the air sacs, can fill with fluid or pus. Bacteria and viruses commonly cause it, and treatment depends on the cause and the severity.
glance: An infection of one or both lungs
Alveoli can fill with fluid or pus
Commonly bacteria and viruses; fungi can also cause it
Cough, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain and tiredness
Young children, older adults, people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease

sections.heading: Infection in the air sacs
body: Pneumonia is an infection of one or both lungs. The alveoli are air sacs that can fill with fluid or pus. Bacteria and viruses commonly cause pneumonia, and fungi can also cause it. Young children, older adults, and people with weakened immunity or chronic lung disease have a higher risk.

sections.heading: Symptoms and assessment
body: Symptoms may include cough, fever, chills, shortness of breath, chest pain and tiredness, and they vary. Clinical assessment may include a chest examination, a chest X-ray and blood tests. Symptoms alone do not establish the diagnosis.

sections.heading: Treatment depends on the cause
body: Bacterial pneumonia is usually treated with antibiotics. Treatment depends on the cause and the severity, so antibiotics are not a universal treatment. Rest and fluids support recovery, and severe illness may require hospital care and oxygen.

sections.heading: Warning signs and risk reduction
body: Severe trouble breathing, blue or pale lips or skin, sudden confusion, or coughing blood require emergency care. Worsening symptoms need prompt medical assessment.
Recommended vaccines can prevent some of the infections that cause pneumonia. Handwashing and not smoking help reduce the risk.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Gout is inflammatory arthritis in which urate can accumulate and form needle-shaped crystals in joints, commonly the big toe joint, triggering painful inflammation. A flare brings sudden severe pain, warmth and swelling.
glance: The big toe joint, though it can affect other joints

Blood urate testing and sometimes joint-fluid crystal testing

sections.heading: Where urate comes from
body: Gout is inflammatory arthritis. Urate can accumulate and form needle-shaped crystals in joints, which triggers painful inflammation. Urate comes from the breakdown of purines in body tissues and in foods, and it normally leaves the body in urine. Too much production or too little removal can raise the level of urate in the blood. Not everyone with high urate develops gout.
Genes, kidney disease, alcohol and some medicines can increase the risk of gout. Gout is not simply a consequence of food choices.

sections.heading: What a flare is like
body: Gout commonly affects the big toe joint, but it can affect other joints. A flare causes sudden severe pain, warmth and swelling. There is sometimes redness, which may be harder to see on darker skin.

sections.heading: Evaluation and treatment
body: First-time symptoms need medical evaluation. Blood urate testing, and sometimes testing of joint fluid for crystals, help evaluate gout. Clinicians treat flares with anti-inflammatory medicines such as NSAIDs or steroids, selected for individual safety. Rest, elevation and a wrapped cold pack can help.

Urate-lowering medicine may be needed for recurrent attacks or high uric acid. The NHS guidance is that it is taken regularly, even when there are no symptoms. Healthy habits support prevention but do not replace needed medicines.

sections.heading: When joint infection is possible
body: A suddenly painful, swollen joint with worsening pain, fever or chills, or feeling sick needs urgent assessment, because joint infection is possible.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Diverticulitis means that diverticula, pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall, have become inflamed. Most people with diverticula do not develop symptoms or problems.
glance: Pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall

sections.heading: Pouches in the colon wall
body: Diverticula are pouches that push outward through weak spots in the colon wall, most often in the sigmoid colon. Diverticulosis means the pouches are present. Most people with diverticula do not develop symptoms or problems. Diverticulitis means the diverticula become inflamed. It is not an inevitable progression of diverticulosis.

sections.heading: Symptoms and assessment
body: Symptoms can include severe, constant abdominal pain, often in the lower left abdomen, and fever. The location is not universal. Assessment may include blood tests and CT imaging to clarify the diagnosis and to distinguish other causes of the symptoms.

sections.heading: Care that depends on severity
body: Treatment depends on severity and on patient factors. Uncomplicated diverticulitis may be managed at home under a clinician's guidance. Treatment may include pain relief selected by a clinician and temporary dietary changes. Antibiotics are not needed for every person.

Severe disease or complications may need hospital treatment, and abscess drainage or surgery can be necessary in selected cases. A perforation of the colon wall or an abscess is a possible complication, not the normal appearance of every case.

sections.heading: Warning signs
body: Worsening persistent pain, fever, or vomiting that prevents keeping fluids down warrants prompt medical assessment. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, a swollen abdomen or an inability to pass stool or gas warrants emergency care.

sections.heading: After an episode
body: After the acute episode, fiber intake as advised by a clinician, physical activity and not smoking may lower future risk. Prevention is not guaranteed. The infographic provides general education, not a diagnosis or an individualized treatment plan.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or the duodenum. Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID medicines are the most common causes, and treatment targets the cause.

sections.heading: Where ulcers form and why
body: A peptic ulcer is a sore in the lining of the stomach or the duodenum. The two locations are alternatives, and an ulcer is not necessarily present in both at once. Helicobacter pylori infection and NSAID medicines are the most common causes. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can make the stomach lining more prone to damage and ulcers. That is a risk, not a universal outcome.

sections.heading: Symptoms
body: Symptoms can include burning or discomfort in the upper abdomen, feeling full early, nausea and bloating. Some people have no symptoms. Food can relieve pain briefly in some people and worsen it in others, so meal timing cannot diagnose an ulcer.

sections.heading: Testing and treatment
body: Evaluation may use breath or stool tests for H. pylori and sometimes upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Treatment targets the cause. It includes antibiotics for H. pylori infection and acid-reducing medicines such as proton pump inhibitors. A clinician may review or change NSAID medicines, and the infographic does not direct anyone to change prescribed medicines independently. Follow-up tests may be needed to confirm that treatment has worked.

sections.heading: The place of diet
body: Diet is not considered an important primary cause of peptic ulcers or an important primary treatment for them. Foods may worsen symptoms for some people, and they do not replace treating H. pylori or medication causes.

sections.heading: Complications and warning signs
body: Ulcers may cause bleeding or perforation. These are possible complications, not present in every ulcer. Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stool, sudden severe persistent abdominal pain or fainting needs urgent or emergency assessment. The infographic provides general education, not a diagnosis or an individualized treatment plan.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A cat's organs work as connected systems. The heart and lungs move blood and exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, the digestive tract handles food, the urinary system removes wastes, and padded paws carry curved, retractile claws.
glance: Two kidneys, ureters, a bladder and a urethra

sections.heading: Organs of the abdomen
body: The liver lies directly behind the diaphragm, on the side toward the tail. The stomach lies behind the liver, and loops of intestine occupy the abdomen.

sections.heading: Heart, lungs and the path of blood
body: The heart pumps blood, and the lungs exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide. Blood returning from the body enters the right side of the heart and travels to the lungs. It then returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it out to the body.

sections.heading: Digestion and the urinary system
body: The digestive tract breaks down food, absorbs nutrients and moves the remaining waste toward elimination. The urinary system includes two kidneys, ureters, a bladder and a urethra. It removes wastes and regulates water and electrolytes.

sections.heading: Paws and claws
body: Cats have curved, retractile claws, which means the claws can be drawn back. The claws provide grip. The paws are padded, and the pads cushion contact.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A cat senses its surroundings with eyes that work in dim light, mobile outer ears that hear higher frequencies than humans do, a nose that reports on food, places and other animals, and whiskers that register touch at the follicle.
glance: Rod photoreceptors and the reflective tapetum contribute; this is not vision in total darkness
Higher sound frequencies than humans hear
Mobile pinnae help collect and locate sound
Receptors associated with the follicle, not nerves inside the hair shaft
Semicircular canals of the inner ear
Backward-facing keratin papillae; not taste buds

sections.heading: Eyes and dim light
body: The cornea and lens direct incoming light to the retina, and the optic nerve carries visual information. The pupil changes size in response to light.
Rod photoreceptors in the retina and the reflective tapetum contribute to vision in dim light. That does not mean a cat can see in total darkness.

sections.heading: Ears, hearing and balance
body: The pinnae, the outer ear flaps, are mobile and help collect and locate sound. The ear canal, the eardrum and the cochlea each have a distinct role in hearing. Cats hear higher sound frequencies than humans.
The semicircular canals are balance structures in the inner ear. They are separate from the cochlea, which is used in hearing.

sections.heading: Smell and whiskers
body: Smell gives a cat information about food, places and other animals. When a whisker is mechanically displaced, the movement stimulates sensory receptors associated with the whisker's follicle. The sensing is not done by nerves inside the hair shaft.

sections.heading: Spines on the tongue
body: The tongue carries backward-facing papillae made of keratin. These visible spines contribute to grooming. They are not taste buds.

2026-10-15-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Cats signal with their ears, eyes, whiskers, posture and tail. The signals are read together and in context, because no single signal stands for one fixed emotion.
glance: Read signals together and in context
Often an upright tail with a softly curved tip and a relaxed body
Soft narrowed eyes and slow blinking can accompany it
Can show as a crouched tense body, ears sideways or back, and a closely held tail
Not automatically an invitation to rub it
Change with lighting and can change with arousal

sections.heading: Why signals are read together
body: A cat's body signals are interpreted together and in context. They are not a fixed code in which one signal equals one emotion.
Pupils are an example. Pupil size changes with lighting and can also change with arousal, so one pupil size does not identify one emotion.

sections.heading: Signs of comfort and interest
body: An upright tail with a softly curved tip, together with a relaxed body, often accompanies a friendly greeting. Soft, narrowed eyes and slow blinking can accompany comfort, and experiments link slow-blink interactions with positive communication between cats and humans.

Ears directed forward and whiskers pointed toward an object can accompany interest or attention. That is not necessarily happiness. A relaxed cat with its belly exposed is not automatically inviting a belly rub.

sections.heading: Signs of unease and when to pause
body: A crouched, tense body, ears turned sideways or back and a tail held close can form a cluster of unease signals.
During contact, body tension, ears turning back and a lashing tail can indicate that the interaction should pause.

2026-10-16-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A domestic cat's claw is pushed out when the deep digital flexor pulls on the last bone of the toe, and elastic ligaments draw it back when it is not in use. Superficial horn caps can shed from the claw, which keeps the tip sharp.
glance: Normal domestic cat forepaw, digits 2 to 5
Distal interphalangeal joint, between the middle and distal phalanges
Contraction of the deep digital flexor
Elastic ligaments, passively; the lateral one is the most important

sections.heading: The bones and the sheath
body: The infographic shows the mechanism in a normal forepaw of a domestic cat, in digits 2 to 5. In each of these toes the middle phalanx and the distal phalanx, the last bone of the toe, form the distal interphalangeal joint.
The cornified claw sheath surrounds living tissues that are supported by the distal phalanx. The horny sheath is not the same thing as the bone.

sections.heading: Pushing the claw out
body: Protrusion is active. The deep digital flexor attaches to the flexor process of the distal phalanx, and when it contracts it protrudes the claw. The digital extensors stabilize the joints nearer the body.

sections.heading: Drawing the claw back
body: Retraction is passive. Elastic ligaments retract the claw, and the lateral elastic ligament is the most important of them. The distal phalanx does not telescope straight into the toe. It comes to overlap the middle phalanx.
Retraction protects the claw from wear when it is not in use. The retracted claw is sheltered in a protective fold of skin.

sections.heading: Shedding the horn caps
body: Superficial caps of horn can shed without injury to the living tissues underneath. This keeps the tips sharp. A shed cap is not the entire claw, and it is not the toe bone.

2026-10-16-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A cat's whisker senses by physical contact. When the shaft bends against an object, the mechanical deformation reaches the follicle at the base of the whisker, where sensory receptors are activated.
glance: At the whisker base, within the follicle

Slowly adapting, to maintained displacement; rapidly adapting, to movement
By physical contact, not remote sensing

sections.heading: From contact to nerve signal
body: Whiskers give a cat tactile contact with its surroundings. In the infographic, a whisker touches an object before the muzzle reaches it. This is sensing through physical contact, not remote sensing without physical input.

Contact bends the whisker shaft, and the mechanical deformation reaches the follicle, where it activates sensory receptors. In the cat, movement of the maxillary whiskers evokes impulses in sensory fibers of the infraorbital nerve.

sections.heading: Where the receptors are
body: The sensory receptors are at the base of the whisker, within the follicle. They are not distributed along the exposed shaft.

sections.heading: Slow and rapid responses
body: The sensory fibers serving cat whiskers include slowly adapting responses, which are to a displacement that is maintained, and rapidly adapting responses, which are to whisker movement. The traces in the diagram are qualitative. They carry no measured scales.

sections.heading: Limits of the diagram
body: The cutaway of the follicle is a simplified schematic and is not to scale. The Northwestern University whisker simulation used data from rats, so it does not demonstrate that a particular S-shaped bend inside the follicle occurs in cats.

2026-10-16-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A cat's tail is read together with its ears, its posture and the situation it is in. A single tail pose is not a guaranteed emotion or a diagnosis.
glance: Read the tail with ear positions, posture and interaction context
Can be a friendly greeting, particularly between cats and humans
With a low crouch and flattened ears, can indicate fear
With ears moving backward during petting, can precede aggression
Can accompany defensive or aggressive displays
Ears predicted cat-cat outcomes better than tails in a shelter study

sections.heading: Reading the tail in context
body: Tails are interpreted together with ear positions, posture and the context of the interaction. A single pose is not a guaranteed emotion or a diagnosis.

In an observational study of cats at a shelter, ear positions were more predictive than tails of how an interaction between cats turned out. The study's exact frequencies should not be generalized, and the finding does not make tails meaningless.

sections.heading: Tail up and tail tucked
body: A cat that approaches with its tail up can be giving a friendly greeting, particularly in interactions between cats and humans. The friendly version shown in the infographic has smooth fur, upright ears and an easy walking posture. A raised tail is not a universal invitation to touch.
A tucked tail combined with a low crouch and flattened ears can indicate fear. These cues occur as a cluster, and they are not a certainty.

sections.heading: Lashing and raised fur
body: During petting, a lashing tail with ears moving backward can come before aggression. Cornell's veterinary guidance is to stop petting and allow a pause with no contact. Tail movement can also occur in play, so context matters.
Raised tail fur with an arched back and ears flattened back can accompany defensive or aggressive displays. A puffed tail does not stand for one unique emotion.

2026-10-16-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Kneading is a paw-pressing behavior related to nursing that can persist into adult life. What it means in an adult cat is a matter of interpretation, not certainty.
glance: Kneading the mother's belly helps stimulate milk flow
Can be a sign of affection, but not a guaranteed reading

sections.heading: What is established
body: Kneading is a paw-pressing behavior related to nursing. Nursing kittens knead their mother's belly, which helps stimulate milk flow. The behavior can persist into adult life.
The infographic shows it as alternating presses of the forepaws on a soft blanket. This is kneading, not walking or scratching. Some cats knead while purring.

sections.heading: What remains interpretation
body: Kneading can be a sign of affection, but it is not a guaranteed reading of a cat's thoughts. The cat's broader engagement and the context matter. No one can get inside a cat's mind, so an adult cat's motive for kneading is an interpretation and not a certainty.
Purring does not settle the question. It occurs in contented cats and in stressed cats, so purring alone does not prove happiness.

2026-10-16-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Cats need taurine in their diet because they have only a very limited ability to make it themselves. Taurine deficiency can cause central retinal degeneration and dilated cardiomyopathy.
glance: Cats have a very limited ability to synthesize taurine from cysteine

Usually unnecessary with a complete balanced diet

sections.heading: Why cats cannot make enough
body: Cats have a very limited ability to synthesize taurine from cysteine, so taurine in the diet is essential. Low activities of cysteine dioxygenase and cysteinesulfinic acid decarboxylase limit how much taurine a cat makes.
The infographic simplifies this to a limited internal supply. It does not mean cats make no taurine at all.

sections.heading: What deficiency can do
body: Taurine deficiency can cause central retinal degeneration, in the eye, and dilated cardiomyopathy, in the heart muscle. The infographic uses the eye and the heart to illustrate why adequate dietary taurine matters. It does not diagnose disease or describe treatment.

sections.heading: Taurine and the whole diet
body: Animal-source foodstuffs supply taurine. A meat ingredient alone does not establish that a diet is complete. Cats are obligate carnivores, and they require a balance of multiple nutrients, not taurine alone.

Cornell's feeding guidance is to choose cat food with a nutritional adequacy statement that indicates complete and balanced nutrition for the appropriate life stage. Ingredients and nutrient balance are distinct things. Supplements are usually unnecessary with a complete, balanced diet and should not be given without veterinary approval.

2026-10-16-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: In Siamese-type colorpoint cats, the cooler extremities have darker fur and the warmer body has lighter fur. The pattern is associated with variants in TYR, and pigment production in these cats is temperature-sensitive.

Cooler extremities: face, ears, paws and tail
