sections.heading: Where it sits
body: The nictitating membrane is the cat's third eyelid. It is a whitish-pink membrane that lies beneath the other eyelids, at the inner corner of the eye near the nose.
The cornea is the clear dome at the front of the eye. The iris is the colored area that surrounds the pupil.

sections.heading: How it protects the eye
body: The third eyelid extends across the eye to help protect the eyeball from scratches. The infographic shows this extension as a schematic. It does not show a timed, voluntary wink.

sections.heading: Tears and blinking
body: Glands within the third eyelid contribute to the watery portion of tears. The upper and lower eyelids blink and spread tears over the surface of the eye. This keeps the surface moist and clears small particles.

sections.heading: When a veterinarian is needed
body: The infographic shows the normal third eyelid. The Cornell source says to seek veterinary care for a cat with apparent eye discomfort and discharge.

2026-11-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Entomophobia is a fear of insects. Seeing insects or thinking about them can provoke extreme fear or anxiety that is out of proportion to the likely real-life harm.
glance: Encounters indoors or outdoors, images, and fears of bites or stings
Palpitations, trembling, chest tightness and dizziness

sections.heading: Fear out of proportion to harm
body: Entomophobia means fear of insects. Seeing insects, or thinking about them, can provoke extreme fear or anxiety. It is a specific phobia.
The fear is out of proportion to the likely real-life harm. It is not proof that an encounter with an insect is dangerous.

sections.heading: Triggers, symptoms and avoidance
body: Triggers can be encounters indoors or outdoors, images, and fears of bites or stings. Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, trembling, chest tightness and dizziness. Avoidance may restrict outdoor exercise, events or leaving home.

sections.heading: What CBT involves
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a recommended treatment for phobias. A therapist helps a person examine thoughts, feelings and actions, and change avoidance, in an individualized plan. The NHS guidance is to seek professional help when symptoms affect daily life.

2026-11-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Microphobia is an extreme fear of small things. Even thoughts of little things can provoke severe anxiety, although most small everyday things cause no harm.
glance: Palpitations, trembling, dizziness and severe anxiety

sections.heading: Fear of small things
body: Microphobia means an extreme fear of small things. It is described as a specific phobia, not a separately named diagnostic category.

sections.heading: Fear and actual danger
body: Thoughts of little things can provoke severe anxiety. The fear can be out of proportion to the actual danger, and most small everyday things cause no harm. The infographic depicts this felt threat with an imagined small-object trigger.

sections.heading: Symptoms and avoidance
body: Phobia symptoms can include palpitations, trembling, dizziness and severe anxiety. Phobias can also involve avoidance that interferes with everyday life.

sections.heading: Talking therapies
body: Talking therapies, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), can help manage phobia symptoms. The sources point to consulting a healthcare provider when fear affects daily life.

2026-11-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Anthophobia is an extreme fear of flowers. Any flower, specific types, or parts such as petals, leaves or stems may trigger it, even though the fear concerns something unlikely to cause harm.
glance: Any flower or specific types; petals, leaves or stems; thinking about flowers
Palpitations, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath
Gradual exposure therapy guided by a mental health professional, often combined with CBT

sections.heading: What can trigger it
body: Anthophobia means an extreme fear of flowers. Any flower may trigger the fear, or only specific types. Parts, including petals, leaves or stems, may trigger it too.
It is described as a specific phobic disorder. The word is a descriptive name for a fear, and it is not a claim of a separate diagnostic category.

sections.heading: Body alarm and actual danger
body: Thinking about flowers can trigger anxiety. Possible bodily symptoms include palpitations, sweating, trembling and shortness of breath. Phobic fear concerns something unlikely to cause harm, and an intense feeling of alarm is not itself proof of actual danger.

sections.heading: Avoidance and professional treatment
body: Avoiding flowers can restrict work and social life and make leaving home difficult. The sources point to professional help when phobia symptoms affect daily life.
A mental health professional can guide gradual exposure therapy. It is often combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) to change perceptions and responses.

2026-11-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Haphephobia is an intense, overwhelming fear of being touched. Touch from friends or family can also cause distress, and the condition differs from allodynia, which is physical pain from touch.
glance: Intense, overwhelming fear of being touched
Severe anxiety, palpitations, trembling and dizziness

sections.heading: Fear of touch, not pain from touch
body: Haphephobia means an intense, overwhelming fear of being touched. Touch from friends or family can also cause distress.
Haphephobia is an anxiety disorder. It is not the same as allodynia, which is physical pain that comes from touch.

sections.heading: Symptoms and daily life
body: Phobia symptoms may include severe anxiety, palpitations, trembling and dizziness. Anxiety may disrupt everyday activities, and it may cause a person to avoid encounters or to avoid leaving home. These points come from general guidance on phobias and on anxiety disorders.

sections.heading: Treatment
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. Professional help is appropriate when symptoms affect a person's life.

2026-11-21-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Pogonophobia is an extreme fear of beards. Real or artificial beards, pictures of them and other facial hair can trigger severe anxiety or panic, though the fear does not establish actual danger from a beard or its wearer.
glance: Real or artificial beards, photos, videos, mustaches and other facial hair
Palpitations, trembling, dizziness and chest tightness
Unpredictable encounters can interfere with work and public or social life

sections.heading: The name and its triggers
body: Pogonophobia means an extreme fear of beards. Real or artificial beards, photos, videos, mustaches and other facial hair can trigger severe anxiety or panic. Specific phobic disorders are anxiety disorders.

sections.heading: Felt threat and body alarm
body: A beard can feel threatening to the person with the phobia. The fear does not establish actual danger from the beard or from the person wearing it.
Phobias can cause palpitations, trembling, dizziness and chest tightness. Unpredictable encounters can interfere with work and with public or social life.

sections.heading: Treatment
body: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a treatment for phobias. The NHS guidance is to seek professional help when symptoms affect a person's life.

2026-11-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Horseshoe crab blood is blue because it carries oxygen with copper-containing hemocyanin. Its clotting responds to bacterial endotoxins, and LAL is used to test medical products for them.
glance: LAL is used to test medical products for bacterial endotoxins

sections.heading: Why the blood is blue
body: Horseshoe crabs are marine arthropods. They have an exoskeleton and jointed appendages. Their blood is blue. The color comes from hemocyanin, which contains copper and carries oxygen in the blood.

sections.heading: Blood that responds to bacteria
body: The clotting of horseshoe crab blood responds to bacterial endotoxins. LAL is used to test medical products for endotoxins.

NOAA Ocean Today and the Smithsonian National Zoo both report that scientists are exploring synthetic alternatives to LAL. The infographic covers both the copper-based transport of oxygen and the detection of endotoxin in horseshoe crab blood.

2026-11-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The oak leafrolling weevil is a small, shiny black weevil with one red spot on each wing cover. The adult cuts an oak leaf, lays an egg on it and rolls it into a neat cylinder, called a nidus, where the larva feeds.
glance: Shiny black, with one red spot on each wing cover
Called a nidus, Latin for nest
Leafrolling weevils: 16 species of oak and 2 species of chestnut
Eastern US oak woodlands, including Massachusetts, Connecticut and North Carolina

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: The oak leafrolling weevil, Synolabus bipustulatus (synonym Attelabus bipustulatus), is a small, stout, shiny black weevil with one red spot on each wing cover. Adults are less than 1/4 inch long. A similar oak leaf-rolling weevil, Homoeolabus analis, is orange-red with a black head and legs.

sections.heading: Rolling the leaf
body: The adult chews slits on either side of the leaf's midrib and lays an egg near the tip of the leaf. The leaf is folded along the midrib and rolled into a neat cylinder, with the egg near the center of the roll. The egg is tiny and shaped like a rugby ball. The finished leaf roll is called a nidus, which is Latin for nest.

The larva is a legless, curved, plump grub with a brown head. It feeds on the leaf tissue inside the roll, out of reach of predators. It pupates inside the roll, and a new adult emerges. There may be more than one generation a year.
The thief weevil, Pterocolus ovatus, preys on eggs and is a kleptoparasite of the nidus. Its attelabid hosts include this species, listed under the synonym A. bipustulatus.

sections.heading: Host trees and range
body: Leafrolling weevils have been recorded on 16 species of oak and 2 species of chestnut. They are rarely pests and typically do not cause noticeable damage to their host trees.

The oak leafrolling weevil is recorded in oak woodlands of the eastern US, including Massachusetts, Connecticut and North Carolina. Its distribution is slightly more northerly than that of Homoeolabus analis, and it is not found in Florida.

sections.heading: The generalized insect body plan
body: The internal view in the infographic is a simplified schematic of a generalized insect, not a dissection of this species. The gut has a foregut, midgut and hindgut, and most digestion and absorption occur in the midgut. Malpighian tubules, which handle excretion, join the gut where the midgut meets the hindgut.

The dorsal vessel, or heart, pumps blood through an open body cavity. Air enters through spiracles and travels through branching tracheae. The nervous system has a brain in the head, which processes sensory information, and a ventral nerve cord of ganglia. The fat body stores energy.

2026-11-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: Along the California coast, winds blowing along the shore can drive surface water offshore. Cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below to replace it, a process called coastal upwelling.
glance: Cold coastal water contributes to San Francisco summer fog

sections.heading: How the water rises
body: Coastal upwelling is driven by wind. Winds blowing along the shore can drive surface water offshore. Deeper water then rises to replace the surface water that has been displaced. The rising water is cold and rich in nutrients. In this way upwelling brings cold, nutrient-rich water to the California coast.

sections.heading: Productivity and fisheries
body: California coastal upwelling supports marine productivity, and it supports fisheries as well. The infographic presents these as ecological consequences of the wind-driven process.

sections.heading: Cold water and summer fog
body: Upwelling brings cold water to the California coast. That cold coastal water contributes to the summer fog of San Francisco.

2026-11-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The wheel bug is a gray to brown assassin bug with a toothed, cog-like crest on the adult's thorax. It seizes insects with its front legs, injects digestive enzymes through a piercing beak and sucks up the liquefied tissue.
glance: Across North America, including the United States, Mexico and Guatemala

sections.heading: The crest and the body
body: The wheel bug, Arilus cristatus, is an assassin bug. The adult has a toothed crest on its thorax that resembles a cog, and a gray to brown body. Adults measure about 1 to 1.25 inches.
Wheel bugs occur across North America, including the United States, Mexico and Guatemala. They live among vegetation, including trees and shrubs.

sections.heading: How it feeds
body: Wheel bugs prey on insects, including caterpillars. The enlarged front legs seize the prey. The piercing beak injects digestive enzymes, and the bug then sucks up the liquefied tissue.

sections.heading: Eggs and nymphs
body: Egg clusters are laid on twigs in fall. They overwinter and hatch in spring. The nymphs are red and black, and they lack the crest of the adult.

sections.heading: The generalized internal view
body: The internal anatomy in the infographic is simplified and generalized for insects. Spiracles lead to branching tracheae. The gut includes a foregut, midgut and hindgut. A dorsal vessel moves hemolymph, and a ventral nerve cord links the ganglia.

2026-11-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: A lichen is a stable partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner: green algae, cyanobacteria or both. The fungus gives the lichen most of its characteristics, and the partner supplies sugars made by photosynthesis.
glance: A fungus and a photobiont (green algae and/or cyanobacteria)

sections.heading: A fungus and its partner
body: A lichen is a stable symbiotic partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, called the photobiont. The photobiont is green algae, cyanobacteria or both. About 90% of lichens use a green-algal photobiont, and some lichens have both green algae and cyanobacteria. The photobiont photosynthesizes and supplies sugars, a source of carbon, to the fungus. The partnership is thought to be a mutualism.

The fungus is the dominant partner. It gives the lichen most of its characteristics, including the shape of its body (the thallus) and its fruiting bodies. By protecting its photobiont, the fungus lets lichens live in dry, sunny places where algae alone could not, recharging with occasional rain.

sections.heading: Inside the thallus
body: Lichens have no roots, stems, leaves, waxy cuticle or vascular tissue. They absorb water and nutrients from air and rain. They are not mosses: mosses are plants with leaf-like structures, and lichens are not plants.

The thallus is layered. On the outside is a cortex of tightly packed fungal cells. Beneath it is an algal layer, and then a medulla of loosely packed, threadlike fungal filaments. When a lichen is wet, the cortex cells become transparent and the color of the algal layer shows through. Green algae often make a wet lichen bright green.

Rhizines are fungal filaments from the medulla that attach the lichen to its surface. They do not move water or nutrients as roots do. Some foliose lichens attach by one central holdfast. These are the umbilicate lichens, such as rock tripe.

sections.heading: Three main growth forms
body: Lichens have three main growth forms. Crustose lichens are pressed against the surface like a crust. Foliose lichens are leafy, with distinct upper and lower sides. Fruticose lichens are hair-like, shrubby or cup-like.

sections.heading: How lichens reproduce
body: The fungus produces spores from fruiting bodies. A new fungus must then find a compatible photobiont partner. Lichens also reproduce vegetatively. Soredia are granules of algae and fungi intertwined for dispersal. Isidia are vegetative outgrowths. Fragments of a lichen can also grow into new thalli.

sections.heading: Lichens and air quality
body: Lichens absorb pollutants such as heavy metals and sulfur from the air, so scientists use them to monitor air quality. Old man's beard (Usnea longissima) is an indicator of air pollution.

2026-11-24-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The elephant mosquito, Toxorhynchites rutilus septentrionalis, is a predatory mosquito. Its larvae hunt other mosquito larvae in water-filled tree holes and containers, and the adults feed on nectar, not blood.
glance: Can exceed 7 mm in body length

sections.heading: A predator in tree holes
body: Toxorhynchites rutilus septentrionalis is a predatory mosquito found north to Connecticut and southern New York. Its larvae inhabit water-filled tree holes and containers, where they prey on mosquito larvae. They locate prey by its movement. The larva's mouth brushes grasp the prey, and its mandibles are powerful.

sections.heading: The nectar-feeding adult
body: Adults feed on nectar, not blood, using a strongly curved proboscis. They bear iridescent scales and can exceed 7 mm in body length.

sections.heading: Life stages and body plan
body: Egg, larva, pupa and adult are the stages of complete metamorphosis in flies. Insects have a head, thorax and abdomen and three pairs of legs. The generalized insect anatomy in the infographic includes a digestive tube, a heart, spiracles and branching breathing tubes.

2026-11-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The sixline wrasse is a small purplish reef fish with six orange stripes. It is shy, swims within the protection of coral branches and feeds on small crustaceans.
glance: Seaward reefs among coral branches, commonly at 2 to 35 m

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: The body is purplish with six orange stripes running lengthwise. The cheek is orange with fine yellow dots, and the eyes are red with two white horizontal stripes. The base of the tail and the tail fin are green, with a black, blue-edged eyespot on the upper part of the tail base. The fish grows to about 7.5 cm, about 3 inches.

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: The sixline wrasse occurs in tropical marine waters of the Indo-West and Central Pacific. It inhabits seaward reefs among coral branches and dense clear coastal reefs, commonly at 2 to 35 m depth.

sections.heading: Behavior and food
body: The sixline wrasse feeds on small crustaceans. It is a shy fish that swims within the protection of coral branches. Small, loose groups occur.

sections.heading: What this means for an aquarium
body: The aquarium points on the infographic are planning inferences from habitat and diet, not a tested prescription for tank size. They are to provide complex shelter, reflecting the branching-coral habitat, and small meaty foods, reflecting the crustacean diet. Small crustaceans are potential prey, so the fish cannot be called safe with all invertebrates. Compatibility with tankmates needs to be assessed individually.

2026-11-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The Midas blenny is a golden-orange Indo-Pacific reef fish. It swims up from the bottom to feed on zooplankton in open water and shelters in crevices in rock or coral.
glance: Indo-Pacific, from the Gulf of Aqaba and southeast Africa to the Marquesas
Coral reefs with moderate currents, at a reported 2 to 40 m

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: The Midas blenny has an elongated body with golden-orange coloration. Adults have a long tail, and a narrow dark margin runs along the front of the dorsal fin. The maximum reported total length is 13 cm, about 5.1 inches.
A hatchery that documents the species describes a golden-yellow body, a blunt face, large blue eyes, comb-like teeth and an eel-like way of swimming.

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: Its Indo-Pacific range runs from the Gulf of Aqaba and southeast Africa to the Marquesas. It lives on coral reefs with moderate currents, from coastal reefs to outer walls, at a reported depth of 2 to 40 m. It shelters in crevices in rock or coral.

sections.heading: Feeding in open water
body: The Midas blenny feeds on zooplankton while swimming 2 to 3 m above the bottom. It can change color when it moves from the bottom into open water, and it may swim with similarly colored anthias.

sections.heading: Husbandry notes from a hatchery
body: The husbandry notes come from the hatchery Sustainable Aquatics. It reports feeding a prepared hatchery diet, Spirulina brine and mysis. It advises rockwork and a tight-fitting lid, because the fish can jump.

The hatchery describes the fish as reef-safe and generally peaceful, but potentially territorial toward its own kind or fish with similar body shapes. Compatibility is to be assessed individually, not guaranteed. The hatchery recommends at least 30 US gallons, approximately 114 liters, with larger preferable to reduce aggression. That is a husbandry recommendation, not a universal biological threshold.

2026-11-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The flame hawkfish is a small scarlet fish of shallow tropical Pacific reefs. It lives among the branches of live Pocillopora and Stylophora corals, and adults eat small crustaceans.
glance: Pacific, from the Ryukyu Islands to the Line Islands and Mangareva

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: The description rests on an adult photographed by Tanya Dewey. That fish has a scarlet body, a dark marking on the upper back and dorsal area, a black ring around the eye, a short snout and a deep, compact body.
The maximum reported total length is 9 cm, approximately 3.5 inches. That is not a guaranteed size for every adult.

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: The flame hawkfish has a Pacific range from the Ryukyu Islands to the Line Islands and Mangareva, and south to the Great Barrier Reef and the Austral Islands. It is a reef-associated fish of shallow tropical habitat, with a typical depth range of 1 to 10 m.
It lives among the branches of live Pocillopora and Stylophora corals. When approached, it retreats deep into the coral.

sections.heading: What it eats
body: Adults eat small crustaceans. A dietary DNA study from Moorea identified a broad assemblage of prey. That result does not make the fish an obligate eater of coral polyps, and it does not show that all prey living with coral are eaten equally.

sections.heading: What this means for an aquarium
body: The flame hawkfish is a commercially kept species that requires well-oxygenated water. Refuge and oxygenation are recommendations informed by its habitat. Because this fish eats small crustaceans, small ornamental crustaceans should not be assumed safe with it. That precaution is inferred from diet. It is not a quantified aquarium trial or a universal reef-safe label.

Taking refuge in coral in the wild does not by itself prove that the fish is compatible with every reef tank. Livestock and individual behavior need to be assessed, and harmlessness to every tank mate cannot be asserted.

2026-11-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The green chromis is a small, pale blue-green reef fish that feeds on plankton above branching coral and retreats into the branches for shelter.
glance: Tropical Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea
Sheltered reef flats and lagoons, 1 to 20 m deep

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: The green chromis has a pale blue-green, iridescent body that is flattened from side to side, with visible scales, translucent fins and a deeply forked tail. Its small mouth sits at the tip of the snout and can extend forward. A similar fish, C. atripectoralis, has a distinct black patch at the base of its pectoral fin. The green chromis does not.
The largest reported total length is 10 cm, about 4 inches. Other guides give smaller maximums, so that figure is an upper limit, not a typical adult size.

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: This is a fish of the tropical Indo-Pacific, including the Red Sea. It keeps to sheltered reef flats and lagoons, at reported depths of 1 to 20 m. Large groups gather above branching Acropora coral and retreat into the branches for shelter. Juveniles stay closely tied to coral heads.

sections.heading: Feeding and nesting
body: The green chromis feeds by day on plankton. It takes both phytoplankton and zooplankton, including copepods, by pushing its mouth forward.
The male prepares a nest and guards the eggs, which are attached to the bottom. He fans them with his tail fin to keep water moving over them.

sections.heading: In an aquarium
body: The aquarium notes on the infographic come from a trade care sheet for chromis and damselfish, not from studies of wild fish. It advises open swimming space with rockwork for cover. Chromis are generally peaceful with peaceful species but may squabble, so check compatibility instead of expecting a harmonious school.

Feed a quality flake or pellet with suitable frozen foods, and avoid overfeeding. Ammonia and nitrite should be zero, in a mature, filtered system. Corals may change the water conditions a tank needs, and schooling in the wild does not make a fish safe for every reef tank.

2026-11-25-factual-infographic-factual-i.dek: The coral beauty, Centropyge bispinosa, is a small angelfish of outer reef slopes. It grazes algae by day, shelters in reef crevices at night and is only conditionally suited to a reef aquarium.
glance: Adults can reach 10 cm, about 4 inches
Outer reef slopes with crevices, at 5 to 45 m
Mainly grazed algae, with plankton and some worms or small crustaceans
Conditional: some individuals nip corals and clams

sections.heading: How to recognize it
body: The coral beauty is a small angelfish with a laterally compressed body. Its head and its dorsal, anal and caudal fins are blue-purple, and the middle of the body is orange-yellow with blue lines or spots. Adults can reach 10 cm, about 4 inches.
FishBase lists Centropyge bispinosa as the accepted name, with the synonyms Holacanthus bispinosus and Centropyge bispinosus and the misspelling Centropyge hispinosus.

sections.heading: Where it lives
body: The species occurs in the tropical Indo-West and Central Pacific, from East Africa to Japan, Australia and the Tuamotu Islands. It lives on outer reef slopes, uses reef crevices for shelter and is found singly or in small groups. The Australian Museum reports depths of 5 to 45 m.

sections.heading: Food and daily routine
body: Grazing on algae is central to its diet. The fish is omnivorous and also takes plankton and some worms or small crustaceans. It feeds during the day and shelters in reef crevices at night. Its feeding territories can lead to mild aggression.

sections.heading: In an aquarium
body: The aquarium guidance comes from an industry care sheet for dwarf angelfish in general, published by the Ornamental Aquatic Trade Association. It recommends a mature, filtered aquarium with plentiful rockwork for cover. Most dwarf angelfish do not tolerate their own or similar species, so the advice is to keep one unless the system is particularly large, has visual barriers and expert compatibility advice has been taken.

Compatibility with a reef aquarium is conditional. Some individuals nip corals and clams, so the fish cannot be guaranteed reef safe. For food, the care sheet suggests varied vegetable matter such as nori together with appropriate meaty frozen feeds, and many dwarf angelfish accept pellets and flakes. Ammonia and nitrite should be zero, and salinity and water quality should be monitored.
